teile.einleitung: In a mine, people dig mineral resources out of the earth, for example ore, coal or salt. The work is often deep underground. Miners have their own words, customs and even their own greeting.
wichtigste: Mineral resources are extracted in a mine.
Someone who works in a mine is called a miner.
A tunnel called an adit runs horizontally, while a shaft runs vertically.
In the past, canaries warned of poisonous gas.
The German miners' greeting is “Glück auf”.
Iron ore was mined for a long time in the Gonzen near Sargans.

abschnitte.text: A **mine** is a place where **mineral resources** are taken from the earth. These can be ores, from which metals are obtained, or coal and salt. Sometimes the raw materials lie close to the surface. But often you have to dig deep into the ground. Miners call working below the ground working **underground**.

An **adit** is an almost horizontal tunnel into the mountain. You can walk into it or ride in on small trains. A **shaft**, on the other hand, leads **vertically** down into the depths. **Cages** carrying people and material travel up and down it. Because it is pitch dark underground, miners wear a **lamp on their helmet**.

Working in a mine used to be very dangerous. Tunnels could collapse, and water could get in. Especially feared was **poisonous gas** that you cannot smell. That is why miners took **canaries** with them. These react quickly to the gas. If the bird became weak, the miners knew they had to get out at once. Today electronic devices measure the air.

German-speaking miners traditionally greet each other with **“Glück auf”**, which means something like “good luck up there”. The greeting wishes that you come back up to the surface safe and sound. Many miners honour **St Barbara** as their patron saint. Her feast day is **4 December**. In some areas miners hold special celebrations on this day.

There were mines in Switzerland too. In the **Gonzen** near **Sargans** in the canton of St Gallen, **iron ore** was mined for a long time. Today the mine is closed, and you can visit it. In **Bex** in the canton of Vaud, salt has been produced for centuries, and there are guided tours through the tunnels there too.

gewusst: The miners' greeting “Glück auf” is still used today, including in songs.
The canaries in the mine were a kind of living gas detector.

teile.einleitung: A rock glacier looks like a huge heap of stones slowly creeping down a slope. But under the blocks of stone there is a lot of ice. Rock glaciers are only found where the ground is permanently frozen.
wichtigste: A rock glacier consists of rock debris with ice in between.
Active rock glaciers need permafrost.
They creep about 10 centimetres to 1 metre a year.
The share of ice beneath the layer of boulders is often 40 to 70 per cent.
Fossil rock glaciers show that it used to be colder.
Rock glaciers are studied particularly closely in the Engadine.

abschnitte.text: A **rock glacier** is a mixture of **rock debris and ice**. It creeps slowly down the slope like a thick porridge. The surface is made of coarse boulders. Underneath, it often contains **40 to 70 per cent ice**, sometimes even more. Because you cannot see the ice, a rock glacier looks like an ordinary **scree slope** to non-experts.

The ice in a rock glacier only survives if the ground is **permanently frozen**. Such ground is called **permafrost**. In the Swiss Alps, permafrost is found mainly at high altitudes and on shady slopes. That is why rock glaciers are seen as typical signs of permafrost. They often have a steep front and wavy ridges on the surface.

Active rock glaciers typically move **0.1 to 1 metre a year**. That is much slower than most ice glaciers. If the permafrost gets warmer, some rock glaciers can speed up. That is why experts watch them closely. If stones come loose at the front, this can be dangerous for paths and buildings below.

Some rock glaciers today contain **no more ice** and do not move. They are called **fossil**. Today they lie outside the permafrost zone. But their shape shows that there used to be permafrost there and therefore a **colder climate**. In this way they help us to understand the history of the climate.

In the **Engadine**, rock glaciers are studied particularly closely, for example the **Murtèl-Corvatsch** rock glacier. Researchers drilled down to the bottom there and installed measuring instruments. In this way they have been measuring temperature and movement for many years. In 2022 the Engadine rock glaciers were put on a list of 100 important geological heritage sites in the world.

gewusst: From the outside you usually cannot see the ice of a rock glacier at all.
The measurements at Murtèl-Corvatsch are among the longest series of permafrost measurements in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Geothermal energy is the use of heat from inside the Earth. It can be used to heat houses and in some areas also to produce electricity.
wichtigste: On average it gets about 3 °C warmer for every 100 m of depth.
About half of the Earth's heat comes from the decay of radioactive substances.
In 1904 electricity was produced from geothermal heat for the first time in Larderello in Italy.
In Iceland about 90 per cent of buildings are heated with geothermal heat.
Ground probes for houses in Switzerland usually go 100 to 300 m deep.
In 2006 the Deep Heat Mining project in Basel set off earthquakes that could be felt.

abschnitte.text: It is very hot inside the Earth. The deeper you drill, the warmer it gets. On average the temperature rises by about 3 °C per 100 m; this is called the **geothermal gradient**. An example: if it is 10 °C at the surface, the temperature rises by 40 times 3 °C, that is 120 °C, down to a depth of 4000 m. So there it is about **130 °C**.

Altogether about **47 terawatts** of heat flow from inside the Earth to the surface. About half comes from the **decay of radioactive elements** in the rock. The rest is heat left over from the formation of the Earth. But per square metre of the Earth's surface, this is on average only just under 0.1 watt.

In Switzerland many houses are heated with **ground probes**. They usually go 100 to 300 m deep. There the rock is about 10 to 15 °C all year round. This heat is not enough for heating directly. That is why a **heat pump** is needed, which raises the heat to the temperature needed for heating and hot water. Switzerland has a particularly large number of ground probes.

To make electricity you need very hot water or steam. In 1904, in **Larderello** in Tuscany, Prince Piero Ginori Conti used steam from the ground to run a generator that lit a few light bulbs. In 1913 the first geothermal power station started work there. **Iceland** lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and above a hotspot. There about 90 per cent of buildings are heated with geothermal heat.

In **hydrothermal** geothermal energy, hot water that is naturally present is brought up. In **petrothermal** geothermal energy this water is missing. So water is pressed into hot, dry rock to create artificial paths. In **Basel** this was tried in the Deep Heat Mining project. On 8 December 2006 it caused an earthquake of magnitude 3.4. After a risk analysis, the project was finally abandoned in 2009.

gewusst: Heat from inside the Earth is available day and night, whatever the weather and the season.
In Iceland many people bathe in warm water that comes from deep underground.

teile.einleitung: Bowen's reaction series describes the order in which minerals crystallise out of a cooling rock melt. It is named after the Canadian geologist Norman L. Bowen. It helps to explain why such different rocks as basalt and granite can form from similar melts.
wichtigste: Olivine is the first mineral to crystallise from a basalt melt.
The discontinuous series leads via pyroxene, amphibole and biotite.
The continuous branch is formed by the plagioclases.
As it cools, plagioclase changes from calcium-rich to sodium-rich.
At the end, potassium feldspar, muscovite and finally quartz crystallise.
Fractional crystallisation makes the remaining melt richer in SiO₂.
Basalt melts begin to crystallise at about 1200 °C.

abschnitte.text: A **magma** is a rock melt deep inside the Earth. When it cools, not all minerals form at the same time. Each mineral crystallises in a certain **temperature range**. Basaltic melts start to crystallise at about **1200 °C**. Granitic remaining melts, on the other hand, only harden at about 650 to 700 °C. **Norman L. Bowen** studied this sequence at the beginning of the 20th century with laboratory experiments.

In the **discontinuous branch**, different minerals, each with a different crystal structure, follow one another. First **olivine** forms, then **pyroxene**, after that **amphibole** and **biotite**. At each step the **silicate tetrahedra** are more strongly linked to each other. Crystals formed early are no longer stable as the temperature falls. If they stay in contact with the remaining melt, they **react** to form a new mineral. That is where the name reaction series comes from.

Alongside this runs the **continuous branch** of the **plagioclases**. Here the crystal structure stays the same; only the chemical make-up of the **solid solution** changes. At high temperature, calcium-rich **anorthite** crystallises. As the temperature falls, the plagioclase becomes more and more sodium-rich, all the way to **albite**. In between there are seamless transitions.

At the end a **remaining melt** is left that is rich in SiO₂, potassium and water. From it, **potassium feldspar** and **muscovite** crystallise. The last mineral to form is **quartz**, pure silicon dioxide. These minerals are typical of **granite**. That is why there is hardly any quartz in basalt, but a great deal in granite.

When heavy crystals formed early sink to the bottom of the magma chamber, they are separated from the melt. They can then no longer react with it. This process is called **fractional crystallisation**. As a result, the melt changes its make-up step by step and becomes **richer in SiO₂**. In this way a basaltic starting melt can gradually turn into a much lighter-coloured melt.

gewusst: Minerals from the start of the series, such as olivine, usually weather faster at the Earth's surface than quartz from the end of the series.
Bowen published his results in 1928 in the book “The Evolution of the Igneous Rocks”.

teile.einleitung: Firn is old snow that has survived at least one summer. It is the stage before glacier ice and is important for the growing and melting of glaciers.
wichtigste: Firn is denser than snow but less dense than ice.
The word firn comes from an old word meaning “of last year”.
Firn becomes ice when the air pores are closed.
The firn line separates the accumulation zone and the ablation zone of a glacier.
At Konkordiaplatz several streams of firn flow together to form the Great Aletsch Glacier.
Ice cores contain air from earlier times.

abschnitte.text: Fresh snow is loose and contains a lot of air. Over time the snowflakes turn into round grains. If the snow stays lying through a summer, it is called **firn**. The word comes from an old German word meaning “of last year”. Firn is an in-between stage: denser than snow, but still much less dense than ice.

Every year new layers of snow are added. Their weight presses the firn beneath them together more and more. The air channels between the grains get narrower. Once they are closed off into small bubbles, it is called **glacier ice**. Air stays trapped in these bubbles. That is why researchers can study air from times gone by in **ice cores**.

At the end of summer, the **firn line** shows how far down the winter snow stays lying on the glacier. Above it lies the **accumulation zone**, where the glacier grows. Below it lies the **ablation zone**, where more ice melts than is added. If the firn line rises, the glacier loses mass.

At the top of the glacier lie large **firn fields**. At **Konkordiaplatz** several of them meet and flow down the valley as the Great Aletsch Glacier. At the upper edge of a firn field, a deep crack often opens up, the **bergschrund**. There the flowing ice separates from the rock or from the ice frozen to it, which stays where it is.

Bright snow and firn reflect a lot of sunlight. If the layer of firn disappears, the darker ice comes to light. It absorbs more radiation and melts faster. That is why a snowy winter is so important for the glaciers.

gewusst: At Konkordiaplatz the ice of the Aletsch Glacier is about 900 metres thick.
Firn is also called firn snow and is popular with ski tourers in spring.

teile.einleitung: An ice-dammed lake is a lake held back by a glacier, as if by a dam. Such lakes can suddenly drain and cause floods. A well-known example in Switzerland is the Märjelensee on the Great Aletsch Glacier.
wichtigste: An ice-dammed lake forms when glacier ice blocks a valley and water collects behind it.
It can suddenly burst out and cause a flood.
The Märjelensee lies on the eastern edge of the Great Aletsch Glacier.
In the 19th century, a lot of water flowed through the Massa gorge during outbursts.
In 1895 a relief tunnel was built against the outbursts.
A sudden outburst of a glacier lake is called by an Icelandic word, jökulhlaup.

abschnitte.text: A glacier can block a **side valley** like a dam. Behind it, meltwater and rainwater collect into an **ice-dammed lake**. But ice is not a solid wall. The water can find its way through cracks or under the ice. Then the lake often drains in a short time and causes a **flood** further down.

The **Märjelensee** lies in a hollow on the eastern edge of the **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais. In the 19th century the glacier was much thicker, and the lake was up to 1.6 kilometres long. During outbursts the water drained through crevasses in the glacier and caused floods in the **Massa**, which flows from the Aletsch Glacier to the Rhône. In 1895 a **relief tunnel** over 500 metres long was built, which limited how high the lake could rise.

Since the 19th century the Aletsch Glacier has **shrunk** a great deal. Today it is much thinner and holds back less water. So the natural Märjelensee is hardly 100 metres long any more and drains almost every year. Because the glacier retreated, the tunnel was only rarely needed. The lake shows clearly how much the glaciers of the Alps have changed.

abschnitte.titel: Huge lakes of the Ice Age
abschnitte.text: In **Iceland**, dammed glacier lakes often burst out. The Icelandic word **jökulhlaup** means something like “glacier run”. After the last cold period, a huge lake was dammed up at the edge of the North American ice sheet. It was named after the Swiss naturalist **Louis Agassiz** and is called **Lake Agassiz**. It was bigger than any lake on Earth today.

gewusst: Louis Agassiz came from the canton of Fribourg and later became a famous scientist in the USA.
Today glacier lakes in Switzerland are monitored by experts so that people can be warned in time before an outburst.

teile.einleitung: Halite is the mineral that our table salt is made of. Chemically it is sodium chloride. Halite forms beautiful cubes and dissolves easily in water.
wichtigste: Halite is sodium chloride, in other words table salt.
Halite grows in cubes.
It dissolves easily in water.
Rocks formed from evaporated salt water are called evaporites.
A rock made almost entirely of halite is called rock salt.
The Schweizerhalle saltworks is in Pratteln in the canton of Basel-Landschaft.

abschnitte.text: The salt in the kitchen is actually a mineral. It is called **halite** and is made of **sodium and chlorine**, chemically **sodium chloride**. The name comes from the Greek word **“hals”** for salt. The term “halogens” also goes back to it. Halite belongs to the cubic crystal system and often forms beautiful **cubes**. Under a magnifying glass you can see that table salt is made of small cubes too.

Halite is different from most minerals: it **dissolves easily in water**, even cold water. That is why it is found at the surface almost only in dry areas. Pure halite is **colourless**. But natural radiation in the rock can create faults in the crystal lattice. Then it turns **blue or violet**.

When seawater evaporates in a closed basin, salts are left behind one after another. The rocks formed in this way are called **evaporites**, from the Latin word for evaporate. A rock that is made almost entirely of halite is called **rock salt**. Rock salt is lighter than most rocks and can be deformed under pressure. Over millions of years it can therefore slowly push its way upwards and form **salt domes**.

There are salt deposits under Switzerland too. **Swiss Saltworks** gets salt for the whole country from them. One of its sites is the **Schweizerhalle saltworks** in Pratteln in the canton of **Basel-Landschaft**. A hole is drilled down to the salt, the salt is dissolved with water and the brine is pumped up. Then the water is evaporated, and the salt is left behind. It is used as table salt, in industry and as **road salt** on wintry roads.

gewusst: Every grain of table salt is a tiny crystal, often shaped like a cube.
Natural radiation can turn halite blue, although it is actually colourless.

teile.einleitung: The Burgess Shale is a famous fossil site in the Canadian Rocky Mountains. It preserves animals from the Cambrian that lived in the sea about 508 million years ago. What is special is that even their soft body parts have been preserved.
wichtigste: The Burgess Shale is in Yoho National Park in British Columbia, Canada.
Charles Walcott discovered the site in 1909.
The fossils are about 508 million years old and come from the middle Cambrian.
Even soft parts such as muscles, gills and guts were preserved.
Well-known animals are Opabinia, Hallucigenia and Pikaia.
Stephen Jay Gould made the site world famous with “Wonderful Life”.

abschnitte.text: The **Burgess Shale** is in **Yoho National Park** in the Canadian province of British Columbia. It is part of the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was discovered in **1909** by the American palaeontologist **Charles Doolittle Walcott**. At that time Walcott was head of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. In the following years he collected tens of thousands of fossils from the shale.

The fossils are about **508 million years** old. They come from the **middle Cambrian**. At that time many new groups of animals appeared in the sea. The Burgess Shale is a little younger than the early Cambrian fauna of **Chengjiang** in China, which is also very well preserved.

Usually only the hard parts of animals, such as shells or bones, are left as fossils. In the Burgess Shale it is different. **Mudflows** buried the animals quickly and **cut off from the air**. That is why even **muscles, gills and guts**, which usually rot away, were preserved. So researchers know what animals that had no hard parts looked like.

**Opabinia** had **five eyes** and a trunk with a grasping claw. When its reconstruction was first presented, the audience laughed, it seemed so strange. Today it is seen as a relative of the early arthropods. **Hallucigenia** was first reconstructed upside down: people thought the spines were legs and the legs were tentacles on its back. Today it is seen as a relative of the **velvet worms**.

**Pikaia** had a rod along its back, the so-called **notochord**, and muscular body segments. It is seen as an early **chordate** and therefore as a distant relative of the vertebrates. In 1989 the palaeontologist **Stephen Jay Gould** made the Burgess Shale world famous with the book **“Wonderful Life”**. He interpreted the strange animals as a sign of how strongly **chance** shapes evolution. In German the book appeared as “Zufall Mensch”, meaning “Humans by chance”.

gewusst: The name Hallucigenia is a reminder of how dreamlike and strange this animal seemed to the researchers.
Tens of thousands of fossils have been collected from the Burgess Shale.

teile.einleitung: A season is a part of the year with typical weather, light and life in nature. In Switzerland there are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. They happen because the Earth's axis is tilted while the Earth travels around the Sun.
wichtigste: Here there are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter.
Spring comes after winter.
In spring the first flowers, such as snowdrops, bloom.
In summer the days are longest.
In autumn the leaves fall from many trees.
Seasons happen because the Earth's axis is tilted.

abschnitte.text: The Earth travels once around the Sun in a year. As it does so, its **axis** always stays tilted in the same way, by about 23.5 degrees. When our Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun shines more steeply and for longer, and it is summer. When it is tilted away from the Sun, the days are short and cold, and it is winter.

Astronomically, **spring** begins around 20 March, when day and night are the same length. The first flowers, such as **snowdrops**, crocuses and spring snowflakes, bloom. The trees get new leaves, and migrating birds such as swallows come back. Many animals now have their young.

**Summer** begins around 21 June, the longest day of the year. In Switzerland this day lasts around 16 hours. It is warm, grain and fruit ripen, and you can swim in lakes and rivers. Summer also has the most thunderstorms.

**Autumn** begins around 22 or 23 September, when day and night are again the same length. The leaves of many trees turn yellow, orange and red and fall off. It is harvest time for apples, grapes and pumpkins. Many migrating birds fly south, and some animals gather food stores.

**Winter** begins around 21 December, the shortest day of the year. It is cold, and there is snow in the mountains and often in the lowlands too. Animals such as the marmot and the edible dormouse **hibernate**. In Switzerland, winter is the time for skiing, sledging and Fasnacht, the carnival.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line through the North and South Poles around which the Earth turns.
A day in spring and autumn when day and night are the same length.
The day with the longest or shortest daytime of the year.
A long, deep sleep of some animals during the cold months.

gewusst: When it is winter here, it is summer in Australia.
In January the Earth is actually a little closer to the Sun than in July.
In many tropical countries, instead of four seasons there is a rainy season and a dry season.

teile.einleitung: On 18 October 1356 a severe earthquake shook the city of Basel. Afterwards the city burned for days. It is the strongest earthquake recorded in the history of Central Europe.
wichtigste: The main earthquake happened on the afternoon of 18 October 1356.
A fire that lasted for days destroyed many wooden houses.
The epicentre was probably a few kilometres south of Basel near Reinach BL.
The choir of Basel Minster collapsed.
Over a wide area, about 40 castles were damaged or destroyed.
The magnitude is estimated at about 6 to 7, with 6.6 often given.
It is the strongest historically documented earthquake in Central Europe.

abschnitte.text: The Basel earthquake happened on **18 October 1356**, the feast day of St Luke the Evangelist. A **foreshock** had already frightened people before that. So many left the city. The main earthquake followed in the afternoon. That is probably why fewer people died than you might expect. The figures for the number of dead vary greatly, between about 100 and 2000.

At that time many houses in Basel were made of **wood**. The earthquake knocked over hearth fires and lamps. The flames spread quickly. According to the old sources, the **city fire** raged for eight days. It destroyed a large part of the city.

At **Basel Minster**, the **choir** collapsed and the roof fell into the nave. Altars, the organ and pictures were destroyed. There was also great damage over a wide area. About **40 castles** were badly hit. Many were rebuilt later, while others remained ruins. On the corner tower of the former city wall near the **Lohnhof**, earthquake damage can still be seen today.

According to today's research, the source of the earthquake was a few kilometres south of Basel near **Reinach BL**. A deep **fault zone** runs through the Earth's crust there. There were no measuring instruments in the Middle Ages. So experts estimate the strength from the damage that was recorded. The values lie between about 6 and 7 on the **magnitude scale**, with 6.6 often given.

No other recorded earthquake in Central Europe was as strong. That is why the Basel earthquake serves as an important **yardstick** for the earthquake risk in the region. Experts know that a similar earthquake could happen again today. That is why there are rules in Switzerland for **earthquake-proof building**. The Basel region is one of the areas with a higher earthquake risk.

gewusst: The earthquake was so strong that it could still be felt clearly far away.
More than 650 years have passed since the Basel earthquake.

teile.einleitung: Limestone is a pale rock that has often formed from the shells of sea creatures. In Switzerland you come across it in the Jura, in the Alps and even in the kettle.
wichtigste: A lot of limestone has formed from the shells of sea creatures.
The Jura is made largely of limestone.
If you drip vinegar on limestone, it fizzes.
Water dissolves limestone and creates caves with stalactites.
Natural chalk is a soft, white limestone.
The Hölloch in the Muota Valley is one of the longest caves in the world.

abschnitte.text: A very long time ago, countless animals with **shells** made of lime lived in warm seas. When they died, their shells sank to the sea floor. Over millions of years these layers were pressed together and turned into **limestone**. Chemically, limestone is made mainly of **calcium carbonate**. That is why you often find **fossilised shells** and other fossils in it.

The **Jura** in north-western Switzerland is made largely of limestone. Many mountains in the Alps, such as **Pilatus** or the **Säntis**, are also built of limestone. Limestone is usually **light grey to whitish**, sometimes yellowish too. That is why limestone cliffs shine brightly in the sun.

Limestone can be recognised with a simple experiment. If you drip **vinegar** on it, it fizzes and bubbles. Vinegar is an **acid** that dissolves the limestone. This produces the gas carbon dioxide in tiny bubbles. Geologists do this test with diluted hydrochloric acid.

Rainwater can slowly dissolve limestone. Over a long time, large **caves** form in this way. When water containing lime drips from the ceiling, a little lime is left behind. **Stalactites** grow down from the ceiling, and **stalagmites** grow up from the floor. The **Hölloch** in the Muota Valley in the canton of Schwyz is one of the longest caves in the world.

In many areas, tap water contains dissolved lime. When it is boiled, it is left behind as a **white coating** in the kettle. Natural **chalk** is a soft, white limestone made of tiny shells of sea creatures. Limestone is also used as a building stone and for making **cement**. When limestone is heated and squeezed deep inside the Earth, **marble** forms.

gewusst: On high limestone mountains in the Alps you can find fossils of sea creatures, because the rock once lay on the sea floor.
The white cliffs on some coasts are made of chalk, in other words of tiny shells.

teile.einleitung: The föhn is a warm, dry wind that blows down the lee side of a mountain range. In Switzerland it is known especially from the valleys on the north side of the Alps.
wichtigste: With a south föhn, the warm downslope wind blows in valleys north of the Alps such as the Reuss Valley.
With a north föhn, it is warm and dry on the south side of the Alps.
Sinking air warms up by 1 °C per 100 m.
A föhn wall often stands over the main ridge of the Alps.
Lens-shaped föhn clouds are called altocumulus lenticularis.
During föhn the humidity falls sharply and the risk of fire rises.
In North America a similar wind is called the chinook.

abschnitte.text: The side of a mountain range facing the wind is called the **windward** side, and the side facing away is the **lee** side. When air rises on the windward side, it cools down. At a certain height the water vapour condenses into clouds, and it rains or snows. Then the air only cools by about 0.5 °C per 100 m (**moist adiabatic**). On the lee side, the dry air sinks and warms up by 1 °C per 100 m (**dry adiabatic**). That is why it arrives at the bottom warmer than it started.

Air starts in Ticino at 400 m at 15 °C. Up to 1400 m it cools by 10 °C to 5 °C. Then clouds form, and up to 2400 m it cools by only 5 °C, to 0 °C. On the north side it sinks 2000 m down to 400 m. In doing so it warms up by 20 °C to **20 °C**. But a föhn can also be warm without much rain on the windward side: then air sinks from greater heights and warms up especially strongly on the way down.

During a **south föhn**, Ticino is on the windward side, with rain or snow. On the north side of the Alps, the air drops into valleys such as the **Reuss Valley**, the Hasli Valley or the Rhine Valley. During a **north föhn** it is the other way round: the air banks up in the north, and in **Ticino** it brings clear, dry weather. In föhn valleys the air often becomes very dry, and the relative humidity sometimes falls below 30 %. Then the **risk of fire** rises.

abschnitte.titel: Föhn wall, föhn window, föhn clouds
abschnitte.text: Clouds banked up on the windward side spill over the main ridge of the Alps and dissolve on the lee side. Seen from the north, this looks like a wall, the **föhn wall**. Behind it a strip of blue sky appears, the **föhn window**. The föhn also creates standing waves in the air. At their crests, smooth, lens-shaped clouds form, called **altocumulus lenticularis** or föhn fish.

There are föhn-like winds on many mountain ranges around the world. On the eastern side of the Rocky Mountains in North America it is called the **chinook**. It can make the temperature rise by more than 20 °C within hours. Some people feel unwell or have a headache during föhn; this is called **föhn sickness**.

gewusst: In winter the föhn can make snow disappear so quickly that people call it the “snow eater”.
The word föhn comes from the Latin “favonius”, a mild west wind.

teile.einleitung: A high-pressure area, or high for short, is an area with high air pressure. In it, air sinks and the clouds usually dissolve. That is why a high often brings fine, calm weather, but in winter it sometimes brings fog as well.
wichtigste: In a high, the air sinks and flows outwards at the ground.
Sinking air warms up and dries out, which is why the clouds dissolve.
In the Northern Hemisphere, the air flows clockwise around a high.
The Azores High often brings fine weather to Switzerland in summer.
In winter, a high often brings low cloud to the Swiss Plateau.
The technical term for a high is anticyclone.

abschnitte.text: Air has weight and presses down on the Earth. This pressure is called **air pressure**. In a **high-pressure area** it is higher than in the surroundings. At the centre of a high, **air sinks** from high up down to the ground and flows outwards there. As it sinks, the air is squeezed together and **warms up**. Warm air can hold more water vapour. The cloud droplets **evaporate**, and the sky becomes clear.

The air does not flow straight out of the high. Because of the **Earth's rotation**, it is deflected. In the **Northern Hemisphere**, this makes it turn **clockwise** around the high. In the Southern Hemisphere it is the other way round. The technical term for a high is an **anticyclone**. “Anti” means “against”, because the high is the opposite of a cyclone, which is a low.

An important high for the weather in Europe is the **Azores High**. It usually lies over the Atlantic west of Portugal, near the group of islands called the Azores. When it spreads as far as central Europe in summer, it becomes **sunny and warm** in Switzerland too. If a high stays in place for a long time, a heatwave can develop.

In winter, a high often brings grey **low cloud** to the **Swiss Plateau**. In calm weather, cold, damp air collects low down between the Jura and the Alps. Above it lies warmer air. Normally it gets colder higher up, but here it is the other way round. This situation is called an **inversion**. The cold air stays trapped at the ground. While it is grey for days on the Swiss Plateau, the sun shines in the mountains above a **sea of fog**.

When a high lies **north of Switzerland**, for example over northern Europe, cold air flows in from the north-east. Between the Jura and the Alps it is squeezed together as if in a funnel. This creates the **bise**, a cold, dry wind. It often blows especially strongly on **Lake Geneva**. In winter, the cold feels even colder when the bise blows.

gewusst: When there is low cloud, it is often warmer on the Säntis or Pilatus than on the Swiss Plateau.
In the Southern Hemisphere, a high turns exactly the other way round from ours.

teile.einleitung: Isobars are lines on a weather map that join places with the same air pressure. They show highs, lows and how strongly the wind is blowing.
wichtigste: An isobar joins places with the same air pressure.
The name comes from Greek: “isos” means equal, “baros” means weight.
When isobars lie close together, a strong wind blows.
Around a high they form closed rings, and the pressure rises towards the inside.
In a low, the values get smaller towards the centre.
Lines of equal temperature are called isotherms.

abschnitte.text: On many weather maps you can see curved lines with numbers. These are **isobars**. Everywhere along one line the **air pressure** is the same. It is given in **hectopascals** (hPa). At sea level, the average air pressure is about 1,013 hPa. Isobars are usually drawn at fixed intervals, for example every 5 hPa.

The word isobar comes from **Greek**. “Isos” means equal, and “baros” means weight. So an isobar is a line of equal weight of air, in other words of equal pressure. There are other terms built in the same way. **Isotherms** join places with the same temperature, because “therme” stands for heat.

Around a **high**, the isobars form closed rings. The highest pressure is in the middle, so the values rise towards the inside. In a **low** it is the other way round: the pressure is lowest at the centre, and the numbers get smaller towards the inside. This lets you see at a glance where the highs and lows are. Highs often bring calm weather, lows often clouds and rain.

Wind happens because air flows from high to low pressure. When the isobars lie **close together**, the difference in pressure over a short distance is large. Then a **strong wind** blows, sometimes even a gale. When they are far apart, it tends to be calm. High up, the **Earth's rotation** deflects the air so that it flows almost parallel to the isobars. At the ground, friction slows it down, and the wind blows at an angle into the low.

You can also calculate with isobars. If they are drawn 5 hPa apart, there are four gaps between the first and the fifth isobar. Four times 5 hPa gives a pressure difference of **20 hPa**. This is how experts estimate how much the pressure changes over a distance.

gewusst: If you see lots of closely packed isobars over Switzerland in the weather forecast, you can expect a gale.
As well as isobars and isotherms, there are also contour lines (isohypses), which are lines of equal height.

teile.einleitung: The glaciers in the Alps are getting smaller because the climate is getting warmer. Glacier melt is changing the landscape and the water supply of Switzerland.
wichtigste: Glaciers are melting because it is getting warmer.
Most ice melts in summer.
Meltwater flows into streams and rivers such as the Rhône and the Rhine.
Where a glacier disappears, a new lake often forms.
Dark dust makes ice melt faster.
At the Rhône Glacier, parts are covered with white sheets.

abschnitte.text: A glacier grows in winter through **snow** and loses ice in summer through **melting**. In a warmer climate, more ice melts in summer than is added in winter. That is why the glaciers are getting smaller. Most ice melts in **summer**, when it is warm in the mountains too. In hot summers, especially large amounts of meltwater flow away.

Bright snow reflects a lot of sunlight. **Dark surfaces**, on the other hand, absorb more sunlight and get warmer. If ice is covered with dark dust or debris, it therefore melts faster. When the bright snow has gone early in the summer, the darker ice appears and melts even more.

At the **Rhône Glacier** in Valais, parts of the ice are covered with **white sheets** in summer. The sheets reflect the sunlight. Underneath them, the ice melts more slowly. This mainly protects an ice grotto that visitors can look at. But the whole glacier cannot be saved this way.

The meltwater gathers into streams. These flow into rivers such as the **Rhône** or the **Rhine**. Where a glacier has melted away, a hollow is often left behind. Water collects in it, and a new **glacial lake** forms. The **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais is the largest glacier in the Alps. It too gets shorter and thinner every year.

Glaciers are like **water stores**. They release a lot of water, especially in hot, dry summers. Once the glaciers have disappeared, this **meltwater** will be missing in high summer. Some rivers will then carry less water. This affects farming, shipping and electricity production from hydropower.

gewusst: The Great Aletsch Glacier is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.
At many glaciers, signs show where the ice still lay a hundred years ago.

teile.einleitung: Pumice is a very special stone: it is so light that it floats on water. It forms during volcanic eruptions from frothed-up lava. Many people know it from the bathroom.
wichtigste: Pumice floats on water.
It is full of small holes filled with air.
Pumice forms when lava froths up because of gas bubbles.
It is usually light grey, white or beige.
Its surface feels rough.
It is used for foot care, for light building blocks and in the past for jeans.

abschnitte.text: Many **gases** are dissolved in the lava of a volcano. In a violent eruption they are suddenly released, rather like when you open a bottle of fizzy water. The lava **froths up**. It cools so quickly that the bubbles stay trapped. This is how **pumice** forms, a volcanic rock full of small holes.

Because pumice has so many air-filled holes, it is very light. It is even lighter than water and therefore **floats**. After some eruptions under water, huge **rafts of pumice** drift on the sea. They can cover hundreds of square kilometres. Over time the stones soak up water and sink.

Pumice is usually **light-coloured**, often light grey, white or beige. That makes it different from dark lava rocks such as basalt. Because of the many holes, the surface has tiny sharp edges. That is why pumice feels **rough**, almost like sandpaper.

In the bathroom, many people use pumice to gently rub away **hard skin** on their feet. On building sites it is used to make **light building blocks** and mortar. In the past some **jeans** were washed together with pumice stones in large machines. The rough stones rubbed off the colour, and the trousers looked faded. This was called **stonewashed**.

gewusst: Pumice is one of the few stones that float on water.
After eruptions, drifting rafts of pumice can travel long distances across the sea.

teile.einleitung: An emissions scenario describes a possible future: how many greenhouse gases people might give off, and how the climate would then change. It is not a forecast but a “what if” calculation. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change IPCC and Switzerland too use such scenarios.
wichtigste: An emissions scenario describes a possible future based on certain assumptions.
In RCP8.5, the number stands for the radiative forcing in the year 2100 in watts per square metre.
SSP means Shared Socioeconomic Pathways.
SSP1 describes a sustainable, green development, SSP5 strong growth with a lot of fossil energy.
In the middle scenario SSP2-4.5, the Earth warms by about 2.7 °C by the end of the century.
For Switzerland, MeteoSwiss and ETH Zurich published the CH2018 scenarios in 2018.

abschnitte.text: Nobody knows exactly how many greenhouse gases humanity will give off in the future. This depends on decisions made by society, for example in politics, technology and ways of life. **Emissions scenarios** therefore describe different possible paths. They answer the question “what if” and do not give a probability. Climate models then calculate how the climate would change on each path.

In 2000 the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change **IPCC** published the **SRES** family of scenarios, with names such as A1, A2, B1 and B2. Later came the **RCPs**, the Representative Concentration Pathways. The number in the name, for example in **RCP8.5**, gives the **radiative forcing** in the year 2100 in watts per square metre. Radiative forcing tells you how strongly greenhouse gases change the Earth's energy balance.

abschnitte.titel: The SSPs in the sixth report
abschnitte.text: The sixth IPCC report used the **SSPs**, the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. They describe possible developments in society, in population, economy and technology. **SSP1** stands for sustainability, cooperation and education. **SSP5** relies on strong growth, driven mainly by fossil fuels. The SSPs are combined with a level of forcing, for example **SSP1-1.9** or **SSP5-8.5**.

In the middle scenario **SSP2-4.5**, which roughly continues the trends so far, the Earth warms by about **2.7 °C** by 2081 to 2100 compared with 1850 to 1900. The scenario **SSP1-1.9** assumes very rapid cuts in emissions and net zero CO2 around the middle of the century. It has the best chance of keeping warming at about **1.5 °C**. With SSP5-8.5 the warming would be much stronger.

In 2018 **MeteoSwiss** and **ETH Zurich** published the climate scenarios **CH2018**. They show how temperature, rainfall and extreme events in Switzerland could develop depending on the emissions path. Above all, they compare a future with determined **climate protection** with a future without climate protection. Authorities use the scenarios to prepare for heat, drought and heavy rain.

gewusst: The abbreviation SRES stands for the “Special Report on Emissions Scenarios”.
According to CH2018, Switzerland is warming faster than the global average, because land areas warm up faster than oceans.

teile.einleitung: A mountain is a rise in the land that is clearly higher than its surroundings. In Switzerland you can see mountains everywhere, from the gentle Jura to the mighty Alps with their glaciers. Mountains form over millions of years, when parts of the Earth's crust are pushed together and lifted up.
wichtigste: A mountain is a rise in the land that is clearly higher than its surroundings.
The highest point of a mountain is called the summit.
The Alps are Switzerland's large mountain range with very high mountains.
The Jura mountains lie in the north-west of Switzerland.
The Matterhorn is world famous for its pointed shape.
The higher you climb, the colder it usually gets.
The highest mountain in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif, at 4634 metres.

abschnitte.text: A **mountain** rises clearly above its surroundings. Its highest point is called the **summit**, and its sides are called slopes or flanks. Several mountains together form a **mountain range**. A saddle between two peaks that you can cross is called a pass. The height of a mountain is measured in metres above sea level.

Most large mountain ranges form when two **tectonic plates** collide. The Earth's crust is pushed together, folded and lifted. This is how the Alps formed, when the African Plate pushed against the Eurasian Plate. This process took many millions of years and is not quite finished yet. Other mountains are **volcanoes**, built up from lava that has flowed out. At the same time, wind, water and glaciers slowly wear the mountains down again.

The **Alps** cover about 60 per cent of Switzerland. There are 48 peaks here that are over 4000 metres high. The highest mountain in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze at 4634 metres, and the most famous landmark is the **Matterhorn** near Zermatt with its pointed shape. In the north-west lies the **Jura**, a lower range of folded mountains with long, wooded ridges. Its highest Swiss peak is Mont Tendre at 1679 metres.

The higher you climb, the **colder** it gets: on average by about 0.6 °C per 100 metres. That is why there is snow on high peaks even in summer. It is also why the plants change with height: lower down there are broadleaved woods, higher up coniferous forests. At about 2000 metres the forest stops; this is the **tree line**. Above it there are Alpine pastures, rock, snow and glaciers.

Animals live in the mountains that are adapted to the cold and to steep ground. They include the **ibex**, the chamois, the marmot and the golden eagle. People have used the mountains for centuries for **Alpine farming**: in summer cows graze on the high pastures, and the milk is made into cheese. Today the mountains are also important for tourism, skiing and hiking. Many reservoirs in the Alps produce electricity from water power.

Mountain hiking is fun but needs preparation. The weather in the mountains can change quickly, and thunderstorms and fog are dangerous. Good shoes, warm clothes, rain protection and enough to drink belong in your rucksack. In Switzerland, paths are marked with colours: yellow for hiking paths, **white-red-white** for mountain paths and white-blue-white for Alpine routes. In an emergency the air rescue service **Rega** helps on the number 1414.

begriffe.erklaerung: The highest point of a mountain.
A large group of connected mountains.
The height above which no forests can grow.
A lower crossing between two mountains, over which paths or roads lead.

gewusst: The rocks on the summit of the Matterhorn originally came from the African Plate.
The Alps are still being lifted by about a millimetre every year.
On many limestone peaks in the Alps you can find fossilised sea creatures, because these rocks once formed on the sea floor.

teile.einleitung: Soil is the top, loose layer of the Earth on which plants grow. It looks plain, but it is full of life. New soil forms only very slowly, which is why it is precious.
wichtigste: Soil is made of broken-down rock, humus, water and air.
Earthworms loosen the soil with their tunnels.
Nature often needs over a hundred years to make one centimetre of new soil.
Plants find support, water and nutrients in the soil.
Millions of tiny living things live in a handful of garden soil.
When rain or wind carries soil away, this is called erosion.

abschnitte.text: Soil is a **mixture**. It contains small stones and grains from broken-down rock. On top of this there is **humus**, a dark mass made of dead plants and animals. **Water** and **air** are held in many small spaces. Depending on the size of the grains, there are different soils: **sandy soil** feels gritty and loose, while loam and clay are finer and stick together.

Frost, heat, water and roots break rock down into small pieces only very slowly. Dead plant parts are turned into **humus** by living things. It often takes **over a hundred years** for one centimetre of new soil to form. That is why good soil is very valuable. Once it has been washed away, it does not come back quickly.

**Millions** of tiny living things live in a handful of good garden soil, mainly **bacteria** and **fungi**. Most of them are so small that you cannot see them. **Earthworms** are important helpers. They dig tunnels, mix the soil and eat plant remains. This lets air and water reach the roots better. The **mole** digs long tunnels with its broad front paws and pushes the earth up into molehills.

Plants need the soil in three ways. Their **roots** hold them firmly so that they do not fall over. From the soil they take **water** and **nutrients**. Almost everything we eat grows directly or indirectly in the soil. That is why healthy soil is also very important for farming in Switzerland.

Rain and wind can **carry soil away**. This process is called **erosion**. On slopes in particular, rain can easily wash the earth away. Plants protect the soil, because their roots hold it in place like a **net**. That is why it is important that fields and slopes are not left without plants for long.

gewusst: A handful of soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth.
Earthworms can dig tunnels that go more than a metre deep.

teile.einleitung: A drought is a long period when there is far too little rain. Soil, plants, streams and lakes dry out. In Switzerland, too, there have been several drought summers in recent decades, for example in 2003 and 2018.
wichtigste: In a drought there is too little rain for weeks or months.
The soil dries out, shrinks and gets deep cracks.
Crops in the fields dry up, and the harvest is small.
The water level in rivers and lakes falls.
When it is very dry, fires in the forest are often banned.
In the summer of 2018 the army flew water to cows on Swiss Alpine pastures.

abschnitte.text: A **drought** happens when there is much less rain than normal for a long time. Often it is also hot, and the Sun makes even more water evaporate. The soil dries out and shrinks. This creates deep **cracks**. Because less water flows out of the soil, the water level in streams, rivers and lakes also falls.

Plants need water to live. Without rain they wilt, and the **harvest** is small. Farmers then have to water their fields or buy in feed for their animals. Fish suffer too: shallow, warm water contains less **oxygen**. But trout and grayling need cool water. In the hot summer of 2018, many grayling died in the Rhine near Schaffhausen.

Dry leaves, grass and wood burn very easily. Even a small spark can start a big **forest fire**. That is why cantons and municipalities often issue a **fire ban** in and near forests when it is very dry. Sometimes fireworks on 1 August are then banned as well. These rules apply to everyone and protect people and nature.

abschnitte.titel: The drought summer of 2018 in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In the summer of 2018 there was very little rain in Switzerland for months. On some **Alpine pastures** the springs dried up. So the **Swiss Army** flew water up by helicopter so that the cows had enough to drink. Experts expect such dry summers to become more frequent because of **climate change**.

Everyone can help to save water when it is dry. In the garden you can collect **rainwater** in a water butt and use it for watering. If you water in the evening, you lose less water through evaporation. A layer of grass cuttings or leaves on the flower beds keeps the soil moist for longer.

gewusst: In the hot summer of 2003 it was also extremely dry and hot in Switzerland.
Dried-out soils cannot soak up rain well at first, so during a thunderstorm afterwards a lot of water runs off over the surface.

teile.einleitung: A flood happens when a river, stream or lake carries much more water than normal and can burst its banks. In Switzerland it is one of the most common and most expensive natural hazards. Dams, retention basins and more space for rivers are used to protect people and houses.
wichtigste: A flood happens when a body of water carries much more water than normal.
In Switzerland, floods are caused mainly by long-lasting, heavy rain.
In August 2005, a flood caused great damage in large parts of Switzerland.
Tarmac and concrete surfaces make floods worse because rain cannot soak away.
Revitalisation gives rivers more space and so protects against floods.
The Jura water correction in the 19th century was meant to protect the Seeland from flooding.

abschnitte.text: Floods are most often caused by **long-lasting, heavy rain** over several days. If snowmelt in spring or early summer is added, rivers rise especially high. Violent thunderstorms can also make small streams swell within minutes. If the ground is already wet or frozen, it cannot take in any more water.

On **tarmac** and concrete surfaces, rainwater cannot soak away and flows straight into the streams. In the past, many rivers were straightened and squeezed into narrow channels, so the water flows away faster. Houses that stand close to the bank or in flood plains are especially at risk. Driftwood can pile up at bridges and dam the water even more.

In August 2005 it rained very heavily for days on the north side of the Alps. Many rivers and lakes burst their banks, and the cantons of Bern, Lucerne, Uri and Obwalden were especially affected. In the Matte quarter of Bern and in Brienz, water and **debris flows** caused severe damage, and several people died. The damage came to around 3 billion francs, more than in any other flood in Switzerland since records began.

In the Seeland between Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Murten there used to be flooding again and again. With the **Jura water correction** from 1868, the River Aare was diverted into Lake Biel, and the lake levels were lowered. Afterwards the marshy Grosses Moos was drained and became Switzerland's fertile vegetable garden. A second correction followed in the 20th century.

Today, besides dams and retention basins, the main approach is **revitalisation**: rivers are given wider beds and floodplain meadows again. This lets the water spread out without flooding towns and villages. **Hazard maps** show where building is not allowed, or only with protective measures. During floods the federal government issues warnings on its natural hazards platform, and you should keep away from riverbanks and cellars.

begriffe.erklaerung: A straightened river is given a more natural course and more space again.
A fast-flowing mush of water, mud and stones.
A basin that holds back water during a flood and releases it slowly.
A map that shows where natural hazards such as floods threaten.

gewusst: Because of the Jura water correction, the level of the three Jura lakes fell by about two and a half metres.
Today a large part of Switzerland's vegetables is grown in the Grosses Moos.
A single cubic metre of water weighs one tonne, which is why floods have so much force.

teile.einleitung: The geodynamo is the process in the Earth's core that produces the Earth's magnetic field. Flowing liquid iron works like a huge dynamo that drives itself.
wichtigste: A dynamo needs a moving liquid that conducts electricity.
Liquid iron flows in the outer core of the Earth.
A permanent magnet is impossible in the hot interior of the Earth.
The Coriolis force arranges the currents into whirls.
The solidifying of the inner core supplies important energy.
In 1919 Joseph Larmor proposed the idea of a self-sustaining dynamo.
Mars no longer has a global magnetic field today.

abschnitte.text: You might think there is a huge magnet inside the Earth. But that is impossible. Above the **Curie temperature**, about 770 °C for iron, materials lose their permanent magnetism. In the Earth's core it is several thousand degrees hot. So the magnetic field has to be produced over and over again.

The **outer core** of the Earth is made of liquid iron. It reaches from a depth of about 2890 km to about 5150 km, so it is about 2260 km thick. The liquid iron conducts electricity. When it moves through a magnetic field, electric currents are produced. These currents in turn produce the magnetic field and keep it going. This is called a **self-sustaining dynamo**.

Because the Earth turns, the **Coriolis force** acts on the currents. It deflects rising and sinking iron sideways. This creates column-like whirls along the Earth's axis, and a large field with a north and a south pole forms. Today the flow is driven mainly by the slow **solidifying of the inner core**. This releases heat, and lighter substances rise in the melt.

In 1919 the physicist **Joseph Larmor** suggested that the magnetic fields of celestial bodies are kept going by a self-sustaining dynamo. He wanted to explain sunspots with this, and later the idea was applied to the Earth. In 1995 **Gary Glatzmaier** and **Paul Roberts** produced a computer simulation in which the field reversed by itself. This showed that **reversals** of the Earth's magnetic field are a natural result of the dynamo.

Magnetised rocks on **Mars** show that it used to have a magnetic field. Its core is smaller and cooled down faster. The currents came to a standstill, and the dynamo died out. Today Mars no longer has a global magnetic field.

gewusst: In the Earth's history the magnetic field has flipped many times.
Without a magnetic field, a compass would not work on Earth.

teile.einleitung: An ice core is a long column of ice that researchers drill out of an ice sheet. Air bubbles, dust and traces of earlier times are trapped in the ice. In this way the ice becomes an archive of the climate going back hundreds of thousands of years.
wichtigste: The EPICA ice core at Dome C in Antarctica goes back about 800,000 years.
At the beginning of 2025 the project “Beyond EPICA” drilled ice that is at least about 1.2 million years old.
The ratio of heavy and light isotopes in the ice reveals the temperature of the past.
In cold periods the CO2 content of the air was about 180 ppm.
Layers with a lot of sulphate show large volcanic eruptions of the past.
Researchers at the University of Bern are leaders in measuring the gases in ice.

abschnitte.text: In Greenland and Antarctica, snow falls every year that no longer melts. Layer by layer it is pressed together, first into **firn** and finally into ice. Small **air bubbles** are trapped in the process. With special drills, researchers bring up long columns of ice, the **ice cores**. The deeper the ice lies, the older it is.

The **temperature** of the past can be worked out from the ice itself. In a colder climate, snow contains fewer heavy **isotopes** of oxygen and hydrogen. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different weights. The air bubbles show how much **CO2** and methane there was in the air in the past. However, the air is younger than the ice around it, because the firn only becomes airtight at a depth of about 50 to 120 metres.

The core from the Russian station **Vostok**, published in 1999, covered about 420,000 years. The core from the European project **EPICA** at Dome C goes back about 800,000 years and shows eight cycles of cold and warm periods. At the beginning of 2025, the project **Beyond EPICA** reached the bedrock at a depth of about 2800 metres at the site Little Dome C. The ice is at least about 1.2 million years old.

The Swiss physicist **Hans Oeschger** from the University of Bern was a pioneer of ice core research. Sudden jumps in climate during the last cold period are named after him and the Dane **Willi Dansgaard**: the **Dansgaard-Oeschger events**. Researchers in Bern also measured the greenhouse gases in the EPICA core. They showed that CO2 and temperature are closely linked: in cold periods the CO2 content was about **180 ppm**, in warm periods much higher.

Large **volcanic eruptions** fling sulphur gases into the air. These fall to the ground as **sulphate** with the snow. In the ice core they can be recognised as layers with a higher sulphate content. Such peaks also help to match up the dates of cores from Greenland and Antarctica.

gewusst: The abbreviation ppm means “parts per million”, so 180 ppm means 180 CO2 particles in a million particles of air.
Today the CO2 content of the air is over 400 ppm, higher than at any time in the known ice cores.

teile.einleitung: Gemstones are rare, beautiful and hard minerals. When cut, they sparkle in the light and are used for jewellery and crowns. Well-known gemstones are ruby, sapphire, emerald and diamond.
wichtigste: The ruby is red; its name comes from the Latin word for red.
The emerald is bright green.
Most sapphires are blue.
The amethyst is purple and a form of quartz.
Gemstones are valuable because they are rare, beautiful and hard.
Cutting gives them many smooth faces, and they sparkle.

abschnitte.text: Gemstones are **minerals** that form in the earth. They are particularly **rare**, beautifully coloured and **hard**. Because they are so hard, they hardly get scratched and stay beautiful for a long time. The hardest natural substance is **diamond**. On the Mohs hardness scale it has the highest value, 10.

The **ruby** is red, and its name comes from the Latin word “ruber” for red. The **sapphire** is usually blue, but there are also other colours. Ruby and sapphire are actually the same mineral, **corundum**. Only tiny added substances give them their colour. The **emerald** is bright green and is one of the most valuable gemstones. The **amethyst** is purple and a form of quartz.

In their raw state, gemstones often look plain. Only the **gem cutter** makes them shine. He grinds many small, smooth faces into the stone. These faces are called **facets**. The light is bent and reflected by them. This makes the stone sparkle and glitter with every movement.

Gemstones are used mainly for **jewellery**, such as rings, necklaces and earrings. The **crowns** of queens and kings are often set with many gemstones. They were meant to show power and wealth. Some gemstones are so famous that they even have their own name.

Beautiful crystals can also be found in the Swiss Alps. Particularly well known is the clear **rock crystal**, a form of quartz. People who search for crystals in the mountains are called **“Strahler”**. They often climb steep rock faces to find crystal fissures.

gewusst: Diamonds are made only of carbon, just like the graphite in a pencil.
The emerald is a green form of the mineral beryl.

teile.einleitung: A glacier is a large mass of ice that slowly moves down the valley. Glaciers form where more snow falls in a year than melts in summer. Switzerland has around 1,400 glaciers, but most of them are getting smaller because of global warming.
wichtigste: A glacier is made of ice that has formed from snow.
Over the years, snow turns into firn and then into glacier ice.
Glaciers move very slowly down the valley.
The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the longest glacier in the Alps.
Deep cracks in the ice are called crevasses.
The debris a glacier leaves behind is called a moraine.
Most Swiss glaciers are currently getting smaller.

abschnitte.text: Glaciers form high in the mountains, where it is so cold that snow stays on the ground even in summer. Every year new snow is added and presses on the old layers. The snow first turns into grainy **firn** and after many years into hard, blue **glacier ice**. The upper part, where snow is added, is called the **accumulation zone**, and the lower part, where ice melts, is the ablation zone.

Glaciers move down the valley like a very slow river of ice. Depending on the glacier, this is a few metres to a few hundred metres per year. Where the ice flows over bumps, it tears open, and deep **crevasses** form. At the lower end, the glacier snout, a meltwater stream often flows out of the **glacier mouth**.

The **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais is the longest glacier in the Alps, at around 20 km. At Konkordiaplatz its ice is almost 900 m thick. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch. Other well-known glaciers are the Gorner Glacier near Zermatt and the **Rhône Glacier** at the Furka Pass.

With stones frozen into them, glaciers grind away the ground beneath and carry rock along with them. They leave the debris behind as a **moraine**, at the sides and at the end of the glacier. Where a glacier flowed through a valley, it leaves a **U-shaped valley**, like the Lauterbrunnen Valley. Many Swiss lakes, such as Lake Zurich, were also formed by Ice Age glaciers.

Swiss glaciers have been getting smaller since about 1850, and especially fast in recent decades. In the record years 2022 and 2023 they lost around 10 per cent of their volume together. The **GLAMOS** network monitors their size every year. Glaciers are important stores of water that feed rivers and power stations in summer.

begriffe.erklaerung: Grainy old snow that has survived at least one summer.
A deep crack in glacier ice.
Debris of stones and sand left behind by a glacier.
A valley with a U-shaped cross-section, carved out by a glacier.

gewusst: Glacier ice looks blue because it absorbs red light and reflects blue light.
In summer, parts of the Rhône Glacier are covered with white sheets so that its ice grotto melts more slowly.
During the last Ice Age, glaciers covered almost the whole of Switzerland as far as the Swiss Plateau.

teile.einleitung: The hypocentre is the place inside the Earth where an earthquake begins. It is also called the focus of the earthquake. How deep it lies has a big effect on how strongly the quake is felt at the surface.
wichtigste: The hypocentre is the place where the break in the rock begins.
Another word for it is the focus.
The epicentre lies directly above it on the Earth's surface.
From around 300 km deep, earthquakes are called deep-focus earthquakes.
The deepest known earthquake foci lie around 700 km deep.
In Switzerland, most foci lie in the top 30 km.

abschnitte.text: An earthquake happens when stress in the rock is suddenly released and the rock **breaks**. The place where this break begins is called the **hypocentre** or **focus**. “Hypo” is Greek and means “under”. From the hypocentre, **seismic waves** spread out in all directions. The point on the Earth's surface directly above it is called the **epicentre**.

The depth of the focus and the distance to the epicentre form a **right-angled triangle**. An example: the focus lies 30 km deep, and a measuring station is 40 km from the epicentre. By **Pythagoras'** theorem, 30² plus 40² equals 900 plus 1,600, which equals 2,500. The square root of this is **50**. So the station is 50 km from the hypocentre.

Earthquakes are grouped by depth. **Shallow earthquakes** lie up to about 70 km deep, **intermediate** ones up to about 300 km. Below that, they are called **deep-focus earthquakes**. No earthquakes have been measured below about **700 km**. There the rock is so hot and under such high pressure that it hardly breaks in a brittle way any more. Deep-focus earthquakes happen mainly in **subduction zones**, where one plate dives down into the mantle. The diving plate is colder and more brittle than its surroundings.

On their way through the rock, seismic waves become weaker. In a **shallow earthquake**, the path to the surface is short. That is why more energy arrives there. A shallow earthquake therefore often causes **more damage** than a deep one of the same strength. Deep earthquakes, on the other hand, are sometimes felt over a very large area.

The ground shakes regularly in Switzerland too, usually so weakly that nobody notices. Swiss earthquakes happen in the **Earth's crust**. Most foci lie in the **top 30 km**, and in the Alps often even less than 15 km deep. The earthquakes are monitored by the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich. The strongest known earthquake in Switzerland destroyed large parts of the city of **Basel** in **1356**.

gewusst: The deepest earthquakes happen around 700 km below the surface, which is around eighty times deeper than Mount Everest is high.
Hundreds of earthquakes are measured in Switzerland every year; nobody feels most of them.

teile.einleitung: In winter, icicles hang from the edges of roofs, fountains and rock faces. They form when dripping water gradually freezes. However beautiful they look, large icicles can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: An icicle forms when dripping water freezes drop by drop.
They grow best when the Sun melts snow but the air is cold.
Because of gravity, icicles grow downwards.
They are pointed at the bottom because the least water reaches there.
When it thaws, they drip and melt.
Large icicles can fall down and injure people.

abschnitte.text: On a sunny winter's day, some snow on the roof melts. The **meltwater** runs to the edge of the roof and drips down. In the cold air, part of it freezes into ice. Drop by drop, new ice is added, and the **icicle** gets longer and longer. Because the water drips downwards due to **gravity**, icicles grow from the top down.

The water flows down the outside of the icicle as a thin film. Much of it freezes on the way. Only a little water reaches the **tip**. That is why the icicle stays thin at the bottom and keeps getting thicker at the top. This creates the typical shape, which looks like an upside-down pyramid or a pointed cone.

Large icicles are heavy and sharp. When it gets warmer or the Sun shines on them, they can suddenly come loose and **fall down**. That is why you should not walk directly under large icicles. House owners sometimes have to have dangerous icicles removed. When it **thaws**, that is, above 0 degrees, icicles drip and get smaller until they fall off.

There are icicles not only on houses. On **rock faces**, water seeps out of cracks in winter. It freezes and sometimes forms icicles several metres long and whole curtains of ice. Frozen **waterfalls** can form in this way too. In the mountains, skilled climbers even climb up such icefalls with ice axes and crampons. This is called **ice climbing**.

gewusst: Some icicles have small ridges all round that look like waves.
Similar-shaped formations of lime in caves are called stalactites, but they grow much more slowly.

teile.einleitung: Rock is the solid material that makes up the Earth's crust, and it is made of minerals. There are three large groups: igneous rocks, sedimentary rocks and metamorphic rocks. Granite, limestone, marble and Nagelfluh are well-known examples.
wichtigste: Rocks are made of one or more minerals.
There are three groups: igneous rocks, sedimentary rocks and metamorphic rocks.
Granite forms when magma solidifies slowly deep underground, basalt when lava solidifies quickly at the surface.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock.
Marble forms from limestone through pressure and heat.
The Rigi is mostly made of Nagelfluh.

abschnitte.text: **Igneous rocks** form when hot molten rock cools down and becomes solid. If magma solidifies slowly deep inside the Earth, a coarse-grained rock such as **granite** forms. If lava solidifies quickly at the surface, a fine-grained rock such as **basalt** forms. In Switzerland, granite is found for example in the Gotthard area and the Grimsel area.

**Sedimentary rocks** form from deposited material such as sand, gravel, mud or shells. Over a long time the layers are pressed together and cemented. **Limestone** often forms from the chalky shells of sea creatures, and the Jura mountains are mostly made of it. **Nagelfluh** is a mixture of round river pebbles and forms, for example, a large part of the Rigi.

**Metamorphic rocks** form when existing rock deep inside the Earth is exposed to great pressure and high heat. It does not melt, but its minerals change. In this way limestone becomes **marble**, and granite or sandstone can become **gneiss**. When the Alps formed, many rocks were changed in this way.

Rocks do not stay the same forever; they change in a long **cycle**. Mountains are weathered, rivers carry away the debris and deposit it as sediment. Deep inside the Earth this can become metamorphic rock or even magma again. Such a cycle takes many millions of years.

People have used rock since the Stone Age, first for tools made of flint. Today we build with granite, sandstone and limestone, and **cement** is made from limestone. The old town of Bern, for example, is built of greenish Bernese sandstone. Gravel and sand from the Swiss Plateau are needed in large amounts for concrete.

begriffe.erklaerung: A natural solid substance with a fixed chemical make-up, for example quartz.
Molten rock inside the Earth; at the surface it is called lava.
The change of rock through pressure and heat.
A sedimentary rock made of cemented, round pebbles.

gewusst: Nagelfluh looks as if someone had hammered nails into the rock, which is where the German name comes from (“Nagel” means “nail”).
The white marble for many famous statues comes from Carrara in Italy.
The summit rocks of Mount Everest are made of limestone that once lay on the sea floor.

teile.einleitung: Diamond is the hardest natural substance on Earth. It is made only of carbon and sparkles especially beautifully when it is cut. Diamonds are precious jewellery and useful tools at the same time.
wichtigste: Diamond is the hardest natural material.
It is made only of carbon.
Its weight is measured in carats; one carat is 0.2 grams.
A diamond with a special round cut is called a brilliant.
Diamonds are very hard, but also brittle.
They are used in drills and saws.

abschnitte.text: A **diamond** is made only of **carbon**. This is the same substance that coal is mostly made of. But in a diamond the carbon particles are joined to each other especially firmly and regularly. Diamonds form deep inside the Earth under very high **pressure** and great **heat**. Sometimes they reach the surface during volcanic eruptions.

Diamond is the **hardest natural material**. On the Mohs hardness scale it has the highest value, **10**. It can scratch almost all other substances, including **glass**. Even so, it is **brittle**. If you hit it hard with a hammer, it can shatter.

Most diamonds in jewellery are **colourless and clear**. But there are also rare coloured diamonds, for example yellow, blue or pink ones. A diamond with a special round cut is called a **brilliant**. The many small faces bounce the light back and forth inside the stone. That is why it sparkles so much.

The weight of diamonds and other gemstones is given in **carats**. **One carat is 0.2 grams**. The name probably comes from the seeds of the carob tree, which were once used as weights. Large diamonds are very rare and therefore especially valuable.

Because diamonds are so hard, they are used in **drills** and **saws**. With them you can even cut hard stone and concrete. For such tools, small diamonds that are not good enough for jewellery are usually used. Today **artificial diamonds** are also made in factories. They are also made of pure carbon.

gewusst: A pencil also contains carbon, as soft graphite. Diamond and graphite are made of the same substance.
At very high temperatures diamonds can burn in air, because they are made of carbon.

teile.einleitung: An ice age is a long period in the Earth's history when there are large ice sheets at the poles. The present ice age began about 2.6 million years ago. Since then cold and warm stages have taken turns, and right now we are living in a warm period.
wichtigste: The present ice age has been going on for about 2.6 million years.
Cold periods are called glacials, and the warm periods between them interglacials.
Today we live in the Holocene, a warm period.
In 1837 in Neuchâtel, Louis Agassiz made the idea of a great ice age well known.
At the peak of the last cold period, sea level was about 120 metres lower.
Erratic boulders in the Central Plateau were brought from the Alps by glaciers.

abschnitte.text: The present ice age began with the **Quaternary** about 2.6 million years ago. Since then **cold periods** and **warm periods** have taken turns many times. In scientific language, cold periods are called **glacials** and the warm periods between them **interglacials**. Today we live in the **Holocene**, a warm period. Because there are still large ice sheets at the poles, the ice age is nevertheless still going on.

abschnitte.titel: Glaciers as far as the Central Plateau
abschnitte.text: In the cold periods, the Alpine glaciers grew far out into the **Central Plateau**. They scooped out valleys and pushed rubble together into **moraines**. Many Swiss lakes lie in basins that the ice dug out. The glaciers also carried large boulders from the Alps. When the ice melted, these **erratic boulders** were left behind, often far from where they came from. Because so much water was locked up in the ice sheets, sea level was about **120 metres** lower than today.

The idea of an earlier great glaciation was developed to a large extent in Switzerland. As early as the 1820s, the Valais engineer **Ignaz Venetz** interpreted erratic boulders and moraines as traces of earlier, much larger glaciers. In 1837 the naturalist **Louis Agassiz** gave a famous speech in **Neuchâtel** about a great ice age. His ideas spread the ice age theory around the world.

In front of the glaciers lay a cold **steppe** with grasses and low plants. Large animals such as **mammoths** and **woolly rhinoceroses** lived there. With their thick coats they were well adapted to the cold. At **Niederweningen** in the canton of Zurich, several mammoth skeletons were found. Today you can visit a small mammoth museum there.

Even in a warm period the climate changes. From about 1350 to 1850 it was a little cooler than before and after. This period is called the **Little Ice Age**, although it was not a real cold period. Many Alpine glaciers reached their greatest length of the last few centuries around 1850. Since then they have been melting back strongly.

gewusst: Because sea level was so low, you could walk from England to France during the last cold period.
The Holocene has already lasted for about 11,700 years.

teile.einleitung: The Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland. It lies in the canton of Valais near Zermatt, close to the border with Italy, and belongs to the mighty Monte Rosa massif. Its summit is covered with snow and ice all year round.
wichtigste: At 4634 metres above sea level, the Dufourspitze is the highest peak in Switzerland.
It is the highest peak of the Monte Rosa massif.
The peak used to be called the Gornerhorn.
In 1863 it was given its present name by decision of the Federal Council.
On 1 August 1855 people stood on the summit for the first time.
The famous Matterhorn stands very close by.

abschnitte.text: The Dufourspitze is **4634 metres** high. No other place in Switzerland is higher. The summit stands in the south of the canton of **Valais**, above Zermatt and very close to the border with Italy. At this height it is always cold. That is why there is **snow and ice** there all year round.

The Dufourspitze belongs to the **Monte Rosa massif**. A massif is a large group of mountains with several peaks. In the Monte Rosa massif there are several peaks over 4000 metres. Large glaciers flow down from the mountains, for example the **Gorner Glacier**. Not far away stands the **Matterhorn** with its pointed pyramid shape. It is world famous, but lower than the Dufourspitze.

The peak used to be called the **Gornerhorn**. In 1863 the Federal Council decided to name it after **Guillaume Henri Dufour**. Dufour was a general and an important mapmaker. Under his direction, the first accurate map of the whole of Switzerland was made, the **Dufour map**. So the name honours a man who had the Swiss mountains measured accurately for the first time.

On **1 August 1855** a roped party reached the summit for the first time. It was made up of British mountaineers and local **mountain guides**. This was a big event at a time when many Alpine peaks were being climbed for the first time. Today the ascent is still a demanding high-altitude climb over glaciers and rock.
