Many mountaineers spend the night before in the Monte Rosa Hut.

gewusst: The first ascent took place, of all days, on 1 August, which is now Switzerland's National Day.
After the Mont Blanc massif, the Monte Rosa massif is the second highest mountain massif in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: A rock face is a very steep slope of bare rock. In Switzerland there are many famous rock faces where people climb and animals live.
wichtigste: A rock face is a steep, often almost vertical surface of rock.
The Eiger North Face in the Bernese Oberland is about 1800 metres high.
Climbers secure themselves with a rope, harness and helmet.
A via ferrata has fixed steel cables, rungs and ladders.
Golden eagles like to build their eyries in rock faces.
Stones can fall at the foot of a rock face.

abschnitte.text: A **rock face** is a very steep slope of rock. Often it is almost vertical. Rock faces form when glaciers, rivers or fractures in the rock shape steep sides. Where the rock is hard, the face stays standing for a long time. You can find rock faces on many mountains and in the Jura too.

The best-known rock face in Switzerland is the **Eiger North Face** in the Bernese Oberland. It is about 1800 metres high and is one of the best-known climbing walls in the Alps. In the **Lauterbrunnen Valley**, steep rock faces tower up on the left and right. Many waterfalls plunge down, for example the **Staubbach Falls**.

**Climbers** go up rock faces with a rope, harness and helmet. The rope catches them if they fall. For less experienced people there is the **via ferrata**. There steel cables, rungs and ladders are fixed firmly into the rock. You clip in with a via ferrata set and are protected the whole time.

The **golden eagle** likes to build its eyrie in steep rock faces. There it is protected from enemies. The **ibex**, with its large, curved horns, climbs amazingly safely over steep rocks. Its hooves have a hard rim and a soft sole that grips the rock well.

abschnitte.titel: Careful at the foot of the face
abschnitte.text: **Stones** keep coming loose from a rock face. Frost and rain loosen the rock. That is why it is dangerous at the foot of the face, even when nobody is climbing. A helmet protects your head. Beneath many rock faces there are scree slopes made of fallen stones.

gewusst: The Eiger North Face was climbed for the first time in 1938.
Ibex even climb almost vertical dam walls to lick salt from the stone.

teile.einleitung: The Folded Jura is the folded part of the Jura mountains in north-western Switzerland and in France. Its long ridges and valleys show the folds in the rock very directly. It was folded up as a late result of the formation of the Alps.
wichtigste: The Folded Jura was folded up mainly in the late Miocene and Pliocene, in the last 10 million years or so.
The cover of sediments slid off the rock beneath it on salt and anhydrite from the Triassic.
In 1907 August Buxtorf founded the distant push hypothesis.
A narrow cross valley that cuts through a Jura ridge is called a cluse.
The northern, unfolded part is called the Tabular Jura.
The highest peak of the whole Jura is the Crêt de la Neige at 1720 metres.

abschnitte.text: The rocks of the Jura mostly come from the **Jurassic** period and are many millions of years old. But they were folded much later, mainly in the late **Miocene** and **Pliocene**, that is, in the last 10 million years or so. The folding was a late result of the **formation of the Alps**. The Alps pushed from the south against the land in front of them, and this pressure reached all the way into the Jura.

Deep beneath the limestone layers lie layers of **salt** and **anhydrite** from the **Triassic**. These rocks are very soft. The package of layers above slid off the rock beneath on them and was folded. The base underneath stayed almost undeformed. The Basel geologist **August Buxtorf** recognised this during studies for tunnel building. In 1907 he founded the **distant push hypothesis**: the push came from the far-off Alps.

In the **Ridge Jura**, the upward-arched folds, the **anticlines**, form the ridges. The dips in between form the long valleys. So the landscape shows the folds directly. Some rivers were older than the folding and cut down into the rock while the ridges slowly rose. This created narrow cross valleys, the **cluses**, for example near **Balsthal**. To the north lies the **Tabular Jura** in Aargau and Basel-Landschaft, with almost flat layers.

abschnitte.titel: Peaks and the Creux du Van
abschnitte.text: The highest peak of the whole Jura range is the **Crêt de la Neige**, at 1720 metres, in the French Jura north-west of Geneva. The highest Swiss Jura peak is **Mont Tendre** at 1679 metres. The **Creux du Van** in the Neuchâtel Jura is also famous. This rocky bowl with vertical limestone walls was cleared out by Ice Age glaciers and their meltwater, with softer layers being worn away faster.

abschnitte.titel: A mountain range gives a period its name
abschnitte.text: In 1795 **Alexander von Humboldt** used the name Jura for layers of rock in the Jura mountains. In 1829 the Frenchman **Alexandre Brongniart** extended it to a whole period of the Earth's history. Since then people have spoken of the **Jurassic** period. It is known around the world, for example as the time of the dinosaurs.

gewusst: The name Jura probably comes from a Celtic word for “forest”.
Because the rock of the Jura is mostly limestone, there are many caves and dolines there.

teile.einleitung: An ore deposit is a place in the Earth's crust where metals are so concentrated that it is worth mining them. Such deposits form in very different ways, for example through hot water, weathering or rivers. They are the source of iron, copper, aluminium and gold.
wichtigste: An ore is a mixture of minerals from which a metal can be extracted economically.
Hydrothermal deposits form when hot watery solutions deposit metals in cracks.
Massive sulphide deposits form at black smokers on the sea floor.
Most banded iron formations formed about 2.8 to 2.5 billion years ago.
Porphyry deposits, as in Chile, mainly supply copper.
Bauxite forms through intense weathering in a tropical climate.

abschnitte.text: An **ore** is a mixture of minerals from which a metal can be extracted **economically**. So what matters is not only how much metal is in the rock, but also whether mining it is worth it. If metal prices rise, a deposit that was worthless before can become an ore. An important iron ore is **haematite**, which contains about 70 per cent iron. **Galena** is a lead ore, **sphalerite** a zinc ore and **cassiterite** a tin ore.

Many deposits formed **hydrothermally**. Deep down, hot water dissolves metals and carries them through cracks. When it cools or through chemical reactions, **ore minerals** come out of solution and form veins. On the sea floor at mid-ocean ridges there are **black smokers**. There hot, metal-rich water comes out and cools suddenly in the seawater. Sulphides of copper, zinc and iron come out of solution and form **massive sulphide deposits**.

**Porphyry deposits** form above bodies of magma at subduction zones, where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. They supply most of the **copper** mined in the world, for example in Chile, often together with molybdenum and gold. Important sources of iron are the **banded iron formations**. Most of them formed about 2.8 to 2.5 billion years ago. At that time dissolved iron in seawater was oxidised and settled out in layers of iron oxides and silica.

**Bauxite**, the most important ore for **aluminium**, forms through intense weathering in a tropical climate. Heavy rain and warmth dissolve almost everything out of the rock, leaving aluminium and iron oxides behind. In **placer deposits**, rivers collect heavy, durable minerals such as **gold** where the current slows down. An example in Switzerland is the **Napf area**, where river gold is still panned today.

Switzerland is poor in ores, but in the past there were some mines. At the **Gonzen** near Sargans, iron ore was mined for centuries until the mine was closed in 1966. Today you can visit it as a **show mine**. There were also smaller mines in Valais and the Grisons.

gewusst: Napf gold is panned from the sand of the streams with pans, as in the days of the gold diggers.
Black smokers give off water that is over 300 degrees hot but does not boil because of the high pressure.

teile.einleitung: An IPCC Assessment Report sums up what science knows about climate change. The IPCC, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, has published such reports since 1990. Governments all over the world use them as a basis for their decisions.
wichtigste: The IPCC's first Assessment Report came out in 1990.
The IPCC has three working groups with different tasks.
The Summary for Policymakers is approved line by line by consensus.
In 2021, the sixth report called the human influence on warming unequivocal.
From 2011 to 2020, the global temperature was around 1.1 °C above the average for 1850 to 1900.
The IPCC uses fixed terms for likelihoods.

abschnitte.text: The **IPCC** was founded in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme. Its secretariat is in **Geneva**. The IPCC does not do research itself. Thousands of experts from all over the world voluntarily review published research and sum it up in **Assessment Reports**. The first came out in **1990**. It was an important basis for the UN **Framework Convention on Climate Change**, which was adopted in Rio de Janeiro in 1992. In 2007 the IPCC received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

Every report is made up of parts from three **working groups**. **Working Group I** describes the physical science basis of climate change. **Working Group II** studies **impacts, adaptation and vulnerability**, in other words how climate change affects people and ecosystems. **Working Group III** deals with how greenhouse gas emissions can be reduced. For the fifth report, the Bernese climate scientist **Thomas Stocker** was one of the leaders of Working Group I.

Each report has a short **Summary for Policymakers**. This is approved by government representatives **line by line by consensus**. They discuss the text together with the authors. The text must agree with the scientific report. In this way, all the countries taking part stand behind the summary.

The IPCC uses **fixed language** when it comes to uncertainty. **“Likely”** stands for 66 to 100 per cent. **“Very likely”** means 90 to 100 per cent. **“Virtually certain”** stands for 99 to 100 per cent. This lets readers understand exactly how certain a statement is.

The **sixth report** came out in several parts from 2021. It states that it is **unequivocal** that humans have warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land. Earlier reports had still given likelihoods for this. From 2011 to 2020, the global surface temperature was around **1.1 °C** above the average for 1850 to 1900, more over land than over the ocean. To limit warming to 1.5 °C with a 50 per cent likelihood, only around **500 gigatonnes** of CO2 could still be emitted from the start of 2020. As early as **2018**, a **Special Report** had compared the effects of 1.5 °C and 2 °C of warming.

gewusst: The IPCC does not do research itself but sums up the work of thousands of researchers.
The secretariat of the IPCC is based in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: A karst spring is a spring whose water flows through caves and cracks in limestone. It reacts quickly to rain and can supply a great deal of water.
wichtigste: Karst cavities form because water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone.
Karst springs react to heavy rain with a fast, strong rise in the amount of water.
The amount of water a spring delivers per unit of time is called its discharge.
After heavy rain, the water of many karst springs becomes cloudy.
Dye tracing experiments show where the water comes from.
The source of the Orbe near Vallorbe is fed with water from the Vallée de Joux.

abschnitte.text: Water takes up **CO2** from the air and soil and forms **carbonic acid**. This dissolves the calcium carbonate in limestone. Dissolved **calcium hydrogen carbonate** is produced, which is carried away with the water. Over a long time, cracks widen into tubes and caves. The water flows through this network to the **karst spring**.

The amount of water a spring delivers per unit of time is called its **discharge**. It is given, for example, in litres per second. In karst springs the discharge varies a lot. After heavy rain it often rises **quickly and strongly** within hours, because the water reaches the spring fast through large tubes. In dry periods, on the other hand, it can be many times smaller.

Shortly after heavy rain, the water of many karst springs becomes **cloudy**. The fast inflow through open karst tubes washes soil particles and sediment along with it. The water is hardly filtered on the way. That is why water suppliers have to monitor karst water carefully and often treat it.

You cannot tell from the outside where the water of a karst spring comes from. That is why a **tracer test** is carried out. A harmless dye such as **uranine** is put into the water where it soaks away. If it turns up again at a spring, the underground connection is proven. The place where a stream disappears into the ground is called a **swallow hole** or **ponor**.

In the Vaud Jura, water from the area of **Lac de Joux** and **Lac Brenet** soaks away into sinkholes in the limestone. Near **Vallorbe** it comes back to the surface as the **source of the Orbe**. In southern Germany, part of the young **Danube** soaks away near **Immendingen**. Most of the water reappears in the **Aachtopf** in the Hegau, the largest spring in Germany. From there it flows via the Radolfzeller Aach into Lake Constance and so to the Rhine.

gewusst: Through the karst, part of the Danube's water ends up in Lake Constance and so flows into the North Sea instead of the Black Sea.
After thunderstorms, karst springs can deliver many times more water within hours.

teile.einleitung: A lagoon is a shallow body of water on the coast that is almost completely cut off from the sea. Famous lagoons are found in Venice, in the South Seas and in Iceland.
wichtigste: A lagoon is a shallow basin of seawater, connected to the sea only by narrow openings.
Often a narrow strip of sand separates the lagoon from the open sea.
The water is often warmer because it is shallow.
Venice was built in a lagoon.
Bora Bora in the South Seas is known for its turquoise lagoon.
Flamingos are often seen in lagoons on the Mediterranean.

abschnitte.text: A **lagoon** is a shallow body of water on the coast. It is almost completely cut off from the open sea. Seawater flows in and out only through **narrow openings**. Often a narrow **strip of sand** separates the lagoon from the sea. Waves and currents have deposited it over a long time.

Because a lagoon is **shallow**, the sun warms the water quickly. That is why it is often warmer there than in the open sea. The waves are usually smaller too, because the strip of sand shields the water. Many fish, crabs and birds find food and shelter in lagoons.

The Italian city of **Venice** was built in a lagoon. It stands on many small islands. Instead of streets there are many **canals**. The black **gondola** is typical of Venice. A gondolier steers it standing up, with a long oar.

There are lagoons around coral islands too. **Bora Bora** in French Polynesia in the Pacific is surrounded by a **coral reef** and a turquoise lagoon. In an **atoll**, the lagoon lies in the middle of a ring of coral. The clear, shallow water shines in many shades of blue.

**Flamingos** are often seen in lagoons on the **Mediterranean**. They stand in the shallow water and eat small shrimps. Their **pink colour** comes from their food. A special lagoon is the **Blue Lagoon** in Iceland. It is a warm bath fed with warm water from deep underground, and it shines a milky blue.

gewusst: Flamingos are not pink from birth; they only get their colour from their food.
In Venice, even ambulances and the fire brigade travel through the canals by boat.

teile.einleitung: A rock crystal is a clear, see-through crystal that looks like glass or ice. It is a particularly pure form of quartz. In the Swiss Alps, crystal hunters have been searching for these glittering treasures for a long time.
wichtigste: A rock crystal is colourless and as clear as glass.
It is a six-sided column with a point at the top.
Rock crystal belongs to the quartz family of minerals.
In Switzerland, crystal hunters are called “Strahler”.
Rock crystals grow in hollows and cracks in the rock.
Large rock crystals need a very long time to grow.

abschnitte.text: A **rock crystal** is colourless and see-through. It is a very pure, clear form of **quartz**. Quartz is one of the most common minerals on Earth. But it is usually cloudy or coloured. Only when it is very pure does it become as clear as a rock crystal.

A rock crystal grows as a **column with six sides**. At the top it comes together in a **point**. This shape is no accident. The smallest building blocks of quartz always arrange themselves in the same pattern. That is why rock crystals from all over the world look similar.

Rock crystals grow in **cracks and hollows** in the rock. There, warm water with dissolved quartz flows through the rock. Over a long time, the quartz is deposited layer by layer. This happens very slowly, and large crystals need a very long time. In Switzerland, rock crystals are found mainly in the **Alps**; the areas around the **Grimsel** and the **Gotthard** are particularly well known.

In Switzerland, people who search for crystals in the mountains are called **“Strahler”**. They climb around the Alps looking for cracks in the rock where crystals might be hidden. The work is tiring and often dangerous. Some finds are so beautiful that they are now on display in museums.

In the past, many people believed that rock crystal was **ice that never melts**. After all, it feels cool and is as clear as ice. The word **crystal** comes from the Greek word for ice. Today we know that rock crystal is a mineral and has nothing to do with frozen water.

gewusst: The word crystal comes from the Greek word for ice.
Very large and famous rock crystals have been found in the area of the Grimsel and the Gotthard.

teile.einleitung: The Great Oxidation Event is an event in the early history of the Earth. Around 2.4 billion years ago, free oxygen built up permanently in the air for the first time. For many living things at that time this was devastating, but it was very important for the later development of life.
wichtigste: The Great Oxidation Event began around 2.4 billion years ago.
It was triggered by cyanobacteria that carried out photosynthesis.
For many microbes that lived without oxygen, oxygen was poisonous.
Banded iron formations formed in the sea.
The long Huronian glaciation happened at the same time.
Only afterwards could the ozone layer form.

abschnitte.text: The early Earth had hardly any free oxygen in the air. Then **cyanobacteria** developed a special kind of **photosynthesis**. In it, they use sunlight and give off **oxygen**. Over a very long time, more and more oxygen got into the sea and the air. From about 2.4 billion years ago, it built up permanently in the **atmosphere**. This happened at the start of the **Proterozoic**. In scientific writing, the event is called the **Great Oxidation Event**, or GOE for short.

Most microbes of that time were adapted to a life **without oxygen**. They are called **anaerobic**. For them, oxygen is strongly oxidising and harmful. Many of them were pushed back into oxygen-free niches, for example into mud or deep waters. The German name, “Grosse Sauerstoffkatastrophe” (Great Oxygen Catastrophe), stresses this devastating effect.

At that time, a lot of **iron** was dissolved in the sea. The oxygen turned it into insoluble **iron oxide**, which settled as a layer on the sea floor. Alternating with layers of silica, this created **banded iron formations**. Much of today's iron is mined from them. From around 2.3 billion years ago, **red sandstones**, the red beds, also formed on land. Their colour comes from iron oxide, which only forms with free oxygen. They are missing from older layers.

The **Huronian glaciation** happened at the same time. It began around 2.4 billion years ago and is named after Lake Huron in North America. It is thought to be one of the longest glaciations in the Earth's history. One possible explanation: oxygen broke down the greenhouse gas **methane**. This produces carbon dioxide and water. Because methane warms much more strongly, the **greenhouse effect** weakened and the climate cooled down.

Under UV radiation, **ozone** can form from oxygen. That is why an **ozone layer** could only form after oxygen had increased. Ever since, it has filtered out a large part of the sun's harmful UV radiation. Together with the oxygen, it created important conditions for later living things, including animals.

gewusst: A large part of the iron used today for steel comes from rocks that formed because of the first oxygen.
Tiny bacteria changed the air of the whole Earth.

teile.einleitung: The Cambrian explosion was a time more than 500 million years ago when a great many new groups of animals appeared. In the rocks, they show up almost suddenly in terms of Earth's history.
wichtigste: The Cambrian explosion began a good 500 million years ago in the geological period called the Cambrian.
During this time, many of the major animal groups that still exist today appeared.
For the first time, many animals formed hard shells, armour and skeletons.
That is why animal fossils are much more common from the Cambrian onwards than before.
Famous fossil sites are the Burgess Shale in Canada and Chengjiang in China.
Possible causes include more oxygen and new predators.

abschnitte.text: The **Cambrian** began around 540 million years ago. In the millions of years that followed, a great many new groups of animals appeared. Among them were ancestors of arthropods, molluscs and echinoderms. Because this happened quickly in terms of Earth's history, it is called the **Cambrian explosion**. But it was not a bang; it was a development over many millions of years.

Before the Cambrian, most living things had soft bodies. From the Cambrian onwards, many animals formed **shells**, **armour** and spines made of lime or phosphate for the first time. Experts call this **biomineralisation**. Hard parts are much more easily preserved as **fossils** than soft ones. That is why many more animal fossils are found from the Cambrian onwards. Even earlier there was the **Ediacaran biota**, whose mostly soft organisms are only preserved as imprints.

Places where soft body parts were also preserved are especially valuable. One of them is the **Burgess Shale** in Canada. Just as famous is **Chengjiang** in the Chinese province of Yunnan, around 518 million years old. **Anomalocaris** was also found there. This animal with grasping limbs on its head is thought to be one of the largest predators of the Cambrian. The well-known **trilobites** also date from this time.

The causes are still not fully understood. An **increase in oxygen** at the end of the Proterozoic is often mentioned, because larger, active animals need more oxygen. The zoologist Andrew Parker supports the **Light Switch hypothesis**. According to it, the first powerful **eyes** set off an arms race between predators and prey. Armour, camouflage and fast movement would then be the results of this. Probably several causes worked together.

**Charles Darwin** was already puzzled by the apparently sudden appearance of the fossils. In his book “On the Origin of Species” he wrote that the lack of older ancestors was hard to explain. He suspected **gaps in the fossil record**. Later finds of older living things such as the Ediacaran biota partly proved him right.

gewusst: Anomalocaris belonged to the radiodonts, early relatives of the arthropods.
Most of the major animal phyla living today already appear in the fossils of the Cambrian.

teile.einleitung: Climate sensitivity tells you how much the Earth warms up if the CO2 content of the air doubles. It is one of the most important figures in climate research.
wichtigste: Equilibrium climate sensitivity describes the long-term warming when the CO2 content doubles.
The sixth IPCC report gives 3 °C as the best estimate.
According to the IPCC, the likely range is 2.5 to 4 °C.
The transient climate response is smaller, around 1.8 °C, because the ocean takes up heat.
Without feedbacks, the Earth would warm by only about 1.2 °C.
The Charney Report of 1979 gave a range of 1.5 to 4.5 °C.

abschnitte.text: **Equilibrium climate sensitivity** tells you by how many degrees the Earth warms in the long term if the **CO2 content doubles**. In the long term means: after the climate has fully adjusted to the new state. The **sixth IPCC report** gives a best estimate of **3 °C** for this. The likely range is **2.5 to 4 °C**. Values below 1.5 °C are considered extremely unlikely.

The **transient climate response** describes the warming at the moment of doubling, if the CO2 content rises by 1 per cent each year. At that point the climate has not yet reached equilibrium. The IPCC gives around **1.8 °C** for this. The value is smaller because the **ocean** takes up a lot of heat. The deep layers of the sea warm only slowly, so the surface only reaches the full warming after centuries.

Without any **feedback**, the Earth would warm by only about **1.2 °C** with doubled CO2. It would then only react by giving off more heat radiation. Feedbacks strengthen this warming. Warmer air can hold more **water vapour**, and water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas. Melting ice and changes in clouds also play a part.

You get the **climate sensitivity parameter** by dividing the warming by the **forcing**. Forcing is given in watts per square metre. If a forcing of 4 W/m² leads to 3.2 °C of warming, this gives **0.8 °C per W/m²**. It is also important that forcing grows **logarithmically** with the CO2 content. Quadrupling equals two doublings. At 2.5 °C per doubling, that would therefore be about 5 °C.

As early as 1979, a report by the US National Academy of Sciences under **Jule Charney** estimated the climate sensitivity. It was based on early climate models and gave a range of **1.5 to 4.5 °C**. This range was confirmed again and again for decades. Only the sixth IPCC report was able to narrow the uncertainty clearly. It is based on several independent lines of evidence, such as measurements, climate models and data from past climates.

gewusst: The range given in the Charney Report of 1979 stayed almost unchanged for around 40 years.
The most important amplifier of warming is water vapour, which is itself a greenhouse gas.

teile.einleitung: GLAMOS is Switzerland's glacier monitoring network. Every year it observes how Swiss glaciers are changing and shows how strongly they are melting.
wichtigste: GLAMOS stands for “Glacier Monitoring Switzerland”.
The network is run by ETH Zurich and the universities of Fribourg and Zurich.
Glacier lengths have been observed systematically in Switzerland since 1880.
The glacier year runs from 1 October to 30 September.
The glacier inventory of 2016 counted around 1,400 glaciers.
In the glacier year 2026, the glaciers lost over 5 per cent of their ice.

abschnitte.text: **GLAMOS** stands for “Glacier Monitoring Switzerland”. Experts from **ETH Zurich** and the universities of **Fribourg** and **Zurich** carry out the measurements. The federal government and the Swiss Academy of Sciences support the network. GLAMOS collects and publishes data on the length, mass and volume of Swiss glaciers.

Systematic observation of **glacier lengths** began in Switzerland in 1880. This makes the Swiss series of measurements among the oldest in the world. According to the **glacier inventory** of 2016 there were around 1,400 glaciers. Many of them are very small. Since 1970, more than 1,000 glaciers in Switzerland have disappeared completely.

To measure how much ice melts in summer, glaciologists drill **stakes** into the ice. Later they check how far the stakes stick out. From this they can tell how many centimetres of ice have melted. In spring they also measure how much snow is lying there. Together this gives the **mass balance**, which shows whether the glacier has grown or shrunk.

The **glacier year** begins on 1 October, when snow starts to fall again in autumn. It ends on 30 September, when the summer melt is over. This period is also called the **hydrological year**. In this way, the winter snow and summer melt of one year can be looked at together.

The measurements show that Swiss glaciers are shrinking fast. According to GLAMOS, over 5 per cent of the remaining ice melted away in the glacier year **2026**. Only in the record year **2022** was the loss even a little bigger. The reasons were a winter with little snow and a hot, dry summer. In the five years up to 2026, the ice volume fell by almost 20 per cent, so by almost a fifth.

gewusst: Some Swiss glaciers have been measured every year for more than 100 years.
The GLAMOS data are added to a worldwide collection of glacier data.

teile.einleitung: A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure. Air pressure tells you a lot about the coming weather and about the height you are at. The barometer was invented in Italy in the 17th century.
wichtigste: In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli built the first mercury barometer.
At normal air pressure at sea level, the column of mercury is 760 millimetres high.
The aneroid barometer works without liquid, using an almost airless metal box.
If the barometer falls quickly, the weather usually gets worse.
Altimeters work on the principle of the barometer.
In 1648 Blaise Pascal showed that air pressure decreases with height.

abschnitte.text: In 1643 the Italian **Evangelista Torricelli**, a pupil of Galileo Galilei, filled a glass tube with **mercury**. Then he stood it upside down in a dish of mercury. The metal only sank a little way and then stayed where it was. This is because the air presses on the dish and holds the column in the tube in place. So for the first time air pressure became visible and measurable.

At normal air pressure at sea level, the column of mercury is **760 millimetres** high. That is where the old unit **millimetres of mercury** comes from. Mercury is very heavy, so a tube of less than a metre is enough. Water is about 13.6 times lighter than mercury. A water barometer would therefore need a column of just over **10 metres**.

In 1648 the French scholar **Blaise Pascal** had a barometer carried up the mountain **Puy de Dôme**. His brother-in-law carried it up. At the top, the mercury column was clearly lower than in the valley. This proved that air pressure decreases with height. The **altimeter**, which mountain walkers and pilots use, is based on this principle.

Many barometers at home are **aneroid barometers**. They contain a thin-walled, almost airless metal box. When air pressure is high, the box is squeezed together; when pressure is low, it expands. A pointer passes this small movement on to a scale. Such instruments are handy and do not need poisonous mercury.

If the barometer falls sharply within a few hours, a **low-pressure area** is usually approaching. Wind, clouds and rain often follow. If the air pressure rises, better weather is often on the way. What matters most is the change, not just a single value. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss measure air pressure at many stations.

gewusst: The word barometer comes from Greek and means roughly “weight measurer”.
The unit of air pressure, the pascal, is named after Blaise Pascal.

teile.einleitung: The Inn is the most important river of the Engadine. It rises in the mountains of the Grisons, flows through Austria and joins the Danube in Germany.
wichtigste: The Inn rises at Lake Lunghin near the Maloja Pass.
It flows through the Upper and Lower Engadine in the canton of Grisons.
In the Upper Engadine it passes through a chain of lakes, including Lake Sils and Lake Silvaplana.
At Zernez, the Spöl from the National Park flows into the Inn.
In Austria, the Inn flows through Tyrol and through Innsbruck.
At Passau, the Inn flows into the Danube.

abschnitte.titel: The source at the Maloja Pass
abschnitte.text: The Inn rises at **Lake Lunghin** by the Lunghin Pass, very close to the **Maloja Pass**. From there it flows north-east. In Romansh the river is called **En**. The name Engadine is often explained as “garden of the Inn”. This shows how closely the valley and the river belong together.

Soon after its source, the Inn flows through **Lake Sils**, **Lake Silvaplana**, Lake Champfèr and **Lake St. Moritz**. These lakes lie high in the Alps and shape the landscape of the Upper Engadine. In winter they often freeze over. Then the Inn flows on through the wide valley towards the Lower Engadine.

abschnitte.titel: The Spöl and the National Park
abschnitte.text: An important tributary is the **Spöl**. It comes from the Livigno area in Italy and is dammed in **Lago di Livigno**. After that it flows partly through the **Swiss National Park**. At **Zernez** it joins the Inn. In the Lower Engadine the valley becomes narrower, and the Inn finally flows into Austria.

After Switzerland, the Inn flows through the Austrian state of **Tyrol**. Its capital, **Innsbruck**, lies there. Its name means “bridge over the Inn”. Later the river forms part of the border between Austria and Germany. Along the Inn there are several hydroelectric power stations that produce electricity.

In the city of **Passau** in Bavaria, three rivers meet: the Inn, the **Danube** and the small Ilz. That is why Passau is also called the City of Three Rivers. On average over the year, the Inn even carries a little more water there than the Danube. Even so, the river is called the Danube afterwards. In this way the water of the Inn reaches the Black Sea.

gewusst: Although the Inn brings more water than the Danube at Passau, the river afterwards is called the Danube.
Water from the Engadine flows via the Inn and the Danube all the way to the Black Sea.

teile.einleitung: The Insubric Line is one of the most important fault zones in the Alps. It runs right across Ticino and separates two very different parts of the mountains.
wichtigste: The Insubric Line separates the Central Alps in the north from the Southern Alps in the south.
It is a section of the Periadriatic Seam, which is around 700 kilometres long.
In Switzerland it runs through Ticino, from the Centovalli via Locarno towards the Valtellina.
The blocks moved sideways, and the north side was strongly lifted.
South of the line, the rocks were hardly changed when the Alps formed.
The name comes from the Celtic people of the Insubres around Milan.

abschnitte.text: The **Insubric Line** is a large **fault**, which means a fracture zone in the Earth's crust. It is part of the **Periadriatic Seam**, which runs for around 700 kilometres through the Alps. The section from Piedmont to the Valtellina is called the Insubric Line. In the west it joins the **Canavese Line**, and in the east, from Sondrio, the **Tonale Line**. The name recalls the **Insubres**, a Celtic people who lived around Milan in ancient times.

In Switzerland the line runs through **Ticino**. It goes from the **Centovalli** via Locarno and the **Magadino Plain** on towards the Valtellina. You can recognise it by straight valley furrows. There the rock has been badly crushed by the movements. That is why erosion has easily carved out valleys here.

Along the line, two blocks of rock moved against each other. They shifted mainly sideways, in a **right-lateral** direction. At the same time, the north side was steeply **lifted up**. That is why rocks come to the surface in the north that were once buried deep and strongly heated. They belong to the nappes of the **Central Alps**.

South of the line lie the **Southern Alps**. These rocks were not buried deep when the Alps formed and so were hardly **metamorphosed**, which means hardly changed. That is why fossils are well preserved there, for example from the **Triassic**. In the **Ivrea Zone** in Piedmont, on the other hand, a piece of deep crust was tipped up steeply. It is seen as a window into the lower crust.

Around 30 million years ago, molten rock rose along the seam. This formed the **Bregaglia granite**. It builds peaks such as **Piz Badile** on the border between the Grisons and Italy. Its smooth granite walls are famous among climbers all over the world.

gewusst: The straight valleys of the Centovalli and the Magadino Plain follow the Insubric Line.
The Ivrea Zone shows rock from the lower crust and even from the mantle at the surface.

teile.einleitung: A river delta forms where a river flows into a sea or a lake and deposits sand, gravel and mud. In Switzerland, too, several deltas are growing out into the lakes.
wichtigste: The delta is named after the Greek letter delta (Δ).
The Nile Delta in Egypt is one of the best known in the world.
The Mississippi forms a bird's-foot delta.
The Maggia has built a large delta between Locarno and Ascona.
The Rhône forms a delta in Lake Geneva and the Camargue on the Mediterranean.
The Rhine builds a delta into Lake Constance.

abschnitte.text: A river carries a lot of **sediment**: gravel, sand and mud. Where it flows into calm water, it slows down. Then the material sinks to the bottom. Over time new land grows out into the water in this way. The river often splits into several **distributaries**. Many deltas have roughly the shape of a triangle, like the Greek letter **delta** (Δ).

Not every delta looks the same. On the **Mississippi**, the distributaries with their banks of sediment stick out into the sea like the toes of a bird. That is why this shape is called a **bird's-foot delta**. Other deltas are more round or fan-shaped. The shape depends on how much material the river brings and how strongly waves and tides carry it away again.

The **Nile Delta** north of Cairo is one of the best-known deltas. The Greek historian Herodotus already compared its shape with the letter delta. On the Mediterranean, the Rhône forms the **Camargue**, known for flamingos and white horses. In the **Netherlands**, the Rhine and the Meuse split into many branches. The large port of Rotterdam is also there.

The **Maggia** brings a lot of sediment from the Maggia Valley. Its delta reaches far into Lake Maggiore and separates Locarno from Ascona. The **Rhône** flows into the eastern end of Lake Geneva at Le Bouveret and deposits material from the Valais Alps there. The **Alpine Rhine** brings large amounts of gravel, sand and mud into Lake Constance every year. As a result, its delta keeps growing out into the lake.

Deltas often have very fertile soils, because the river deposits fine mud. That is why many people live in many deltas and farm there. At the same time, deltas are valuable **habitats** for birds, fish and plants. That is why many delta areas are nature reserves.

gewusst: The word delta for a river mouth goes back to the ancient Greeks.
A large part of Egypt's people live in the fertile Nile Delta.

teile.einleitung: The Coriolis force deflects moving bodies on the rotating Earth. It decides how winds flow around high and low pressure areas. In physics it is an apparent force that only appears in a rotating frame of reference.
wichtigste: The Coriolis force is an inertial force, that is, an apparent force.
The Coriolis parameter is f = 2Ω·sin φ.
At the equator the horizontal Coriolis force is zero, at the poles it is greatest.
In the Northern Hemisphere it deflects to the right, in the Southern Hemisphere to the left.
In the geostrophic wind, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force balance each other.
It is named after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who described it in 1835.

abschnitte.text: The **Coriolis force** only appears in a **rotating frame of reference** such as the Earth. Seen from outside, a body moves straight ahead while the Earth keeps turning beneath it. To an observer on the Earth, it looks as if the body is being deflected. That is why it is called an **inertial force** or **apparent force**. It was described in 1835 by the French physicist **Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis** in a paper about rotating machines.

The strength of the horizontal deflection is described by the **Coriolis parameter** f = 2Ω·sin φ. Here Ω is the angular velocity of the Earth, about 7.29 · 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹, and φ is the latitude. At the **equator**, sin 0° equals 0, so there is no horizontal deflection there. At the **poles**, f is greatest. At 45° latitude you get f = 2 · 7.29 · 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ · 0.707, about **1.0 · 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹**. Switzerland lies close to 46° latitude, so the value is very similar.

In the **Northern Hemisphere**, moving air is deflected to the **right** of its direction of motion. In the **Southern Hemisphere** the sign of f is negative, and the deflection is to the **left**. That is why low-pressure areas turn anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. According to **Buys Ballot's law**, if you stand with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, the low lies to your **front left**. It is shifted forwards because of friction with the ground.

In the free atmosphere, high above the ground, there is hardly any friction. There the **pressure gradient force** and the **Coriolis force** balance each other. The wind that results is called the **geostrophic wind**. It does not blow straight from the high into the low, but **parallel to the isobars**, the lines of equal air pressure. That is why weather maps are easy to read: isobars that are close together mean strong wind.

The Earth's rotation can be made visible with a **Foucault pendulum**. The plane in which it swings seems to turn slowly, because the Earth is turning beneath it. At the **North Pole**, a full turn takes about one **sidereal day**, about 23 hours 56 minutes. At middle latitudes it takes longer, because the effect decreases with the sine of the latitude. At the equator the plane of swinging does not turn at all.

gewusst: The Coriolis force is far too weak to decide which way water spins down the plughole of a bath; other influences decide that.
Léon Foucault demonstrated his famous pendulum in Paris in 1851.

teile.einleitung: Climate change means that the Earth's climate changes over a long time. Today the Earth is mainly getting warmer, and this can be felt in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: With climate change, the typical weather changes over many decades.
Today the Earth is getting warmer on average.
Burning coal, oil and gas contributes especially strongly to this.
Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the global average.
There is less snow at low altitudes, and heatwaves are becoming more frequent.
Everyone can help by walking, cycling and saving energy.

abschnitte.text: **Weather** is what we experience outside today: sun, rain or wind. **Climate** is the typical weather in a place over many years. With **climate change**, this typical weather changes over many decades. Today the Earth is mainly getting **warmer**. That is why people also speak of **global warming**.

Burning **coal, oil and gas** produces exhaust gases such as **carbon dioxide**. These gases hold heat back in the air, a bit like the glass of a greenhouse. That is why they are called **greenhouse gases**. Cars, heating systems, factories and power stations give off a lot of them. The average temperature of the Earth has risen clearly over the last 150 years.

According to **MeteoSwiss**, Switzerland has become around **2.9 degrees** warmer since the time before industrialisation. Worldwide it is about 1.3 degrees (as of 2024). So Switzerland has warmed about **twice as much**. On the Swiss Plateau, rain falls more often instead of snow, and low-lying ski areas often lack snow. The **glaciers** are also melting fast.

Because it is getting warmer overall, there are more very hot days. **Heatwaves** happen more often and get stronger. This is especially tiring for older people, small children and animals. Plants and forests also suffer from long droughts. That is why it is important to protect yourself well in hot weather and drink plenty.

Everyone can do something. If you **walk** or **cycle**, you produce no exhaust fumes and stay fit. At home you can **save energy**, for example by switching off the light when you leave a room. **Trees** help too: they take carbon dioxide out of the air and store it in their wood. Countries and municipalities also take action, for example with solar panels and good public transport.

gewusst: Since 1850, many Swiss glaciers have lost a large part of their ice.
A single large tree can store a lot of carbon dioxide in its wood over its lifetime.

teile.einleitung: A greenhouse, also called a glasshouse, is a house made of glass or see-through plastic. Inside it, plants grow protected and warm, even when it is still cool outside.
wichtigste: Greenhouse and glasshouse mean the same thing.
The walls are made of glass or see-through plastic.
Sunlight comes in, and the warmth stays inside.
In Switzerland, tomatoes, for example, are often grown in greenhouses.
On hot days the windows are opened so that it does not get too hot.
Certain gases in the air act in a similar way to the glass: this is the greenhouse effect.

abschnitte.text: A **greenhouse** or **glasshouse** is a house in which plants are grown in the warmth. Its walls and roof are made of **glass** or see-through **plastic**. This lets in a lot of sunlight, which the plants need to grow. There are small greenhouses in gardens and huge ones on vegetable farms.

The **sunlight** shines through the glass and warms the soil and the plants. The warm air can hardly escape through the glass. That is why it is warmer in a greenhouse than outside. Exactly the same thing happens in a **car** that stands in the sun in summer with its windows closed. It gets very hot inside. That is why you must never leave children or animals in a car.

**Tomatoes** like it warm. That is why in Switzerland they are often grown in greenhouses. Cucumbers, peppers, lettuce and herbs grow there too. A greenhouse is especially useful in **spring**, when it is still cold outside. You can sow early in the year, and the young plants are protected from frost.

In strong sunshine it can get too hot in a greenhouse. Then the plants suffer. That is why a gardener opens the **windows** on hot days. Fresh air cools things down. Large greenhouses often have automatic ventilation, shade nets and watering systems.

The Earth also has a kind of glass roof. Certain **gases** in the atmosphere, for example carbon dioxide and water vapour, hold back heat. This is called the **greenhouse effect**. Without it, it would be very cold on Earth. When people release more of these gases into the air, the Earth gets warmer.

gewusst: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the average temperature on Earth would be far below zero degrees.
Some botanical gardens have huge glasshouses in which rainforest plants grow.

teile.einleitung: Climate neutrality means that, overall, no additional greenhouse gases get into the air. Switzerland has set itself this goal for 2050.
wichtigste: Climate neutral means emitting no more greenhouse gases on balance.
Switzerland wants to reach net zero by 2050.
In June 2023, voters approved the Climate and Innovation Act.
With offsetting, you pay for climate protection projects elsewhere.
Emissions that are hard to avoid, for example from cement production, have to be balanced out.
In Switzerland, heat pumps are increasingly replacing oil heating.

abschnitte.text: A country is **climate neutral** when it does not emit more **greenhouse gases** than are removed from the air again. The balance is then at **net zero**. This does not mean that no gases at all are produced any more. But a remainder is balanced out by removing gases from the air. Many countries have set such goals since the **Paris Agreement** of 2015.

In 2019 the **Federal Council** decided on the goal of **net zero by 2050**. On 18 June 2023, around 59 per cent of voters approved the **Climate and Innovation Act**. It sets the goal of net zero by 2050 and interim targets in law. Supporters see it as an important step for climate protection. Opponents feared higher costs and an uncertain electricity supply.

With **CO2 offsetting**, you pay for projects that save or store the same amount of greenhouse gases elsewhere. An example would be a forest project or replacing old stoves. But your own emissions do not get smaller this way. That is why it is disputed how much offsetting should count towards climate neutrality.

abschnitte.titel: Emissions that are hard to avoid
abschnitte.text: Some emissions can hardly be avoided. When **limestone** is burnt to make **cement**, chemically bound CO2 is released, no matter what fuel is used for heating. Such leftover emissions have to be balanced out with **negative emissions**. One option is **CCS**, which stands for “carbon capture and storage”. In this, CO2 is captured and stored deep in the rock. In **direct air capture**, fans and filters take CO2 directly out of the air. An early plant of this kind was developed in Switzerland.

A large share of emissions comes from heating and transport. A **heat pump** uses a little electricity to take heat from the air, the ground or water. With electricity from renewable sources, this lets you heat almost without CO2. In Switzerland, heat pumps are increasingly replacing **oil heating**. Well-insulated houses, electric cars, bikes and public transport also reduce emissions.

gewusst: With cement, a large share of the CO2 comes not from heating but from the limestone itself.
One of the first plants to filter CO2 directly out of the air was developed in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Global warming is the rise in the average temperature on Earth since the beginning of industrialisation. The main cause is greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, which people release mainly by burning coal, oil and natural gas. The effects can be felt in Switzerland too, for example in melting glaciers.
wichtigste: Since industrialisation, the global temperature has risen by a good 1 °C.
Before industrialisation, the CO2 content of the air was around 280 ppm.
Over 100 years, methane has an effect about 28 times stronger than CO2.
Since 1988, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has summed up the state of climate research.
The Paris Agreement of 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 °C, if possible at 1.5 °C.
Switzerland is warming more than the average because land areas warm up faster than oceans.
Sea level is rising because water expands and ice on land melts.

abschnitte.text: Burning coal, oil and natural gas produces **carbon dioxide** (CO2). Before industrialisation, the CO2 content of the air was around 280 ppm; today it is over 420 ppm (as of about 2025). On top of this comes **methane** from livestock farming, rice fields and natural gas leaks, which over 100 years has an effect about 28 times stronger than CO2. These gases strengthen the **greenhouse effect** and hold back more heat in the atmosphere.

The **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)** was founded in 1988 and sums up the results of thousands of studies. According to its reports, it is clear that humans are causing the warming. The years since 2015 are among the warmest since measurements began. Important data come from weather stations, satellites, buoys and ice cores.

**Sea level** is rising because warm water expands and ice on land melts. Heatwaves, droughts and heavy rain are becoming more frequent or stronger. Many coral reefs are bleaching, and some kinds of animals and plants have to move to cooler areas. Low-lying island states and coastal cities are especially affected.

Since pre-industrial times, Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the global average. The reason is that **land areas** warm up faster than oceans. According to the **GLAMOS** network, the glaciers lost around 10 per cent of their volume together in the record years 2022 and 2023. There are fewer days with snow, and thawing permafrost is making some mountain slopes unstable.

abschnitte.titel: What is being done about it
abschnitte.text: In the **Paris Agreement** of 2015, almost all countries agreed to keep warming well below 2 °C, if possible at 1.5 °C. To do this, greenhouse gas emissions must fall sharply until **net zero** is reached. In 2023, Swiss voters approved the Climate and Innovation Act, which aims for net zero by 2050. In everyday life it also helps to save energy, travel by bike and train and waste less.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat, for example CO2 or methane.
Parts per million, used to measure tiny amounts of a gas in the air.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which sums up knowledge about climate change.
No more greenhouse gas is released than is removed from the air again.

gewusst: Ice cores show that today's CO2 content of the air is the highest for at least 800,000 years.
Swiss researchers at the University of Bern have studied important ice cores from Antarctica.
In summer 2022, the freezing level over Switzerland was at times above 5,000 m.

teile.einleitung: On 28 May 2025, the Birch Glacier above Blatten in the Lötschental broke off. A huge mass of ice and rock buried a large part of the village, which had been evacuated beforehand thanks to good monitoring.
wichtigste: Blatten is the village furthest up the Lötschental in Valais.
Rockfalls from the Kleines Nesthorn loaded the Birch Glacier with debris.
On 19 May 2025, around 300 people were evacuated from Blatten.
Before it broke off, the glacier sped up to around 10 metres per day.
Experts call the event a rock and ice avalanche.
The debris dammed the River Lonza into a lake.

abschnitte.text: **Blatten** is the village furthest up the **Lötschental**. The valley is a side valley on the north side of the Rhône Valley in the canton of Valais. High above the village lies the **Birch Glacier**, below the Kleines Nesthorn. The **Lonza** flows through the valley.

abschnitte.titel: A glacier under a heavy load
abschnitte.text: From mid-May 2025, masses of rock kept breaking loose from the **Kleines Nesthorn**. The debris stayed on the Birch Glacier and pressed heavily on it. The glacier then slid down the valley faster and faster. Measurements at the front of the glacier showed it speeding up from a few metres to around **10 metres per day**. Such an acceleration is seen as a typical warning sign before a collapse.

Experts watched the slope closely. On 17 May, part of the village was cleared. On **19 May 2025**, nine days before the collapse, the whole village with around **300 people** was evacuated. Animals were also taken to safety. In this way, the monitoring prevented a much bigger disaster.

On 28 May 2025 the glacier broke off. A mixture of glacier ice and rock crashed and flowed into the valley. Experts call this a **rock and ice avalanche**. The masses buried a large part of Blatten. The cone of debris blocked the valley and dammed the **Lonza**. Behind it a lake formed, which flooded more houses.

Villages further down were evacuated as a precaution, because people feared the water might suddenly break through. However, the Lonza gradually found its way through the debris. At the end of May, the canton had the sluice gates of the **Ferden reservoir** opened. In this way the empty reservoir could take in water and debris and pass them on.

gewusst: The Blatten event attracted attention all over the world because the warning came so early.
Radar devices, cameras and drones helped with the monitoring.

teile.einleitung: Graupel, also called soft hail or snow pellets, are small, white balls of snow and ice. They fall from shower clouds, usually when it is cool. In Switzerland, graupel is often part of changeable April weather.
wichtigste: Graupel are small, round grains of snow and ice.
The grains are about 1 to 5 millimetres in size.
Graupel is smaller and softer than hail.
On hard ground, graupel grains bounce up.
Graupel is white because there is a lot of air inside the grains.
Graupel only rarely causes damage.

abschnitte.text: In a cloud there are snow crystals and very cold **water droplets**. The droplets are colder than zero degrees, but still liquid. When they collide with a snow crystal, they **freeze on at once**. More and more droplets stick to it, and the snow crystal turns into a round grain. This is how **graupel** forms.

Graupel grains are about **1 to 5 millimetres** in size, as small as pinheads or small peas. They are **white** and not see-through, because there is a lot of air inside them. You can easily crush them between your fingers. When they fall on a hard road, they **bounce up** like little balls.

Graupel and hail are often mixed up. **Hailstones** are hard and can get very big. They form in strong thunderstorms, mostly in summer. **Graupel** is smaller, softer and lighter. It falls more slowly than hail and so only **rarely causes damage** to cars, roofs or plants.

In **April**, the weather in Switzerland often changes quickly. One moment the sun is shining, then a dark cloud moves in. Short **showers** bring rain, graupel or even snow. Shortly afterwards it is bright again. This changeable **April weather** fits the German saying “April, April, der macht, was er will”, which means “April, April, does whatever it likes”.

gewusst: Graupel grains bounce on the ground, while snowflakes simply stay where they land.
There is so much air in graupel that it looks white and not see-through like ice.

teile.einleitung: Inside, crystals have a regular order. According to their symmetry, they are divided into seven crystal systems.
wichtigste: In a crystal, the building blocks are arranged regularly.
There are seven crystal systems.
The smallest repeating unit is called the unit cell.
Quartz belongs to the trigonal system, topaz to the orthorhombic and gypsum to the monoclinic system.
The cubic system has the highest symmetry.
Substances without a regular structure, such as glass, are called amorphous.

abschnitte.text: In a **crystal**, atoms or ions are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern. This pattern is called the **crystal lattice**. The smallest unit that repeats in all directions is called the **unit cell**. It is like a building block from which the whole lattice is put together. Its shape gives the **crystal system**.

In mineralogy there are **seven crystal systems**: cubic, tetragonal, hexagonal, trigonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic and triclinic. Each has its own **symmetry**. They are described using imaginary axes, their lengths and the angles between them. In the **cubic** system, all three axes are the same length and are at right angles to each other. It has the highest symmetry, and in the **triclinic** system the symmetry is lowest.

**Rock salt** and **pyrite** belong to the cubic system and often form cube-shaped crystals. Ordinary **quartz** forms six-sided crystals, but its symmetry is threefold. That is why it belongs to the **trigonal** system. **Topaz** forms long, column-like crystals and is **orthorhombic**. **Gypsum** is a well-known example of the **monoclinic** system, in which two axes are at a slant to each other.

Not all solid substances are crystals. In **amorphous** substances, the particles are disordered, a bit like in a liquid that has set. Well-known examples are **glass** and **opal**. That is why amorphous substances have no regular crystal faces. When they break, they often have curved fracture surfaces.

The science of the structure of crystals is called **crystallography**. It studies shape, symmetry and lattices. An important tool is **X-ray diffraction**. In this, X-rays are bent by the crystal lattice, and from the pattern the structure can be calculated. In the Swiss Alps, crystal hunters called **Strahler** search for beautiful crystals, especially **rock crystal**, a clear form of quartz.

gewusst: Cube-shaped pyrite crystals look as if someone had cut them artificially, but they grow like that in nature.
Rock crystal from the Alps is nothing other than especially clear quartz.

teile.einleitung: A doline is a funnel-shaped or bowl-shaped hollow in the ground. It forms in areas with easily dissolved rock such as limestone or gypsum. Such landscapes are called karst.
wichtigste: Dolines are hollows in karst areas.
A solution doline forms when rock is slowly dissolved from above.
A collapse doline forms when the roof of a hollow space caves in.
Dolines form in limestone, and especially quickly in gypsum.
Several dolines that have grown together make an uvala.
The word doline comes from Slovenian.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater takes up a little carbon dioxide from the air and the soil and so becomes slightly acidic. This means it can slowly dissolve **limestone**. **Gypsum** dissolves even more easily than limestone. That is why caves, cracks and hollows form in areas with such rock. These landscapes are called **karst**. Typical karst areas in Switzerland are in the **Jura** and in the **limestone Alps**.

In places where especially large amounts of water soak away, the rock is dissolved more strongly. The surface there sinks very gradually. This creates a bowl-shaped hollow, a **solution doline**. This process takes a very long time. Some areas are dotted with hundreds of such hollows.

Sometimes water dissolves a **hollow space** beneath the surface. If the roof above it becomes too thin, it caves in. A steep funnel forms, a **collapse doline**. This can happen suddenly. That is why dolines can be dangerous for **houses and roads**, because buildings or roadways can sink.

At the bottom of a doline there is often a **swallow hole**, also called a **ponor**. There a stream suddenly disappears into the ground and flows on underground. If several neighbouring dolines grow together, a larger, irregular hollow forms. It is called an **uvala**.

The word **“doline”** comes from **Slovenian**. There “dolina” means valley or hollow. Many technical words for karst come from the **Karst plateau** in Slovenia. These landforms were studied there early on. The word karst itself also goes back to this region.

gewusst: In karst areas there are often hardly any streams on the surface, because the water disappears underground.
The word uvala also comes from a South Slavic language.

teile.einleitung: The mantle is the thickest layer of the Earth and lies between the Earth's crust and the core. It reaches down to a depth of about 2900 km and makes up most of the Earth's volume. Although it is solid almost everywhere, its rock flows very slowly.
wichtigste: The mantle lies beneath the Earth's crust and goes down to about 2900 km.
It makes up about two thirds of the Earth's mass.
The upper mantle is made mainly of the rock peridotite.
The mantle is mostly solid, but over long periods it can slowly change shape.
Heat currents move the rock in the mantle by a few centimetres a year.
The boundary with the core is called the Gutenberg discontinuity.

abschnitte.text: The **mantle** begins below the Moho, that is, at a depth of 5 to 70 km depending on the place. It goes down to about 2900 km, where the core begins. It is divided into the **upper mantle** and the **lower mantle**. In between lies a transition zone at a depth of about 410 to 660 km.

The upper mantle is made mainly of **peridotite**, a greenish rock. Peridotite contains a lot of the mineral **olivine**, which is known as the gemstone peridot. Sometimes pieces of the mantle reach the surface through volcanoes or mountain building. In Switzerland, such mantle rocks can be found, for example, on the Totalp near Davos.

In the mantle, temperatures range from about 1000 °C at the top to about 4000 °C at the boundary with the core. Even so, the rock is **solid** almost everywhere, because the enormous pressure stops it melting. But over millions of years it changes shape like very stiff dough. Only in a soft zone beneath the lithosphere, the **asthenosphere**, is a small part melted.

Hot rock slowly rises, cools down and sinks again. This movement is called **mantle convection**, similar to water in a cooking pot. It is only a few centimetres a year fast, about as fast as fingernails grow. The currents help to move the **continental plates**.

Nobody has ever drilled down into the mantle. Researchers study it with **seismic waves**, which travel at different speeds depending on the rock. In this way, in 1913, Beno Gutenberg discovered the boundary with the core, which today is called the **Gutenberg discontinuity**. There certain waves stop, because the outer core is liquid.

begriffe.erklaerung: A greenish rock that makes up most of the upper mantle.
A cycle in which warm material rises and cold material sinks.
A soft zone in the upper mantle on which the tectonic plates glide.
The boundary between the mantle and the core, at a depth of about 2900 km.

gewusst: The mantle is so thick that it is greater than the distance from Zurich to Moscow.
The gemstone peridot is made of olivine, a typical mineral of the mantle.
The solid rock of the mantle flows about as fast as your fingernails grow.

teile.einleitung: A heatwave is a period of several very hot days in a row. Often it hardly cools down even at night. Heat can be tiring and dangerous for the body, so it is important to protect yourself well.
wichtigste: During a heatwave it is very hot for several days in a row.
From 30 °C, a day is called a hot day.
On a tropical night it does not cool down below 20 °C.
The highest temperature in Switzerland was measured in Grono in 2003: 41.5 °C.
In hot weather you should drink lots of water, even if you are not thirsty.
Babies and older people are especially at risk.

abschnitte.text: During a **heatwave** it stays very hot for several days. A day with at least **25 °C** is called a **summer day**. From **30 °C**, it is called a **hot day**. A night when it does not cool down below **20 °C** is called a **tropical night**. Then many people sleep badly. It is usually hottest in the **afternoon**, because the sun heats the ground and air all day long.

In summer **2003**, Europe had a very strong heatwave. On **11 August 2003**, **41.5 °C** was measured in **Grono** in the Misox valley, canton of Grisons. This is the highest temperature ever measured in Switzerland (as of 2026). There were several hot summers in the years that followed too. Experts expect heatwaves to become more frequent with **climate change**.

In hot weather the body **sweats** a lot. Sweat cools the skin, but you lose water. That is why you must **drink regularly**, even if you are not thirsty. Water or unsweetened tea is best. Tiring sport belongs in the cool morning hours. **Babies** and **older people** find it harder to cool down. They need special attention in hot weather.

In great heat, **light, pale clothing** is best. Light fabrics let air reach the skin, and pale colours heat up less. A **hat** protects your head from the sun. Sun cream protects your skin from sunburn. Around midday it is best to find some **shade**.

To keep it pleasant indoors, close the **windows and shutters** during the day. That keeps the sun out. It is best to air the rooms during the **cool night** or early in the morning. Shade helps in towns too: trees and green spaces cool the surroundings, while tarmac and concrete store the heat.

gewusst: The Swiss heat record was measured not in Ticino but in Grono in the Misox valley in the Grisons.
In hot weather, towns are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, because stone and tarmac store heat.

teile.einleitung: A carbon sink is a store that takes in more carbon dioxide from the air than it gives off. Oceans, forests and peat bogs are the most important natural sinks.
wichtigste: A sink removes more greenhouse gas from the air than it releases.
Together, oceans and land ecosystems take up about half of human CO2 emissions.
In the sea, the solubility pump and the biological pump are at work.
Peat bogs store a particularly large amount of carbon on only around 3 per cent of the land area.
A forest can become a source if it gives off more CO2 than it takes in.
Direct air capture filters CO2 out of the air using technology.

abschnitte.text: In climate policy, a **sink** is a process or store that removes more greenhouse gas from the atmosphere than it releases. Sinks store carbon in soils, plants or seawater, for example. A **source**, on the other hand, gives off greenhouse gases. Together, oceans and land ecosystems take up about **half** of human CO2 emissions. Without them, the CO2 content of the air would rise twice as fast.

Cold water can dissolve more CO2 than warm water. At high latitudes, cold surface water rich in CO2 sinks into the depths. This process is called the **solubility pump**. In addition, **plankton** binds CO2 through photosynthesis. Dead parts sink down and lock carbon away in the deep sea or in sediment. This is the **biological pump**.

Plants take in CO2 and store carbon in wood, leaves and the soil. A higher CO2 content makes it easier for many plants to grow. This is called the **CO2 fertilisation effect**, but it is limited by water and nutrients. **Peat bogs** store especially large amounts of carbon. In wet bogs, plant remains are hardly broken down and pile up as **peat**. On only around 3 per cent of the land area, they store more carbon than all the Earth's forests put together.

abschnitte.titel: When a sink becomes a source
abschnitte.text: Sinks are not safe forever. **Drought**, **fires** or **pests** can kill many trees. As the wood breaks down, more CO2 is then released than the forest still takes in. In this way the forest turns from a sink into a **source**. Drained peat bogs also give off large amounts of CO2. In Switzerland, many bogs used to be drained; today the remaining ones are protected.

In **direct air capture**, fans suck air through filters that bind CO2. It can then be stored permanently, but the process needs a lot of energy. A worked example shows what sinks do: if 40 gigatonnes of CO2 are emitted and half stays in the air, that is 20 Gt. If 1 ppm equals about 7.8 Gt of CO2, the content rises by around **2.6 ppm**.

gewusst: Peat bogs cover only a small part of the land, but they store more carbon than all forests together.
Without seas and forests, the CO2 content of the air would rise about twice as fast.

teile.einleitung: Gravimetry is the measurement of gravity. Gravity is not equally strong everywhere on Earth, because rocks have different densities and the Earth is not exactly round. From tiny differences, scientists can work out what the ground below is made of.
wichtigste: The unit of gravimetry is the gal; 1 gal equals 1 cm/s².
Usually milligals, thousandths of a gal, are used.
Gravity decreases with height, by around 0.3086 mGal per metre.
Under the Alps, the Bouguer anomaly shows strongly negative values because light crust reaches far down.
Salt domes produce a negative gravity anomaly.
At the poles, the acceleration due to gravity is greater than at the equator.
From 2002, the GRACE satellite mission measured changes in the gravity field.

abschnitte.text: The **acceleration due to gravity, g,** is around 9.8 m/s² on Earth. In gravimetry, very small differences from this are measured. For this the unit **gal** is used, named after **Galileo Galilei**. 1 gal equals 1 cm/s², and usually **milligals** are used. A **relative gravimeter** compares gravity at two places. An **absolute gravimeter** lets a mirror fall freely in a vacuum chamber and follows it with a laser. From the distance and time, g is worked out to within a few billionths.

The further you are from the centre of the Earth, the weaker gravity becomes. The **free-air gradient** is around **0.3086 mGal per metre**. So if you carry a gravimeter 200 m higher, you measure around 62 mGal less. That is why the height must be known very precisely during measurements. If the mass of the rock is also taken into account, you get the **Bouguer anomaly**. Under the Alps it is strongly negative. This is because mountains float on the denser mantle like icebergs, which is called **isostasy**. Their light root of crust reaches far down.

Rocks with low density weaken gravity slightly, and dense rocks strengthen it. A **salt dome**, for example, is made of rock salt with a density of around 2.2 g/cm³. It is lighter than the surrounding sedimentary rock. That is why a **negative anomaly** is measured above a salt dome. Such differences are used when searching for raw materials and when exploring the ground below.

The Earth is flattened at the poles. The poles are around 21 km closer to the centre of the Earth than the equator. In addition, there is no **centrifugal force** from the Earth's rotation there. That is why g is greater at the poles, at around 9.83 m/s², than at the equator, at around 9.78 m/s². The **geoid** is the surface of equal gravitational potential at sea level. It roughly matches the calm surface of the sea, imagined as continuing under the continents. Because masses are unevenly spread, it differs by up to around 100 m from a smooth ellipsoid.

From **2002**, in the **GRACE** mission, two satellites flew one behind the other around the Earth. When they fly over areas with more or less mass, the distance between them changes slightly. From these changes, the gravity field and how it changes were calculated. In this way, for example, **ice loss in Greenland** and changes in groundwater became visible.

gewusst: At the equator you weigh a tiny bit less than at the North Pole, because gravity is weaker there.
With satellites, scientists can measure how much ice Greenland is losing without touching the ice.

teile.einleitung: Eutrophication means that a body of water contains too many nutrients. Then algae and water plants grow too much, and oxygen is missing in the depths. Many Swiss lakes were heavily over-fertilised in the 20th century and have recovered since then.
wichtigste: Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen in a body of water.
In most Swiss lakes, phosphorus limits the growth of algae.
In 1986 the ban on phosphate in laundry detergents came into force in Switzerland.
When dead algae are broken down, bacteria use up a lot of oxygen.
A clear lake poor in nutrients is called oligotrophic.
Lake Baldegg and Lake Sempach have been artificially aerated since the 1980s.

abschnitte.text: Algae and water plants need nutrients to grow, especially **phosphorus** and **nitrogen**. Through fertiliser from fields and through waste water, too much of them gets into the water. Then algae grow too much, and the water becomes cloudy and greenish. This process is called **eutrophication**. In freshwater lakes phosphorus is usually the scarce nutrient. That is why even a little extra phosphorus sets off strong growth of algae.

abschnitte.titel: Lack of oxygen in the depths
abschnitte.text: Dead algae sink to the bottom of the lake. There they are broken down by **bacteria**, which use up a lot of **oxygen** in the process. Especially in summer, when the warm surface water does not mix with the cold deep water, oxygen soon runs short in the depths. Fish and other animals can no longer live there. Experts divide lakes into **trophic levels**: from **oligotrophic**, that is, poor in nutrients and clear, through mesotrophic and eutrophic to hypertrophic.

In the past, **phosphates from detergents** were a main source of over-fertilisation. In 1986 the **ban on phosphate** in laundry detergents came into force in Switzerland. At the same time, many **sewage treatment plants** were built and extended. In the chemical treatment stage, they remove phosphate through **precipitation** with iron or aluminium salts. This creates compounds that hardly dissolve and settle out as sludge. After that, the phosphorus levels in many lakes fell clearly.

Some lakes recover only slowly. In **Lake Baldegg** and **Lake Sempach** in the canton of Lucerne, oxygen was missing in the deep water because of over-fertilisation. That is why they have been **artificially aerated** since the 1980s, with oxygen being added. At the same time, efforts are made to let fewer nutrients from farming get into the lakes. Many Alpine lakes, on the other hand, are naturally oligotrophic.

In **Lake Murten** and other lakes, the cyanobacterium **Planktothrix rubescens** can multiply strongly. It then colours the water reddish. It is popularly called the **Burgundy blood alga**. The name recalls a legend: after the Battle of Murten in 1476, the lake is said to have been red with the blood of the Burgundians.

gewusst: The word “eutrophic” comes from Greek and means “well fed”.
Cyanobacteria are often called blue-green algae, but they are not real algae; they are bacteria.

teile.einleitung: In the mountains, masses of rock can break off and crash down into the valley. Experts watch dangerous slopes with measuring instruments so that people can be warned in time.
wichtigste: Unstable slopes are monitored with extensometers, radar and GNSS stations.
An extensometer measures how much a crack in the rock opens.
Ground-based radar measures almost without a break, satellites only every few days.
Threshold values automatically set off alarms or road closures.
During the rockfall at Piz Cengalo in 2017, the village of Bondo had been evacuated in time thanks to monitoring.
At Brienz/Brinzauls, a drainage tunnel greatly slowed down the landslide.

abschnitte.text: Rock often moves slowly for a long time before it breaks off. Water, frost and disappearing **permafrost** weaken the rock. If you measure these movements, you can recognise a fall early. In Switzerland, cantons, the Confederation and research institutes monitor many dangerous slopes. This makes it possible to protect villages, roads and railway lines.

An **extensometer** bridges a crack with a measuring wire or rod. If the crack widens, the instrument shows the movement to a fraction of a millimetre. **GNSS stations** use satellite navigation such as GPS. They work out their position all the time and so show the direction and speed of the movement in three dimensions. A **ground-based radar** opposite the slope measures every few minutes or so and also detects small changes.

The measurements are linked to **threshold values**. If the speed or the width of the crack reaches a set value, systems set off warnings, traffic lights or closures. Experts also use calculation methods to make predictions. In Fukuzono's **inverse velocity** method, the inverse of the speed is plotted against time. If the line heads towards zero, the approximate time of the fall can be estimated.

Near **Randa** in the Matter Valley, about 30 million cubic metres of rock fell in two events in 1991. They buried the railway line and dammed the River Vispa. Since then the rock face has been monitored scientifically. In August 2017 about 3 million cubic metres of rock broke off **Piz Cengalo** in the Val Bregaglia. Eight hikers died, and debris flows reached Bondo. Thanks to monitoring and warnings, the village had been evacuated in time.
