This time is called the **gold rush**. For Sutter himself the gold brought no luck, because the gold seekers took over his land.

gewusst: The California gold rush began on the land of a Swiss man, Johann August Sutter.
Gold still shines even after a very long time in water because it does not rust.

teile.einleitung: Ekman transport describes how the wind moves the water at the surface of the sea. The surprising thing is that, overall, the water does not flow in the direction of the wind but at right angles to it. The reason for this is the rotation of the Earth.
wichtigste: Ekman transport is caused by wind friction and the Coriolis force together.
In the Northern Hemisphere, water is carried at 90 degrees to the right of the wind direction.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the transport goes 90 degrees to the left.
The Ekman spiral shows how the direction of the current turns with depth.
The current gets weaker with increasing depth.
Fridtjof Nansen observed the effect, and Vagn Walfrid Ekman explained it in 1905.

abschnitte.text: When the wind blows over the sea, it drags the top layer of water along with it. Through **friction**, this layer passes the movement on to deeper layers. At the same time the **Coriolis force** is at work. It is caused by the rotation of the Earth and deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The interplay of these forces is called **Ekman transport**.

Each deeper layer of water is driven by the layer above it and is deflected further. That is why the direction of the current turns with depth like a spiral. This is called the **Ekman spiral**. At the same time each layer loses momentum through friction, so the current gets weaker further down. According to the ideal theory, the top layer flows at an angle of **45 degrees** to the wind. Averaged over the whole layer, the result is a transport at **90 degrees** to the wind direction.

The Norwegian polar explorer **Fridtjof Nansen** let his ship **Fram** drift in the pack ice of the Arctic Ocean. He noticed that the drifting ice did not move exactly with the wind, but a little to the right of it. In **1905** the Swedish scientist **Vagn Walfrid Ekman** explained this observation mathematically. The effect is named after him.

Ekman transport has big effects. If the wind blows parallel to a coast, it can drive the surface water away from the land out to sea. Then cold, **nutrient-rich deep water** rises. This is called **upwelling**. Such areas, for example off Peru, are particularly rich in fish. In the large **subtropical ocean gyres**, Ekman transport carries water towards the middle. Floating **plastic waste** collects there, for example in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

gewusst: Below about one hundred metres deep, you can often hardly feel the wind-driven current at all.
Nansen's Fram expedition lasted from 1893 to 1896.

teile.einleitung: Fossils are remains or traces of living things that lived a very long time ago and were preserved in rock. Thanks to them we know what dinosaurs, ancient fish or ammonites looked like. They are like windows into the Earth's past.
wichtigste: Fossils are the petrified remains or traces of living things from prehistoric times.
They are found most often in sedimentary rocks.
Ammonites were sea creatures with a spiral shell.
The science that studies fossils is called palaeontology.
Monte San Giorgio in Ticino is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its fossils.
Fossils help to work out the age of layers of rock.

abschnitte.text: A **fossil** is the remains of a living thing that is older than about 10,000 years. It can be bones, teeth, shells, leaves of plants or whole imprints. **Trace fossils** such as footprints or feeding tunnels count too. The word comes from the Latin fossilis and means “dug up”.

Usually an animal or a plant dies and is quickly covered by mud or sand. Over a long time these layers are pressed into **sedimentary rock**. Water with dissolved minerals gradually replaces the hard parts, and so they turn to stone. Soft body parts are only very rarely preserved, for example in **amber** or in mud with little oxygen.

**Ammonites** were sea creatures with a spiral shell and were relatives of today's squid and octopuses. They lived for over 300 million years and died out about 66 million years ago, together with the dinosaurs. Because there were many different species, they are well suited as **index fossils** for working out the age of rock. Other common fossils are shark teeth, sea urchins and trilobites.

**Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003. Fish and marine reptiles about 240 million years old from the Triassic were found there, for example the long-necked reptile Tanystropheus. In Frick in Aargau, many skeletons of the dinosaur **Plateosaurus** were discovered. In the Jura and the Alps, too, ammonites and shells are often found.

The science of fossils is called **palaeontology**. Palaeontologists carefully dig fossils out, clean them and compare them with living things today. In this way **evolution**, the development of life, can be traced over hundreds of millions of years. Fossils also show how the climate and the seas changed in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies living things of prehistoric times from fossils.
A fossil that only existed at a particular time and so reveals the age of a layer of rock.
Rock made of layers that were deposited and pressed together.
Fossilised tree resin in which insects are sometimes trapped.

gewusst: On high Alpine peaks you can find fossils of sea creatures, because the rocks used to be sea floor.
In Frick in Aargau there is a dinosaur museum with finds of Plateosaurus.
Some insects in amber are over 40 million years old and look almost alive.

teile.einleitung: The carbon footprint shows how many greenhouse gases a person, a product or a company causes. It helps us to understand which activities put a heavy burden on the climate. These include heating, travelling, eating and shopping.
wichtigste: The carbon footprint adds up all the greenhouse gases caused.
It is usually given in tonnes of CO2 equivalents per year.
Other gases such as methane or nitrous oxide are converted into their CO2 effect.
The bicycle has a very small footprint per passenger kilometre.
Beef usually has the largest footprint per kilogram of any food.
Embodied energy is the energy used to make, transport and dispose of products.
The oil company BP made the personal footprint well known from 2004.

abschnitte.text: The **carbon footprint** adds up all the **greenhouse gases** that someone or something causes. Greenhouse gases hold heat in the atmosphere and so warm the climate. The footprint includes, for example, **heating**, **transport**, **food** and **consumption**. You can calculate it for a person, a family, a product or a company. For a person it is usually given in **tonnes per year**.

As well as carbon dioxide, there are other greenhouse gases such as **methane** or **nitrous oxide**. For the same amount, they cause more warming than CO2. So that everything can be added up, their amount is converted into the equivalent amount of CO2. The result is called **CO2 equivalents**. In this way very different activities can be compared with each other.

Means of transport cause very different amounts of greenhouse gases. When you **cycle**, no fuel is burned. Only making the bike and a little extra food count. That is why the footprint per passenger kilometre is very small. Trains and buses also usually do better than cars, while air travel has a large footprint.

There are big differences in food too. **Cattle** need a lot of feed and land and give off methane. That is why a kilogram of **beef** causes many times the emissions of plant foods. The **season** also matters. In winter, no strawberries grow outdoors in Switzerland. They then often come by aeroplane or from heated greenhouses, which uses a lot of energy.

Every product contains **embodied energy**. This is the energy needed to make, transport and dispose of it, for example with a mobile phone or a house. It often makes up a large part of the footprint. The personal footprint became well known from **2004** through an advertising campaign with a calculator by the oil company **BP**. Critics say that this shifted responsibility from companies onto individual people. Others still find the calculator useful for understanding their own behaviour.

gewusst: A mobile phone causes a large part of its footprint while it is being made, before you even switch it on.
Methane from the stomachs of cattle is an important greenhouse gas.

teile.einleitung: Climate is the average weather in a place over a long time, usually over 30 years. While the weather changes every day, the climate describes what is typical for a place. The climate in the desert, for example, is hot and dry, while in Switzerland it is temperate.
wichtigste: Climate is the weather in a place averaged over at least 30 years.
Weather is what is happening outside right now; climate is what is normally the case there.
The climate depends on how close a place is to the equator, its height, the sea and the winds.
It gets about 0.6 °C colder for every 100 metres of height.
The Gulf Stream gives western Europe a milder climate.
Since pre-industrial times, Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the global average (as of 2024).

abschnitte.text: **Weather** describes the state of the air at a particular moment: rain, sun, wind or snow. **Climate**, on the other hand, is the average of the weather over at least 30 years. To work it out, measurements such as temperature, rainfall and hours of sunshine are compared. So a cold day in summer does not change the climate.

At the **equator**, sunlight hits the ground steeply, which is why it is hot there. Towards the poles it strikes at a slant and warms less. This creates **climate zones** such as the tropics, the subtropics, the temperate zone and the polar zone. Switzerland lies in the temperate zone, with four clear seasons.

With **height**, the temperature drops by about 0.6 °C per 100 metres. That is why it is much colder on the Jungfraujoch, at around 3,500 m, than in Bern. Seas also affect the climate, because they store heat. The **Gulf Stream** brings warm water from the Caribbean northwards and makes winters in western Europe milder.

Switzerland has very different climates in a small space. On the Swiss Plateau it is mild and damp, in the Alps cold and snowy. South of the Alps, in Ticino, it is sunnier and warmer, and even palm trees grow there. Inner Alpine valleys such as Valais are especially dry, because the mountains keep the rain off.

Since industrialisation, the climate has been getting warmer because of greenhouse gases. Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the global average (as of 2024). **MeteoSwiss** measures the climate with a dense network of weather stations. The series of measurements in Basel and Geneva goes back to the 18th and 19th centuries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The average weather in a place over at least 30 years.
A large area of the Earth with a similar climate.
A warm ocean current in the Atlantic that brings Europe a mild climate.
Water that falls from the air, for example rain, snow or hail.

gewusst: Without the Gulf Stream, western Europe would be much colder in winter, similar to parts of Canada.
Valais is one of the driest areas of Switzerland, even though it is surrounded by high mountains.
A saying goes: climate is what you expect, weather is what you get.

teile.einleitung: Granite is a very hard stone that formed deep inside the Earth from hot, liquid rock. It looks speckled and often glitters. There is a lot of granite in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: Granite is speckled and made of many small grains.
It cooled slowly from liquid rock deep inside the Earth.
Granite is very hard and is used for stairs, fountains and paving stones.
Small flakes of mica in granite glitter in the light.
Most granites are grey, some are reddish.
In the Alps, for example at the Grimsel and the Gotthard, there is a lot of granite.

abschnitte.text: Deep inside the Earth it is so hot that rock can melt. This liquid rock is called **magma**. When magma stays deep below the Earth's surface, it cools very slowly. Many crystals grow as it does so, and **granite** forms. Only much later does the granite reach the surface, when the rock above it is worn away.

If you look closely at granite, you can see many small **grains** in different colours. That is why it looks **speckled**. The light grains are mostly **quartz** and **feldspar**. Between them lie small flakes of **mica**, which glitter in the light. Many granites are **grey** with light and dark dots, but there is also reddish granite.

Granite is **very hard** and hardly wears down. That is why stairs, fountains and kitchen worktops are made from it. Many streets and squares are laid with granite **paving stones**. Bridges, walls and gravestones are also often made of granite, because they last so long.

There is a lot of granite in the Alps, for example in the area of the **Grimsel** and the **Gotthard**. There you can see large grey rock faces and slabs that have been ground smooth. The glaciers of the Ice Age polished the rocks round. The stone often called “Ticino granite” in Ticino, on the other hand, is mostly gneiss.

Because granite is so hard, there is a German saying, **“auf Granit beissen”**, which means “to bite on granite”. Nobody can bite into granite. Someone who “bites on granite” has **no success** with what they want. For example, if you ask your parents to let you go to bed late and hear a clear no, you are biting on granite.

gewusst: Deep inside the Earth, granite cools so slowly that the crystals have time to grow big enough to see clearly.
The stone in many old Swiss fountains and stairs is granite from the Alps.

teile.einleitung: A cold front is the boundary where cold air pushes forward against warm air. It often brings thunderstorms, gusts and then a noticeable drop in temperature.
wichtigste: At a cold front, cold air pushes under warm air like a wedge.
In summer it often brings thunderstorms and heavy showers.
After it has passed, the temperature falls and the air pressure rises.
On a weather map it is a blue line with triangles.
Cold fronts usually move faster than warm fronts.
Towering thunderclouds called cumulonimbus are typical.

abschnitte.text: A **front** is the boundary between two air masses. At a **cold front**, cold air pushes forward against warm air. Cold air is heavier. That is why it pushes under the warm air like a **wedge** and lifts it quickly. Cold fronts usually belong to a **low-pressure area**.

Because the warm air is lifted quickly and steeply, tall heaped clouds grow. The **cumulonimbus**, a towering thundercloud, is typical. It can reach up to the top of the lower atmosphere. That is why in summer a cold front often brings **thunderstorms**, heavy showers and sometimes hail. The wind picks up in **gusts** and usually turns from south-west to west or north-west.

Behind the cold front comes cooler air. In summer, the **temperature** can fall by ten degrees or more in a short time. Because the cold air is heavier, the **air pressure rises** again. Often the air becomes clear afterwards, and you can see a long way. In between, there may still be a few showers.

On a weather map, a cold front is drawn as a **blue line with triangles**. The triangles point in the direction in which the front is moving. The blue colour stands for cold air. A **warm front**, on the other hand, is red and has semicircles. This lets you see quickly which front is coming.

The heavy cold air pushes forward strongly. That is why the cold front usually moves **faster** than the warm front ahead of it. It often catches up with the warm front. Then an **occlusion**, a mixed front, forms. In Switzerland, cold fronts usually cross the country from the west or north-west.

gewusst: On a hot summer's day, a cold front can lower the temperature by ten degrees in one hour.
The cumulonimbus thundercloud can be more than ten kilometres tall.

teile.einleitung: A thunderstorm is a weather event with lightning and thunder, often together with heavy rain, hail and strong gusts of wind. Thunderstorms form in tall, towering clouds called cumulonimbus clouds. In Switzerland they happen mostly on hot summer days.
wichtigste: During a thunderstorm, flashes of lightning light up the sky.
The loud crash after a flash of lightning is called thunder.
The lightning arrives first because light is much faster than sound.
The safest place during a thunderstorm is inside a house.
In Switzerland there are most thunderstorms in summer.
A lightning conductor protects a house from lightning strikes.

abschnitte.text: On hot days, warm, moist air rises quickly. As it does so, it cools down, and a huge, tower-like cloud forms: the **cumulonimbus**. It can be over 10 km tall and take on the shape of an anvil at the top. Inside the cloud, ice grains and water droplets collide and become **electrically** charged.

A flash of **lightning** is a giant electrical discharge between a cloud and the ground or within the cloud. It heats the air in an instant to around 30,000 °C. The air expands explosively, and we hear this as **thunder**. Because light is much faster than sound, you always see the lightning first.

abschnitte.titel: How far away is the storm?
abschnitte.text: Sound travels about one kilometre in three seconds. If you count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder and divide by three, you get the **distance** in kilometres. If you hear the thunder less than about ten seconds after the lightning, the storm is already dangerously close. Then you should look for shelter at once.

The safest place is in a **house** or a closed car. Outdoors you should not stand under single trees, and you should leave lakes, rivers and mountain summits. If there is no shelter nearby, crouch down with your feet together. A **lightning conductor** on the roof leads the lightning current safely into the ground.

In Switzerland there are most thunderstorms in **summer**, especially in the afternoon and evening. They are particularly common in Ticino and along the Prealps. Thunderstorms often bring **hail**, which can damage fields, cars and roofs. MeteoSwiss warns of strong thunderstorms with storm warnings in its app.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tall, tower-like thundercloud.
An electrical discharge between clouds or between a cloud and the ground.
A loud bang caused when the air heated by lightning suddenly expands.
A metal rod with a wire that leads lightning safely into the ground.

gewusst: A flash of lightning is several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
A car protects you from lightning because its metal shell leads the current around the outside.
Around the world there are about 2,000 thunderstorms happening at any one moment.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's core is the innermost part of our planet, deep beneath our feet. It is made mainly of iron and nickel and is almost as hot as the surface of the Sun. No person has ever seen it, yet researchers know an amazing amount about it.
wichtigste: The Earth's core is the innermost layer of the Earth.
It is made mainly of the metals iron and nickel.
The Earth's core makes up about a third of the Earth's total mass.
It is about 5000 to 6000 °C hot in the Earth's core.
The outer core is liquid, the inner core is solid.
Despite the heat, the inner core is solid because the pressure there is enormous.
Currents in the liquid outer core produce the Earth's magnetic field.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is built in layers, like an onion or a peach. Right on the outside lies the thin **crust**, on which we live. Beneath it comes the thick **mantle** of hot rock. From a depth of about 2900 kilometres, the **core** begins. Its radius is about 3500 kilometres, so it is a little bigger than the Moon.

The Earth's core is made mainly of **iron** and **nickel**. It also contains smaller amounts of lighter elements such as sulphur or oxygen. These heavy metals sank to the middle when the Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, while the young Earth was still largely molten. Although the core takes up only about a sixth of the Earth's volume, it makes up about a third of the Earth's total **mass**. So it is much denser than the rock above it.

The core has two parts. The **outer core** is about 2200 kilometres thick and liquid. The **inner core** in the middle has a radius of about 1200 kilometres and is solid. It is about 5000 to 6000 °C hot in the core, similar to the surface of the Sun. Even so, the inner core stays solid, because the enormous **pressure** squeezes the iron particles together so strongly that they cannot become liquid.

In the liquid outer core, the hot metal is constantly flowing around. Because iron conducts electricity, these currents create electric currents and a **magnetic field**. This process is called the **geodynamo**. The Earth's magnetic field makes the compass needle point north. It also protects the Earth from the solar wind, which would otherwise slowly strip away the atmosphere.

Nobody can travel to the Earth's core; the deepest borehole goes down only just over 12 kilometres. That is why researchers use **seismic waves**, which travel through the whole Earth. Depending on the material, they become slower, faster or are bent. Certain waves cannot travel through liquids, and this is how it was recognised that the outer core is liquid. In this way the Danish scientist **Inge Lehmann** discovered the solid inner core in 1936.

Without the Earth's core there would be no magnetic field, and life on Earth would be more exposed to radiation from space. Many animals such as migratory birds, sea turtles or homing pigeons find their way using the **Earth's magnetic field**. The heat from inside the Earth also drives the movement of the tectonic plates, and with it volcanoes and earthquakes. Geothermal heat can also be used to heat houses. By the way, the magnetic poles slowly wander, and over the Earth's history the magnetic field has flipped many times.

begriffe.erklaerung: The innermost part of the Earth, made of iron and nickel.
The thick layer of hot rock between the Earth's crust and the core.
The process in which flowing liquid metal in the Earth's core produces the magnetic field.
The force with which something presses on a surface; unimaginably great in the Earth's core.

gewusst: The inner core is growing very slowly, because liquid iron at its edge gradually becomes solid.
Iron meteorites from space give researchers clues about how the Earth's core might be built.
It is about 6370 kilometres from the ground to the centre of the Earth, roughly as far as from Zurich to New York.

teile.einleitung: An island is a piece of land that is completely surrounded by water. There are islands in seas, in lakes and even in rivers.
wichtigste: An island is surrounded by water on all sides.
The largest island in Lake Zurich is Ufenau.
A group of many islands is called an archipelago.
An atoll is a ring-shaped island made of coral.
Iceland is a large volcanic island in the North Atlantic.
Giant tortoises live on the Galápagos Islands.

abschnitte.text: An **island** is land that is surrounded by water on all sides. It can be tiny or huge. The largest island on Earth is **Greenland**. Very large land masses such as Australia, on the other hand, are counted as continents. Many islands lie in the sea, others in lakes or rivers.

Islands form in different ways. Some are pieces of a continent that have been cut off by the sea. Others are **volcanic islands** that have grown up from the sea floor. One example is **Iceland** in the North Atlantic, with many volcanoes and hot springs. In warm seas, corals build ring-shaped islands called **atolls**. In their middle lies an area of water.

When many islands lie close together, they are called an **archipelago** or a group of islands. Greece, for example, has a great many islands in the Aegean Sea. The **Galápagos Islands** in the Pacific are an archipelago too. Famous **giant tortoises** live there, which can live to be over 100 years old.

Switzerland has islands too, in its lakes. The largest island in Lake Zurich is **Ufenau**. It belongs to the **canton of Schwyz** and can only be reached by boat, because there is no bridge to it. In Lake Maggiore lie the **Brissago Islands**, with a botanical garden. In Lake Lauerz lies the small island of Schwanau, with a ruined castle.

On remote islands there are often animals and plants that are found nowhere else. Because the sea separates them, they have developed in their own way over a long time. The Galápagos Islands are a well-known example. Many such islands are protected today.

gewusst: Greenland is the largest island in the world.
Ufenau in Lake Zurich does not belong to the canton of Zurich but to the canton of Schwyz.

teile.einleitung: An iceberg is a huge block of ice floating in the sea. It has broken off a glacier. The dangerous thing about it: most of it lies hidden under water.
wichtigste: Only about a tenth of an iceberg can be seen above the water.
Icebergs are made of fresh water, not of frozen seawater.
When a piece of ice breaks off a glacier into the sea, this is called calving.
Most large icebergs come from Greenland and Antarctica.
In warmer water an iceberg slowly melts.
Very old, dense ice can glow blue.

abschnitte.text: In **Greenland** and **Antarctica**, huge glaciers flow all the way into the sea. At the edge, large pieces of ice keep breaking off and crashing into the water. This process is called **calving**. This is how a new iceberg forms. In Antarctica, flat, very large icebergs sometimes break off; these are **tabular icebergs**.

abschnitte.titel: Only the tip can be seen
abschnitte.text: Ice is a little lighter than water, which is why it floats. But it is only a little lighter. That is why most of an iceberg is **under water**, and only about a tenth sticks out. This is where the saying “only the tip of the iceberg” comes from. It means that only a small part of a problem can be seen.

abschnitte.titel: Fresh ice in the salty sea
abschnitte.text: Although icebergs float in the salty sea, they are made of **fresh water**. Their ice formed from **snow** that built up on the glacier over many years. Very dense, old ice contains hardly any air bubbles. It swallows red light and therefore looks **blue**. When an iceberg drifts into warmer water, it melts bit by bit until nothing is left.

Because you cannot see most of an iceberg, icebergs are dangerous for ships. In 1912 the **Titanic** hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank. After that an international **ice patrol** was set up, which watches icebergs and warns ships. Today satellites and radar also help with this.

gewusst: Some icebergs from Antarctica are bigger than a whole Swiss canton.
When glacier ice melts it crackles, because old air bubbles under pressure burst.

teile.einleitung: Garnet is the name of a group of minerals with the same crystal structure. Many people know garnet as a red gemstone, but it comes in many colours. Garnet is hard and is also used in technology.
wichtigste: Garnet is a group of similar minerals with the same crystal structure.
Typical are roundish crystals with twelve diamond-shaped faces.
The name recalls the red seeds of the pomegranate.
Almandine is the most common garnet; pyrope is known as “Bohemian garnet”.
The rare demantoid is green.
Garnet is found especially often in metamorphic rocks such as gneiss.

abschnitte.text: Several minerals are grouped together under the name **garnet**. They have the **same crystal structure**, but a different make-up. That is why garnets come in many colours: red, orange, yellow, green and even almost black. Garnets often form roundish crystals with **twelve diamond-shaped faces**. This shape is called a **rhombic dodecahedron**.

Red garnet grains in rock look like the seeds of a **pomegranate**. Both names go back to the Latin word for **grain**. Anyone who sees a piece of rock with lots of small red garnets understands the comparison at once.

The most common garnet is **almandine**. It is deep red to purplish red and contains iron and aluminium. The fiery red **pyrope** was mined for centuries in Bohemia, in today's Czech Republic. As **“Bohemian garnet”**, it was made into traditional jewellery. **Demantoid** is rare and valuable. It is green and sparkles especially brightly.

Garnet often forms when rocks are changed deep inside the Earth under high pressure and high temperature. Such rocks are called **metamorphic**. Typical examples are **gneiss** and mica schist. In the Swiss Alps, small red garnet crystals turn up again and again in such rocks.

Garnet is **hard** and breaks into sharp-edged grains. That is why it is used as a **grinding and blasting material**. You find it on sandpaper. In **water jet cutting**, fine garnet sand is mixed with a very powerful jet of water. This can even cut through metal and stone.

gewusst: With garnet sand and a jet of water, thick steel plates can be cut.
Many people only know red garnet, but there are also green and yellow garnets.

teile.einleitung: Extreme weather means weather events that are much more violent than normal, for example tropical storms, tornadoes, heatwaves, heavy rain or hail. They can cause great damage and put people in danger. With climate change, some of these events are becoming more frequent or stronger.
wichtigste: Extreme weather means particularly violent and rare weather events.
Tropical storms are called hurricanes in the Atlantic and typhoons in the western North Pacific.
They typically only form when the sea temperature is about 26.5 °C or more.
Tornadoes are classified by their damage on the Enhanced Fujita scale.
In the summer of 2003 a long-lasting high-pressure area brought an extreme heatwave to Europe.
For every 1 °C of warming, air can hold about 7 per cent more water vapour.

abschnitte.text: Tropical storms form over warm seas with a water temperature of about 26.5 °C or more. In the Atlantic they are called **hurricanes**, in the western North Pacific **typhoons** and in the Indian Ocean cyclones. They do not form right at the equator, because the **Coriolis force** is zero there and the storm cannot start spinning. They bring hurricane-force winds, storm surges and huge amounts of rain.

A **tornado** is a narrow, fast-spinning whirl of air that reaches from a thundercloud down to the ground. Tornadoes are classified by their damage on the **Enhanced Fujita scale** from EF0 to EF5. Most occur in the USA, but weak tornadoes also happen in Switzerland. A **downburst**, on the other hand, is a strong gust that shoots down from a thundercloud and can knock down trees in rows.

In the summer of 2003 a long-lasting **high-pressure area** lay over Europe and brought weeks of heat. Record temperatures were measured in Switzerland, and tens of thousands of people in Europe died as a result. 2018 and 2022 were also very hot and dry in Switzerland. In a **drought** there is no rain for a long time, rivers carry little water and harvests suffer.

Warmer air can hold more water vapour: according to the **Clausius-Clapeyron relation**, about 7 per cent more for every 1 °C. That is why thunderstorms and rainfall can become more violent as the climate warms. **Heavy rain** leads to floods, debris flows and landslides. Hailstones can become as big as tennis balls and damage cars, roofs and fields.

In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss** warns of dangerous weather on five danger levels. The warnings appear in the MeteoSwiss app and on the federal natural hazards platform. During a storm, you should go into buildings, keep away from streams and follow the instructions of the authorities. Better **weather models** today help to predict extreme weather earlier.

begriffe.erklaerung: The deflection of winds by the rotation of the Earth.
A strong gust that rushes down from a thundercloud.
An area with high air pressure, usually with dry, sunny weather.
A long time without enough rain.

gewusst: No tropical storm can form right at the equator itself.
A downburst can produce winds as strong as a tornado.
In August 2003, 41.5 °C was measured in Grono in the canton of the Grisons, a Swiss heat record.

teile.einleitung: If you dig a deep hole in the ground, you can see layers of different colours. In scientific language these layers of soil are called horizons. Each layer is different and has its own job.
wichtigste: The layers of the soil are called horizons.
At the very top lies the dark topsoil, rich in humus.
Below it comes the lighter subsoil.
At the very bottom lies the solid parent rock.
Most earthworms live in the upper layers.
On building sites the topsoil is removed and stored.

abschnitte.text: You can see the layers of soil best if you dig a **deep hole**. In the wall of the pit you can make out stripes of different colours from top to bottom. Experts call these layers **horizons**. All the horizons together make up the **soil profile**. Every soil has a slightly different profile, depending on the rock, the climate and the plants.

At the very top lies the **topsoil**. Leaves and plant remains fall here. Small animals, fungi and bacteria break them down into **humus**. That is why this layer is usually the darkest and most fertile. Most **earthworms** also live here, because they eat plant remains and humus.

Below the topsoil lies the **subsoil**. It is **lighter** because it contains less humus. On the other hand, substances that rainwater has washed out from above often collect here. The roots of large plants reach down into the subsoil. There they find water and nutrients.

At the very bottom lies **solid rock**. The soil once formed from it, which is why it is called the **parent rock**. Over a very long time, the rock breaks down because of water, frost and plant roots. Slowly, new soil forms from it. One centimetre of soil often takes many decades or even longer to form.

The humus-rich topsoil is very valuable. That is why on **building sites** it is often removed first and stored. Later it can be used again for gardens and fields. In Switzerland there are rules so that this soil is not simply thrown away.

gewusst: A single spoonful of good garden soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth.
In scientific language, soil layers have letters; the topsoil, for example, is called the A horizon.

teile.einleitung: Erosion is the wearing away of soil and rock by water, wind, ice and gravity. Over thousands and millions of years it shapes valleys, gorges and strange rock formations. At the same time it can destroy fertile farmland.
wichtigste: Erosion is the wearing away of soil and rock.
Water, wind, glaciers and gravity are the main forces of erosion.
Before that, weathering breaks the rock into smaller pieces, for example through frost shattering.
The Colorado River carved out the Grand Canyon.
A thick covering of plants protects the soil best against erosion.
The earth pyramids of Euseigne in Valais were formed by erosion.

abschnitte.text: Before rock can be carried away, it first has to be broken into smaller pieces; this is called **weathering**. In **frost shattering**, water freezes in cracks in the rock, expands and splits the rock. Roots, heat, cold and chemicals in the rain also loosen rocks. **Erosion** then carries the loose pieces away.

Rivers and streams carry sand and stones along and so grind their beds deeper and deeper. In this way the **Colorado River** in the USA carved out the Grand Canyon, which is up to about 1800 m deep. In Switzerland, gorges such as the Aare Gorge near Meiringen or the **Viamala** in the Grisons were formed by water. Sea waves also gnaw at coasts and shape cliffs.

In dry areas, the wind blows sand away and grinds rocks as if with sandpaper. **Glaciers**, with the rubble they carry, scoop out whole valleys, which then have a U shape. Because of gravity, slopes slide down or stones fall. Rockslides and debris flows are fast forms of erosion in the Alps.

In the Val d'Hérens in Valais stand the **earth pyramids of Euseigne**. They are tall columns of soft moraine material that a glacier deposited in the Ice Age. On top of each column lies a large **capstone**, which protects it from the rain like a hat. All around, the rain has washed the soft material away; only under the stones has it stayed standing.

When rain or wind carries fertile farmland away, this is called **soil erosion**. New soil forms very slowly; a few centimetres take hundreds of years. A thick **covering of plants** protects the soil best, because roots hold it in place and leaves slow down the rain. That is why farmers plant cover crops or hedges and do not plough down the slope.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wearing away of soil and rock by water, wind, ice or gravity.
The breaking down of rock where it is, caused by weather, water and plants.
Freezing water expands in cracks and splits the rock.
Deposited material such as sand, gravel or mud.

gewusst: Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes and can split whole rocks in this way.
If the capstone of an earth pyramid falls off, the column is soon washed away by the rain.
The sand on the seashore is often the result of erosion that began in mountains long ago.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake drill, children at school learn what to do in an earthquake. If you have practised beforehand, you know straight away how to protect yourself in an emergency. The most important rules are simple.
wichtigste: In an earthquake at school, you first get under the table.
Under the table you protect your head and hold on.
Keep away from windows.
After the earthquake, do not use the lift but the stairs.
Outside, an open space is safest.
At the assembly point, wait until everyone is there.

abschnitte.text: When the earth shakes, things can fall from shelves and the ceiling. That is why at school you go straight **under a sturdy table**. With one arm you protect your **head**, and with the other hand you hold on to the **table leg**. That way the table does not slide away. You can remember this with three words: **drop, cover, hold on**.

Window panes can **break** in an earthquake. The splinters of glass are dangerous. That is why you keep away from windows, glass doors and tall cupboards. If you are in bed, it is best to **stay lying down** and protect your head with your **pillow**. Walking around in the dark would be more dangerous.

When the shaking is over, you leave the building calmly. You do not use the **lift**, because it can get stuck if the power fails. You go out by the **stairs**. Outside, you look for an **open space**, because nothing can fall on you there. Walls, trees and power lines can fall over.

Every school has an **assembly point**. There the teacher counts whether all the children are there. That is why you wait there until everyone has arrived, and do not simply run off. This way everyone knows for sure that nobody is missing. During a drill you also learn the way to the assembly point.

In a real earthquake you get a fright. If you have **practised** beforehand, you still do the right thing. There are a great many earthquakes in **Japan**. That is why all children there practise regularly how to protect themselves. There are earthquakes in Switzerland too, mainly in Valais, the Grisons and the Basel region.

gewusst: In Japan there is a national disaster prevention day with many drills every year on 1 September.
Many injuries in earthquakes are caused by objects falling down or toppling over.

teile.einleitung: A geyser is a hot spring that shoots a fountain of water and steam into the air from time to time. Geysers exist in only a few places in the world, for example in Iceland and in the USA.
wichtigste: A geyser shoots hot water and steam into the air.
The name comes from the Icelandic word “geysa”, meaning to gush out.
Strokkur in Iceland erupts about every 5 to 10 minutes.
Old Faithful in Yellowstone National Park erupts fairly regularly.
There are no natural geysers in Switzerland.
The water of a geyser is almost boiling hot.

abschnitte.text: Under a geyser there is a narrow channel, the **vent**, full of water. Deep down, the water is heated by hot rock. Because a lot of water presses down from above, it can get hotter than 100 °C without boiling. At some point steam forms and pushes the water upwards. Then a hot **fountain** with steam shoots into the air.

After the eruption, water flows back into the vent. There it is heated again. When it is hot enough, the geyser spouts once more. Even between eruptions you can often see **steam** above the pool, especially on cold days. The hot water in the pool steams all the time.

The word geyser comes from **Iceland**. The Icelandic word “geysa” means to gush out violently. The famous **Geysir** in Haukadalur gave its name to all the others. Right next to it lies **Strokkur**. It erupts about every 5 to 10 minutes and is therefore very popular with visitors.

In **Yellowstone National Park** in the USA there are a great many geysers. The best known is called **Old Faithful**. It erupts fairly regularly, which is how it got its name. Geysers need hot rock close to the surface. This is found in volcanic areas such as Iceland, Yellowstone or New Zealand.

The water of a geyser can be almost **boiling hot**. Anyone who goes too close can be badly scalded. That is why there are barriers and paths at geysers that you must not leave. In **Switzerland** there are no natural geysers because the hot rock lies too deep. There are warm springs, though, for example in thermal baths.

gewusst: More than half of all the geysers in the world are in Yellowstone National Park.
Strokkur often shoots its water 15 to 20 metres high.

teile.einleitung: A groundwater flow is groundwater that flows slowly underground through gravel and sand. In many Swiss valleys, such an invisible stream flows down the valley under the river. It is an important source of drinking water.
wichtigste: A groundwater flow moves underground through gravel and sand.
It flows very slowly, often only a few metres per day.
New water comes from rain soaking into the ground and from river water.
Clay lets almost no water through and dams the groundwater.
Around 80 per cent of Swiss drinking water comes from groundwater and springs.
Around groundwater sources there are the protection zones S1, S2 and S3.

abschnitte.text: In valleys there are often thick layers of **gravel and sand**. They have many spaces and let water through well. Such layers are called **aquifers**. In them, the groundwater flows slowly down the valley. This underground river is called a **groundwater flow**. The upper boundary of the water in the ground is the **water table**.

The groundwater has to squeeze through the narrow gaps between the grains. That is why it flows **very slowly**, often only **a few metres per day**. At the bottom, the groundwater flow is often bounded by a layer of **clay**. Clay is made of tiny particles with very small pores. Water can hardly get through, so the groundwater is dammed above it.

A groundwater flow constantly receives new water. **Rain** and **meltwater** soak into the ground. In many valleys, **water from the river** also seeps into the groundwater. In dry periods the water table falls, and after lots of rain it rises. Where a water-bearing layer reaches the surface, the groundwater comes out by itself. This place is called a **spring**.

According to the **Federal Office for the Environment**, around **80 per cent** of Swiss drinking water comes from groundwater, including spring water. The rest is mainly taken from lakes. Many municipalities pump their water from groundwater flows or use springs. Because gravel and sand filter the water, it is usually very clean.

To keep drinking water clean, there are **protection zones** around every groundwater source. The innermost one is **zone S1**, the area around the well itself. It is strictly protected and usually fenced off. Around it lie **zones S2 and S3**. There the rules are less strict but clear, for example for buildings, fertiliser or dangerous substances.

gewusst: Under many Swiss rivers flows a second, invisible stream of groundwater.
Groundwater often needs days to flow as far as you can walk in one minute.

teile.einleitung: Remote sensing means studying the Earth from a distance, usually from satellites or aircraft. Sensors measure light, heat or radar echoes and so show forests, cities, glaciers and seas.
wichtigste: Passive sensors measure sunlight or heat radiation; active ones send out radiation themselves.
Radar and lidar are active systems.
The vegetation index NDVI uses red light and near infrared.
The first Landsat satellite was launched in 1972.
Many satellites fly in a sun-synchronous orbit.
Hyperspectral sensors measure hundreds of narrow channels.

abschnitte.text: **Passive** sensors, for example optical cameras, measure the sunlight that the Earth reflects or the heat that it gives off. **Active** systems send out radiation themselves and measure the echo. These include **radar**, using microwaves, and **lidar**, using laser pulses. Radar also works at night and through clouds.

Healthy green leaves absorb red light strongly and reflect **near infrared** very strongly. The vegetation index **NDVI** compares these two values. This shows how thickly and healthily plants are growing. Pictures in the **thermal infrared** can be used to work out the surface temperature, for example to find warm cities or warm springs in lakes.

The **spatial resolution** tells you how big one pixel is on the ground. The **temporal** resolution says how often a place is photographed, and the **radiometric** resolution how finely the brightness is graded. The **spectral resolution** describes the number and width of the wavelength ranges measured. Multispectral sensors usually have 4 to 15 broad channels. **Hyperspectral** sensors measure hundreds of narrow channels and can even tell minerals apart.

abschnitte.titel: Orbits and long series of pictures
abschnitte.text: Many Earth observation satellites fly in a **sun-synchronous orbit**. They pass over every place at the same local time. This means the position of the Sun and the shadows are similar in repeated pictures and easy to compare. In 1972 the first **Landsat** satellite was launched. Since then the Landsat series has been delivering pictures that show changes on Earth over decades.

In **lidar** from an aircraft, a great many laser pulses are sent to the ground. Some of them get through gaps in the treetops down to the forest floor. Each pulse can produce several echoes, and the last ones often come from the ground. From this a **terrain model** without trees is calculated. Switzerland has also had its land surface measured precisely in this way.

gewusst: With lidar, researchers discover old paths and walls hidden under thick forest.
Radar satellites can measure whether the ground is rising or sinking by a few millimetres.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is not a country with a great many strong earthquakes, but it is not safe from them either. Hundreds of small earthquakes are measured every year, and now and then there is one that causes damage. The areas most at risk are Valais, the Grisons and the Basel region.
wichtigste: An earthquake of magnitude 6 or more can be expected in Switzerland about every 50 to 150 years.
An earthquake that causes damage is expected about every 8 to 15 years.
The areas most at risk are Valais, the Grisons and the Basel region.
Basel lies on the Upper Rhine Graben, where the Earth's crust is being pulled apart.
Since 2003 modern rules for earthquake-proof building have applied under the building standard SIA 261.
In March 2023 the Swiss Seismological Service published an earthquake risk model.

abschnitte.text: The Alps are forming because the African Plate is pushing against Europe. This builds up strains in the rock, which are released in earthquakes. The areas most at risk are **Valais**, the **Grisons** and the **Basel region**. Basel lies on the **Upper Rhine Graben**, a zone where the Earth's crust is being pulled apart. In the Central Plateau and in Ticino the hazard is lower, but not zero.

The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes all over the country. Most earthquakes are so weak that you cannot feel them. An earthquake that causes **damage** can be expected about every 8 to 15 years. A very strong earthquake of **magnitude 6** or more happens about every 50 to 150 years. Such an earthquake hit the city of **Basel** in 1356 and caused great destruction.

Experts distinguish between two terms. The **hazard** describes how often and how strongly the earth shakes in a place. The **risk** also says how great the damage to people and buildings would be. That is why the risk is higher in densely populated cities, because more people and property would be affected there. In March 2023 the Seismological Service published an **earthquake risk model** for the whole of Switzerland. It combines hazard, ground conditions, building methods and population.

It is not only the strength of an earthquake that counts, but also the **ground**. Soft ground such as **lake deposits** or river gravel can make the shaking up to about **ten times** stronger than on rock. The waves build up in it. That is why areas on lakeshores and in river valleys are hit harder in an earthquake. Many Swiss towns lie in exactly such places.

The first earthquake rules appeared in the Swiss building standards in 1989, but they were often not followed closely. Since **2003** modern requirements have applied under the standard **SIA 261**. A building survives an earthquake better if its floor plan is **regular** and the load-bearing walls run all the way from the roof to the foundations. Many older buildings were built without such rules.

gewusst: The Basel earthquake of 1356 is regarded as the strongest known earthquake in Central Europe north of the Alps.
About a thousand earthquakes are measured in Switzerland every year, and most of them are far too weak to be felt.

teile.einleitung: Karst is the name for landscapes in which water dissolves limestone. Caves, grooves in the rock and springs form, while often hardly any streams flow at the surface.
wichtigste: Karst forms when water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone.
Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide and can then dissolve limestone.
Caves, dolines, karren and karst springs are typical.
The water soaks away and flows off underground.
The Jura and parts of the Alps are important karst areas in Switzerland.
The Hölloch in the Muota Valley is one of the longest cave systems in Europe.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater takes up **carbon dioxide** from the air and the soil. This forms a weak **carbonic acid**. It can dissolve **limestone** very slowly. Over thousands of years, the water widens cracks in the rock in this way. Landscapes shaped like this are called **karst**. The name comes from a limestone landscape in today's Slovenia.

When rainwater runs over bare limestone, it etches sharp grooves and furrows into it. These are called **karren** or, in German, **Schratten**. The **Schrattenfluh** in the Entlebuch is named after them. **Dolines** are typical too: these are funnel-shaped hollows in the ground. In karst areas there are only a few streams at the surface.

Underground, large **cave systems** form. More than 200 kilometres of the **Hölloch** in the Muota Valley in the canton of Schwyz have been surveyed. It is the second-longest cave system in Europe (as of 2022). On the northern shore of Lake Thun you can visit the **St. Beatus Caves**. Dripstones grow in many caves: **stalactites** hang from the ceiling, and **stalagmites** grow up from the floor.

In karst areas, rainwater quickly **soaks away** into cracks and caves. It flows on underground and comes out again at **karst springs**. Because it flows so fast, it is hardly filtered by fine layers of soil. That is why drinking water from karst springs is **easily polluted**. If harmful substances get into the ground, they often reach the spring quickly.

The **Jura** is built mainly of limestone. That is why there are many caves, dolines and karst springs there. Karst is also widespread in the limestone Alps, for example in the Muota Valley or at the Schrattenfluh. Cave explorers in Switzerland keep discovering new passages.

gewusst: Cave explorers are still exploring the Hölloch, and it keeps getting longer as they do.
In some karst areas, a whole stream suddenly disappears into the ground.

teile.einleitung: A thin section is a wafer-thin slice of rock that is glued onto a glass slide. When ground so thin, most minerals let light through. Under the microscope you can then see what a rock is made of.
wichtigste: A standard rock thin section is about 30 micrometres thick, that is, 0.03 millimetres.
Only when they are this thin do most minerals become see-through.
In the past the slices were glued on with Canada balsam, today mostly with epoxy resin.
Between crossed polarisers, minerals show typical interference colours.
From about 1850 Henry Clifton Sorby made thin sections usable for the study of rocks.
Archaeology also uses thin sections, for example of pottery fragments.

abschnitte.titel: How a thin section is made
abschnitte.text: First a small slab is sawn from the rock. One side is ground smooth and glued onto a glass **microscope slide**. Then the slab is ground thinner and thinner until it is only about **30 micrometres** thick. Traditionally **Canada balsam**, a clear resin from the balsam fir, was used as the glue. Today **epoxy resin** is mostly used.

The thin section is studied with a **polarising microscope**. It only lets through light that vibrates in one particular direction. When two such filters are crossed, many minerals show glowing **interference colours**. These colours depend on the **double refraction** of the mineral and on the thickness of the section. That is why the same standard thickness is so important. Quartz, for example, appears grey to white at standard thickness.

Some minerals, especially **ore minerals**, stay black even in a thin section. They are called **opaque**. They are studied in **reflected light** on polished sections. Researchers look at how strongly and in what colour they reflect light. To work out the shares of the minerals, there is the **point counting method**: at many points on a grid, you count which mineral is under the crosshairs.

From about 1850 the British natural scientist **Henry Clifton Sorby** from Sheffield was the first to study rocks systematically under the microscope. He is regarded as the founder of microscopic **petrography**, the study of rocks. Today geologists use thin sections all over the world. **Archaeology** also uses them: the grains in the clay of pottery fragments reveal where the raw material came from.

gewusst: A thin section is thinner than a human hair.
Sorby also studied steel under the microscope and is therefore also seen as a pioneer of metallography.

teile.einleitung: A mountain lake lies high up in the mountains. It is often small, cold and very clear. There are hundreds of such lakes in Switzerland, and many of them formed in the Ice Age.
wichtigste: A mountain lake is a lake high up in the mountains.
Many mountain lakes are filled with meltwater from snow and glaciers.
During the Ice Age, glaciers scooped out many hollows.
Fine rock flour colours some mountain lakes turquoise.
When there is no wind, the mountains are reflected in the still water.
The Oeschinensee lies above Kandersteg in the Bernese Oberland.

abschnitte.text: Many mountain lakes formed during the **Ice Age**. At that time huge **glaciers** covered the Alps. The heavy ice ground deep hollows into the rock. When the glaciers melted, these hollows filled with water. Other mountain lakes formed because a rockslide or glacier rubble blocked a valley.

The water in mountain lakes is usually very cold. It often comes from **snow and glaciers**. Also, it is cool high up, and many mountain lakes are frozen over for months. Because little dirt gets in, the water is often very clear. When there is no wind, the surface is as smooth as a **mirror**, and you can see the mountains in it.

Some mountain lakes glow **turquoise**. The reason is fine **rock flour**. Glaciers grind the rock beneath them into very fine dust. This floats in the water and scatters the sunlight. That makes the lake look a glowing colour.

One of the best-known mountain lakes in Switzerland is the **Oeschinensee** above **Kandersteg** in the Bernese Oberland. It is surrounded by high rock walls. In summer many people hike there, and in winter it freezes over.

Only animals that can cope with the cold live in the cold water. One of them is the **trout**. It likes cold water that is **rich in oxygen**. This is because cold water can hold more oxygen than warm water. That is why trout like living in mountain lakes and mountain streams.

gewusst: Some mountain lakes are covered with ice for more than half the year.
The turquoise colour of many glacier lakes comes from tiny grains of rock in the water.

teile.einleitung: A river is a larger flowing body of water that flows from a source to a mouth. Rivers shape landscapes, supply water and energy and are home to many animals. Switzerland is often called the water tower of Europe, because large rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhône rise here.
wichtigste: A river begins at its source and ends at its mouth.
A small river is called a stream.
The edge of a river is called its bank.
The Rhine, one of the largest rivers in Europe, flows through Basel.
The Rhine, Rhône, Inn and Ticino rise in Switzerland.
Rivers supply drinking water and electricity and are home to fish and other animals.

abschnitte.text: A river begins at its **source**, where water comes out of the ground or a glacier melts. Many small **streams** gradually turn into a larger river. At the end it flows at its **mouth** into another river, a lake or the sea. The Aare, for example, flows into the Rhine at Koblenz in the canton of Aargau.

The water flows in the **riverbed**, and the edges on the left and right are called **banks**. Smaller rivers that flow into a larger one are called **tributaries**. All the areas from which water reaches a river together form its catchment area. In its upper course a river flows steeply and fast, in its lower course wide and slowly.

The **Rhine** rises in the Grisons, flows through Lake Constance and past Basel to the North Sea. The **Rhône** begins at the Rhône Glacier and flows through Valais and Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean. At about 290 km, the **Aare** is the longest river that runs entirely within Switzerland. The Inn flows via the Danube into the Black Sea, and the Ticino via the Po into the Mediterranean.

Fish such as trout, grayling and barbel live in rivers. On the banks, kingfishers, grey herons and beavers hunt. In the past many rivers in Switzerland were straightened and dammed, so animals lost their habitat. Today, through **river restoration**, rivers are being given more space again.

Many cities such as Basel, Bern or Geneva lie on rivers, because water used to be a trade route and a source of energy. Today rivers drive **hydroelectric power stations** that produce electricity. Cargo ships sail on the Rhine from Basel to Rotterdam. In summer, swimming in the Rhine in Basel and in the Aare in Bern is very popular.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place where a river or stream begins.
The place where a river flows into another body of water.
A river that flows into a larger river.
The area from which all the water flows into a particular river.

gewusst: Water from Switzerland flows into the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Adriatic and the Black Sea.
At Koblenz AG, the Aare often carries more water than the Rhine, which it flows into.
From Basel onwards, the Rhine can be used by large cargo ships.

teile.einleitung: Lake Maggiore is a large, long lake at the southern foot of the Alps. Its northern part lies in Ticino, but most of it belongs to Italy.
wichtigste: About a fifth of the lake's area belongs to Switzerland.
The Ticino town of Locarno lies at its northern end.
The lake is around 64 kilometres long and up to 372 metres deep.
Its bottom lies well below sea level.
It is the second-largest lake in Italy after Lake Garda.
The Brissago Islands are in the Swiss part, and the Borromean Islands in the Italian part.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Maggiore** lies at the southern foot of the Alps. About **a fifth** of the lake's area belongs to the **canton of Ticino**, and most of it to Italy. By area it is the **second-largest lake in Italy**; only Lake Garda is bigger. Its name means “bigger lake”. The shore of the lake is also the lowest point in Switzerland.

Lake Maggiore is around **64 kilometres** long, but only up to 10 kilometres wide. It reaches from Ticino far into Italy. At its deepest point it is **372 metres** deep. Because the surface of the lake lies just under 200 metres above sea level, its bottom is well **below sea level**. It formed when glaciers carved out a deep valley during the Ice Age.

Several large rivers flow into the lake. From Switzerland come the **Ticino** and the **Maggia**. From Italy, the **Toce** flows in from the Ossola Valley. On average it even brings a little more water than the Ticino. At the southern end, the Ticino leaves the lake again and later flows into the Po.

The Ticino town of **Locarno** lies at the northern end. Its Piazza Grande is famous for the **film festival**. Other places on the Swiss shore are Ascona and Brissago. Thanks to the mild climate, palm trees and camellias grow here. Many people from German-speaking Switzerland spend their holidays here.

The **Brissago Islands** lie in the Swiss part. A **botanical garden** grows on them, with plants from many warm parts of the world. You can reach them by boat, for example from Brissago or Locarno. In the Italian part, off Stresa and Verbania, lie the **Borromean Islands**. The best known is **Isola Bella**, with a palace and magnificent gardens.

gewusst: The lowest point in Switzerland lies on the shore of Lake Maggiore, at about 193 metres above sea level.
The bottom of Lake Maggiore lies lower than sea level, although the lake is far inland.

teile.einleitung: Normally the air gets colder the higher you climb. In a temperature inversion it is the other way round: warmer air lies above cold air at the ground.
wichtigste: Inversion means reversal: the temperature rises with height instead of falling.
A ground inversion forms on clear nights when the ground gives off heat.
A subsidence inversion forms in high-pressure areas because of sinking air that warms up.
The inversion layer acts like a lid and stops air from rising.
That is why in winter there is often low cloud over the Swiss Plateau while the mountains are in the sun.
A cold front with wind often ends the inversion.

abschnitte.text: In the lower layer of air, it normally gets a little colder with every metre of height. In an **inversion** it is the other way round: above the cold air at the ground lies a **warmer layer**. The word inversion means reversal. Warm air is lighter than cold air. That is why this situation is very **stable**, and the air hardly mixes.

On clear nights without clouds, the ground gives off a lot of heat as radiation. This makes the lowest air cool down strongly. That creates a **ground inversion**. In a **high-pressure area**, on the other hand, air sinks over a large area. As it sinks, it is squeezed together and warms up. This forms a warm barrier layer above the cooler air at the ground: the **subsidence inversion**.

abschnitte.titel: Low cloud over the Swiss Plateau
abschnitte.text: In winter, cold, damp air often collects on the **Swiss Plateau**. Above it lies a warm, dry layer. The **low cloud** reaches exactly up to the underside of the inversion. Anyone who travels up the **Rigi** or another mountain gets above the sea of fog into the sun. Up there it can be warmer than in Lucerne. In hollows and valleys, **cold air pools** also form, where frost and fog are more common.

The inversion layer works like a **lid**. Rising air is held back, and exhaust fumes stay trapped underneath. That is why **air pollution** rises during long inversions. A well-known example is the **“Great Smog”** in London in December 1952. At that time, an inversion trapped smoke from coal fires over the city for days. Thousands of people died as a result.

An inversion can last for days or even weeks. Often a passing **cold front** with wind ends it. The wind mixes the cold air at the ground with the air above. After that the low cloud also clears. Sometimes the **foehn** helps to drive the cold air out of the valleys.

gewusst: During an inversion, it can be several degrees warmer on a mountain top than in the valley below.
Seen from mountain tops, the sea of fog over the Swiss Plateau looks like a white lake.

teile.einleitung: The Keeling Curve shows how much carbon dioxide there is in the air. It is based on measurements on a volcano in Hawaii that have been running since 1958.
wichtigste: The Keeling Curve shows the CO2 content of the air.
It is measured on the volcano Mauna Loa in Hawaii.
It is named after the chemist Charles David Keeling.
The measurements began in 1958 at around 315 ppm.
The annual average for 2024 was just under 425 ppm (as of 2024).
Every year the curve shows a small up and down, because plants take up CO2 in summer.

abschnitte.text: The **Keeling Curve** shows the measured amount of **carbon dioxide** (CO2) in the atmosphere. Since measurements began, it has been rising steadily. It is the longest unbroken series of direct measurements of CO2 in the air. That is why it is seen as one of the most important records in climate research.

The values are measured on **Mauna Loa**, a volcano in **Hawaii**. The observatory lies at a height of around 3,400 metres, far from large cities. There the air is well mixed and hardly affected by exhaust fumes from nearby. That is why the measurements show well how the air of the whole Earth is changing.

The curve is named after the American chemist **Charles David Keeling**. He began the precise measurements in **1958** and continued them until his death in 2005. Today his son, among others, carries on the work. CO2 is also measured in many other places, in Switzerland for example on the **Jungfraujoch**.

The curve does not rise evenly but shows a small **wave** every year. There are far more land plants in the Northern Hemisphere than in the Southern Hemisphere. When they grow in summer, they take up CO2, and the value falls. In autumn and winter, CO2 is released again as the leaves rot. That is why the value reaches its peak each year in **May**, before the plants grow strongly.

The unit **ppm** stands for **parts per million**. 420 ppm means that out of a million particles of air, 420 are carbon dioxide. When measurements began in 1958, the value was around **315 ppm**. The annual average for 2024 was just under **425 ppm** (as of 2024). The rise comes mainly from burning coal, oil and gas.

gewusst: The CO2 content of the air is higher today than it has been for hundreds of thousands of years.
The Keeling Curve looks like a rising saw, because summer and winter show up every year.

teile.einleitung: A mountain pass is a way across the mountains from one valley to another. In Switzerland many passes connect the parts of the country, for example the north with Ticino.
wichtigste: A pass is a lower place between mountains over which a path leads.
A pass connects two valleys.
The Gotthard Pass connects Uri with Ticino.
Many passes are closed in winter because of snow and avalanches.
On passes there were hospices where travellers found shelter.
The Julier Pass leads from Tiefencastel to the Upper Engadine.

abschnitte.text: A **pass** is a lower place between mountains. There a path or road leads up from one valley and down the other side into another valley. In this way a pass connects **two valleys**. Thousands of years ago people were already using passes to cross the Alps. Traders carried goods over the mountains with pack animals.

The **Gotthard Pass** leads from Andermatt in the canton of Uri to Airolo in Ticino. It is one of the best-known passes in the Alps. Over the **Julier Pass** you drive from Tiefencastel to Silvaplana in the Upper Engadine and on to St Moritz. Other well-known passes are the Great St Bernard, the Simplon, the San Bernardino and the Furka Pass.

abschnitte.titel: The hospice and the St Bernard dogs
abschnitte.text: A **hospice** is an inn on a pass. In the past travellers found food and a warm bed there. The hospice on the **Great St Bernard** is famous. The monks there bred the **St Bernard dogs**. In the past the dogs helped to find travellers in the snow.

On steep slopes the road winds back and forth in many tight bends. These bends are called **hairpin bends** or switchbacks. This makes the road less steep. So that people can get through the Alps safely in winter too, **tunnels** were built. Today railway and road tunnels lead through the Gotthard.

In winter there is a lot of **snow** on the passes. **Avalanches** make the roads dangerous. That is why many pass roads are closed in autumn and only opened again in late spring or early summer. Some passes, for example the Julier Pass, are also kept open in winter when the weather allows.

gewusst: At 57 km, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
The Romans already built paths over Alpine passes such as the Great St Bernard.

teile.einleitung: A hot spring is a spring from which warm water comes out of the ground. The water is heated deep down by warm rock. Even the Romans bathed in such water in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The heat deep inside the Earth warms the water of a hot spring.
Minerals such as lime or sulphur are often dissolved in the water.
In Baden in Aargau, even the Romans bathed in the warm spring water.
Leukerbad in Valais is known for its many hot springs.
The warm spring in the Tamina Gorge supplies the thermal baths in Bad Ragaz.
In Japan, a bath in a hot spring is called an onsen.

abschnitte.text: The deeper you go into the Earth, the **warmer** it gets. Rainwater soaks away and can get very deep into the rock. There it is heated by the warm rock. It rises up again through cracks and comes out as a **hot spring**. On its long journey, the water dissolves **minerals** such as lime or sulphur. That is why some spring water smells of sulphur.

In the town of **Baden** in the canton of Aargau there are hot springs that even the **Romans** knew about. They built baths there. The name of the town recalls bathing (“baden” means “to bathe” in German). A bath with warm water from the ground is called a **thermal bath**. “Thermal” means warm. Today there is a modern thermal bath in Baden again.

In Valais, **Leukerbad** is known for its many hot springs. There are large thermal baths where you can lie in warm water in the middle of the mountains. A warm spring also rises in the wild **Tamina Gorge** near Bad Ragaz. Its water is piped all the way to **Bad Ragaz**, where it fills a well-known thermal bath.

In **Japan** there are thousands of hot springs. A bath in one is called an **onsen** and is very popular with many people. **Snow monkeys** also live in the mountains of Japan. In the cold winter they like to sit in hot springs to warm up. Photos of them are famous all over the world.

In winter, hot springs **steam** especially strongly. The warm water gives off water vapour. In the **cold air**, this cools quickly and becomes visible as mist. That is why you often see thick clouds of steam above thermal baths on cold days. In summer the same steam can hardly be seen.

gewusst: The Romans called Baden “Aquae Helveticae”, which means “waters of the Helvetii”.
Snow monkeys in Japan warm themselves in hot springs in winter.

teile.einleitung: Calcite is one of the most common minerals on Earth. It is made of calcium carbonate and builds up limestone, marble and stalactites and stalagmites. Clear calcite crystals play an amazing trick with light.
wichtigste: Calcite is made of calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3.
It is also called calc-spar.
On the Mohs scale it has a hardness of 3.
Calcite fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid.
Clear calcite shows double refraction: writing appears twice.
Limestone, marble and dripstones are made mainly of calcite.
Aragonite has the same formula but a different crystal structure.

abschnitte.text: **Calcite** is made of **calcium carbonate** with the formula **CaCO3**. Another name for it is **calc-spar**. On the **Mohs scale**, calcite is the reference mineral for hardness 3. You can only just scratch it with a copper coin, and easily with a knife. Calcite is often white or colourless, but it can also be yellow, pink or other colours.

If you put a drop of **dilute hydrochloric acid** on calcite, it foams and fizzes. The acid breaks down the calcium carbonate. In doing so, **carbon dioxide** escapes in small bubbles. With this simple test, geologists can recognise limestone rocks even out in the field.

If you look at writing through a clear calcite crystal, you see it **twice**. The crystal splits every ray of light into two rays. This is called **double refraction**. It is especially clear in **Iceland spar**. When calcite is split, it breaks into **slanted cubes**, so-called **rhombohedra**, because it splits in three directions that are not at right angles.

**Limestone** often forms from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. **Marble** forms when limestone is changed by pressure and heat. Both are made mainly of calcite. Large parts of the Jura and of the limestone Alps of Switzerland are built of limestone. That is why calcite plays a big part in the Swiss landscape.

Rainwater dissolves lime in the rock. When it drips down in a cave, the dissolved mineral is deposited again. This is how **stalactites and stalagmites** grow, for example in the **Hölloch** cave in the Muotathal. The mineral **aragonite** has the same formula as calcite but a different crystal structure. Mussels build their shimmering **mother-of-pearl** from tiny plates of aragonite.

gewusst: Limescale in a kettle is also mostly calcium carbonate.
Centuries ago, researchers were already studying double refraction in Iceland spar.

teile.einleitung: An erratic boulder is a large stone that does not match its surroundings. Glaciers often carried it a long way during the Ice Age and left it behind when they melted.
wichtigste: Erratic boulders were carried long distances by glaciers.
Experts call them erratic blocks; erratic means “strayed”.
In Switzerland there are particularly many erratic boulders in the Central Plateau.
Erratic boulders show how far the glaciers used to reach.
Some erratic boulders are as big as a house.
The Pierres du Niton lie in the harbour of Geneva.

abschnitte.titel: A stone in the wrong place
abschnitte.text: An **erratic boulder** is often made of a different rock from the ground around it. It lies there as if someone had put it down, as if it had been found. That is why in German it is called a “Findling”, a foundling. Experts also say **erratic block**. Erratic means “strayed”: the stone lies far away from its home.

During the **Ice Age**, the glaciers from the Alps reached far into the Central Plateau. Boulders fell onto the ice or were dragged along by the glacier. Glaciers usually flow only a few metres to a few hundred metres a year. So the stones needed many hundreds of years or longer for a long journey. When the ice melted, the boulders were simply left lying there.

In Switzerland there are particularly many erratic boulders in the **Central Plateau** and at the foot of the Jura. Glaciers carried the stones to their edges. That is why erratic boulders show how far the ice used to reach. If you identify the rock, you also know which Alpine valley it came from. In this way erratic boulders helped people to discover the ice ages in the first place.

In the harbour of **Geneva**, two large erratic boulders stick out of Lake Geneva, the **Pierres du Niton**. A glacier carried them there from the Mont Blanc area. Some erratic boulders are huge, weigh many tonnes and are as big as a house. Many are protected today.

In the past people did not know that glaciers had brought the stones. That is why **legends** told of giants or the devil who had thrown the boulders. Only in the 19th century did researchers realise that the ice had carried the stones. Some erratic boulders still have names from such stories today.

gewusst: The Pierres du Niton were for a long time the starting point for measuring heights in Switzerland.
Some erratic boulders in the Central Plateau have travelled more than a hundred kilometres.

teile.einleitung: A floodplain is an area beside a river that is flooded again and again. Floodplains are among the habitats with the most species in Switzerland, and at the same time they protect against floods.
wichtigste: Floodplains lie along rivers and are regularly flooded during high water.
Willows and poplars are typical of the softwood floodplain forest.
Floodplains hold back floodwater and slow down the flood wave.
Floods keep creating new habitats for many species.
Since 1992 the most important floodplains have been listed in a federal inventory.
Well-known floodplains are the Bolle di Magadino and the Pfynwald.

abschnitte.text: **Floodplains** lie along rivers and streams. During **floods** they are regularly covered with water and then dry out again. The river deposits gravel and sand, tears away trees and digs new channels. So a floodplain is always changing. This **dynamism** is what makes it special.

Right next to the water grows the **softwood floodplain forest**. **Willows** and **poplars** are typical. They can bear long floods and grow quickly. A little further away from the river, where water reaches less often, comes the **hardwood floodplain forest** with trees such as ash and oak.

Floods keep creating new and varied habitats: **gravel banks**, **ponds**, wet and dry places, young and old woods. In this **patchwork** a particularly large number of animal and plant species live. The **beaver** also helps to shape floodplains. It had died out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from **1956**. With its dams it holds back streams and creates new wetlands.

In a floodplain, a river can **spread out** during a flood. The water is held back, and downstream the water levels rise less. Many rivers in Switzerland were straightened and dammed in the past. Today some are being **restored** so that they get more space.

Since **1992** the most valuable floodplains have been listed in the **Federal Inventory of Alluvial Zones of National Importance**. The cantons have to preserve them and, where possible, improve them. In Ticino, the **Bolle di Magadino** lie where the River Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore, a resting place for many migratory birds. In Valais, the Rhône is still allowed to split into branches in the **Pfynwald**, in the **Pfyn-Finges** nature park.

gewusst: A large part of Switzerland's former floodplains has disappeared because of river engineering.
