The Bolle di Magadino are also protected internationally as a wetland.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's crust is the outermost, solid shell of our Earth. Mountains, cities and forests stand on it, and the sea floor belongs to it too. Compared with the whole Earth, it is as thin as the skin of an apple.
wichtigste: The Earth's crust is the top layer of the Earth and is made of solid rock.
There is the thin oceanic crust and the thicker continental crust.
The oceanic crust is about 5 to 10 km thick.
The Earth's crust is thickest under high mountains, often 60 to 70 km.
The most common element in the Earth's crust is oxygen, the most common metal is aluminium.
The boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle is called the Moho.

abschnitte.titel: The thin skin of the Earth
abschnitte.text: The Earth is built like an onion, with several shells: the **crust**, the mantle and the core. The crust is the outermost and thinnest of these shells. The Earth's radius is about 6370 km, and the crust makes up only a tiny part of it. Together with the top, solid part of the mantle, it forms the **lithosphere**.

The **oceanic crust** lies beneath the oceans and is about 5 to 10 km thick. It is made mainly of dark, heavy rocks such as **basalt** and gabbro. At the mid-ocean ridges, new oceanic crust is constantly forming from rising magma. Because it dives back down into the mantle, it is nowhere older than about 200 million years.

The **continental crust** forms the continents and is usually 30 to 40 km thick. Under high mountains such as the Alps or the Himalayas it is thickest, reaching deep down like a root. It is made of lighter rocks such as **granite** and gneiss. Some rocks of the continental crust are older than 4 billion years.

abschnitte.titel: What the crust is made of
abschnitte.text: The most common chemical element in the Earth's crust is **oxygen**; it is found in almost all rocks and minerals. Next comes silicon, and together they form the silicate minerals such as quartz and feldspar. The most common metal is **aluminium**, ahead of iron. We get many raw materials we need from the Earth's crust, for example ores, salt and gravel.

The boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle is called the **Moho**, after the Croatian scientist Andrija Mohorovičić. He discovered it in 1909, because seismic waves suddenly become faster at this boundary. It is hardly possible to drill into it directly: the deepest borehole in the world, on the Kola Peninsula in Russia, reached about 12 km. That is why most of what we know about the depths comes from measuring **seismic waves**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The solid rocky shell of the Earth, made of the crust and the uppermost mantle.
The boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle.
A dark rock made of hardened lava, typical of the sea floor.
Minerals made of silicon and oxygen; most rocks are made of them.

gewusst: If the Earth were the size of an apple, the Earth's crust would be thinner than the apple's skin.
The borehole on the Kola Peninsula took about 20 years and still only got about 12 km deep.
The sea floor is much younger than the oldest rocks on the continents.

teile.einleitung: Gneiss is a metamorphic rock, which means a rock that was changed by pressure and heat deep inside the Earth. You can usually recognise it by its light and dark stripes. Gneiss is very common in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: Gneiss has typical light and dark stripes.
It forms during strong metamorphism and at high temperatures deep in the Earth's crust.
Orthogneiss forms from granite, paragneiss from sedimentary rock.
So-called “Ticino granite” is geologically mostly gneiss.
The summit pyramid of the Matterhorn is made of gneiss that once belonged to the African Plate.
The Acasta Gneiss in Canada is one of the oldest known rocks on Earth.

abschnitte.text: In gneiss, light minerals such as **quartz** and **feldspar** and dark ones such as **mica** lie side by side in layers. This gives it its **striped appearance**. Sometimes single feldspar crystals are shaped into oval lenses. The stripes flow around them so that they look like eyes. Such a rock is called **augen gneiss**, from the German word “Augen”, meaning “eyes”.

Gneiss forms during **strong metamorphism**. This is the name for the change of rock through pressure and heat. Temperatures of several hundred degrees are often involved. Shale forms with weak change, gneiss only with much stronger change. When **granite** is squeezed and heated, **orthogneiss** forms. Gneiss made from sedimentary rocks, on the other hand, is called **paragneiss**.

In Switzerland there is particularly a lot of gneiss in the **Central Alps**, for example in the Gotthard area or in Ticino. There, rocks that were once buried deep have come to the surface as the Alps were lifted up. The summit pyramid of the **Matterhorn** is also made of gneiss. This rock once belonged to a piece of the **African Plate**. When the Alps formed, it was pushed over European rock.

Gneiss can be split along its layers into thick slabs. The roofs of many **rustici** in Ticino, which are old stone houses, are covered with such heavy stone slabs. Gneiss is still quarried in the valleys of Ticino today. In the trade it is often called **“Ticino granite”**, although geologically it is mostly a gneiss. It is used for stairs, walls and floor tiles.

Gneiss can be very old. The **Acasta Gneiss** in north-western Canada is around **4 billion years** old. This makes it one of the oldest known rocks on Earth. Such rocks help experts understand how the Earth's crust formed in its early days.

gewusst: The Matterhorn has rock on its summit that originally belonged to Africa.
The Acasta Gneiss is almost as old as the Earth itself, which is around 4.6 billion years old.

tpdu5z4.t: Tipping point in the climate system

teile.einleitung: A tipping point in the climate system is a threshold. If it is crossed, part of the climate changes abruptly and can hardly be turned back.
wichtigste: A tipping point is a threshold with consequences that can hardly be reversed.
Self-reinforcing feedbacks can push a system over the tipping point.
Thawing permafrost could release methane and carbon dioxide.
Parts of the Amazon rainforest could turn into savannah.
The Atlantic overturning circulation could weaken because of meltwater.
Coral reefs die from coral bleaching when the water is too warm.

abschnitte.text: You can imagine a **tipping point** like a chair that you tilt backwards. For a long time not much happens, but at a certain point it falls over. In the climate this means: one part of the system changes **abruptly**. The change often cannot be undone, even if the warming later goes down again. Such parts are called **tipping elements**.

Behind tipping points there are often **reinforcing feedbacks**. In these, an effect strengthens its own cause. An example: warming makes ice melt. Less bright ice reflects less sunlight, and it gets even warmer. Such cycles can push a system over the threshold.

The **West Antarctic Ice Sheet** rests on bedrock below sea level and is therefore vulnerable to warm seawater. If it broke up, it would in the long term cause a **sea level rise** of several metres. **Permafrost** is ground that stays frozen without a break for at least two years. It contains huge amounts of plant remains. If it thaws, microorganisms release **methane** and carbon dioxide, which increases the warming.

The **Amazon rainforest** produces part of its own rain. Because of deforestation and drought, this might no longer be enough. Then parts of it could turn into dry **savannah**. The **Atlantic overturning circulation**, which includes the Gulf Stream, is also seen as a tipping element. A lot of fresh water from Greenland could slow it down, which would change the climate in Europe.

When water temperatures are too high, **corals** push out their colourful algae and turn white. This is called **coral bleaching**. If the heat lasts, they die, and whole reefs can be lost. Switzerland is affected too: there is permafrost high in the **Alps**. If it thaws there, **rockfalls** can become more frequent.

gewusst: The Earth's permafrost stores a great deal of carbon in the form of plant remains.
There is permafrost in the Swiss Alps too, mainly in shady, high places.

teile.einleitung: On 2 September 1806, an enormous mass of rock broke away from the Rossberg in the canton of Schwyz. It buried the village of Goldau and other hamlets. The Goldau landslide is one of the greatest natural disasters in Swiss history.
wichtigste: The landslide happened on 2 September 1806.
The mass of rock broke away from the southern flank of the Rossberg.
457 people died in the disaster.
Almost 40 million cubic metres of rock crashed into the valley.
Softened layers of marl acted as a slide for the conglomerate rock.
Part of the mass rushed into Lake Lauerz and set off a flood wave.
Today the Goldau Nature and Animal Park lies in the field of rubble.

abschnitte.titel: Between the Rossberg and the Rigi
abschnitte.text: **Goldau** belongs to the municipality of **Arth** in the canton of **Schwyz**. The village lies between **Lake Zug** and **Lake Lauerz**. On one side of the valley rises the **Rossberg**, on the other the **Rigi**. On 2 September 1806 a huge mass of rock broke away from the southern flank of the Rossberg, below the Gnipenspitze. It raced into the valley and on the other side even surged up the Rigi.

The Rossberg is made of tilted layers of **Nagelfluh**, a conglomerate. This is a rock made of cemented pebbles that is widespread in the foothills of the Alps. Between these layers lie thin layers of **marl**. After a lot of rain, water got in through cracks and softened the marl. The blocks of rock then slid off it as if on a **slide**.

Experts estimate the mass at almost **40 million cubic metres**. It buried an area of about 6.5 square kilometres. As a rule, a **landslide** of this kind is defined as at least about one million cubic metres. Smaller falls are called **rockfalls**. So Goldau was far bigger than the threshold for a landslide.

**457 people** died in the landslide, and over 300 animals were killed too. Several villages and hamlets were buried. Part of the mass rushed into **Lake Lauerz**. As a result, the lake became about one seventh smaller. Eyewitnesses reported a **flood wave about 20 metres high**.

The large boulders still shape the landscape today. Right in the middle of the field of rubble lies the **Goldau Nature and Animal Park**. Native animals live there between the boulders. A museum recalls the disaster of 1806. You can still see the traces of the place where the rock broke away on the Rossberg.

gewusst: The mass of rock was so enormous that it surged up the Rigi on the other side of the valley.
The landslide made Lake Lauerz about one seventh smaller.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's atmosphere is the layer of air that surrounds our planet. It gives us oxygen to breathe, protects us from dangerous radiation from space and keeps the Earth warm. Without it there would be no weather, no blue sky and no life as we know it.
wichtigste: The Earth's atmosphere is the layer of air around the Earth.
Dry air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen, 21 per cent oxygen and almost 1 per cent argon.
The weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere.
In the troposphere the temperature falls on average by about 0.65 °C per 100 metres.
In the stratosphere it gets warmer higher up, because ozone absorbs UV radiation.
Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere.
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 set out the phasing-out of ozone-damaging CFCs.

abschnitte.text: Dry air consists of about 78 per cent **nitrogen** and about 21 per cent **oxygen**. The third most common gas, at almost 1 per cent, is the noble gas **argon**. There are also small amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases. The air also contains water vapour, from which clouds and rain form. Higher up the air gets thinner and thinner until it gradually turns into space.

The lowest layer is called the **troposphere**, and here it reaches up to about 11 kilometres. All the weather happens here, with clouds, rain, snow and thunderstorms. The temperature falls on average by about 0.65 °C per 100 metres as you go up. If you calculate with 0.6 °C per 100 metres, you get an example: if it is 15 °C in Zurich at 400 metres, it is about minus 3 °C on a summit 3400 metres high. Passenger aircraft usually fly in the top part of the troposphere.

Above the troposphere, up to about 50 kilometres, lies the **stratosphere**. It contains the **ozone layer**. Ozone absorbs a large part of the dangerous ultraviolet radiation from the Sun. This warms the air, which is why the temperature in the stratosphere rises with height. Without the ozone layer, life on land would hardly be possible.

Between about 50 and 85 kilometres lies the **mesosphere**, the coldest layer, with temperatures down to minus 90 °C. Most **meteors**, which we see as shooting stars, burn up here. Above it comes the thermosphere, in which the International Space Station orbits at about 400 kilometres. The **auroras** also form there. Right on the outside, the exosphere merges gradually into space.

The atmosphere works like a blanket. Gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide hold back heat; this is the natural **greenhouse effect**. Without it, the Earth would be about minus 18 °C on average instead of about plus 15 °C. Because people put more carbon dioxide into the air by burning coal, oil and gas, this effect is getting stronger. This leads to **climate change**, which can be seen in Switzerland, for example, in the melting of the glaciers.

In the 1980s, researchers discovered an **ozone hole** over Antarctica, a strong thinning of the ozone layer. It was caused mainly by **CFCs**, gases from spray cans and fridges. In 1987 many countries agreed in the **Montreal Protocol** to ban these substances step by step. Since then the ozone layer has slowly been recovering. The agreement is regarded as one of the most successful environmental agreements in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lowest layer of the atmosphere, in which the weather happens.
A layer in the stratosphere that catches dangerous UV radiation.
Gases in the air hold heat and so warm the Earth.
Artificial gases that used to be in spray cans and fridges and destroy ozone.

gewusst: The sky is blue because the air scatters blue sunlight more strongly than red.
If you squeezed the whole ozone layer to the pressure at the ground, it would only be about 3 millimetres thick.
On the summit of Mount Everest, each breath of air contains only about a third as much oxygen as by the sea.

teile.einleitung: El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific. During El Niño, the sea water in the central and eastern Pacific becomes unusually warm. This changes winds and rainfall in many parts of the world.
wichtigste: During El Niño, the surface water in the central and eastern Pacific becomes unusually warm.
The name comes from Peruvian fishermen and means “the child”.
The cool counterpart is called La Niña.
ENSO stands for El Niño Southern Oscillation.
During El Niño the trade winds weaken.
El Niño events happen about every 2 to 7 years.

abschnitte.text: Normally the **trade winds** blow from east to west over the equatorial Pacific. They push warm surface water westwards, towards Indonesia and Australia. Off South America, cold deep water rises in its place. During **El Niño** the trade winds weaken or partly reverse. The warm water sloshes back east, and the central and eastern Pacific become unusually warm.

**El Niño** means “the child” in Spanish and refers to the **Christ Child**. Peruvian fishermen noticed that the water off their coast often warmed up around Christmas time. The cool counterpart is called **La Niña**, “the girl”. During La Niña the trade winds are stronger, and the water in the eastern Pacific is colder than normal.

The abbreviation **ENSO** stands for El Niño Southern Oscillation. The **Southern Oscillation** is a seesaw of air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin in Australia. Ocean and atmosphere influence each other. El Niño does not happen regularly, but about every **2 to 7 years**. An event usually lasts nine to twelve months.

Off Peru, the **thermocline** lies deeper than normal during El Niño. This is the boundary between warm surface water and cold deep water. That is why hardly any nutrient-rich water rises any more. **Plankton** is missing, and fish stocks fall sharply. For fishing in Peru these are difficult years.

El Niño changes air pressure, winds and rain all over the Earth. In some areas, for example on the west coast of South America, there is heavy **rain** and flooding. Elsewhere, for example in Australia and Indonesia, **droughts** and forest fires threaten. Because warm sea water gives off a lot of heat to the air, El Niño years are often especially warm around the world. In Europe the effects are much weaker and hard to prove.

gewusst: There were especially strong El Niño events in 1997/98 and 2015/16.
The fishermen in Peru mainly catch anchovies, which live on plankton in the cold upwelling water.

teile.einleitung: The Lengenbach Quarry in the Binn Valley is one of the most famous mineral sites in the world. In this small quarry in Upper Valais, many minerals were discovered for the very first time. Today digging continues there for research and collections.
wichtigste: The Lengenbach Quarry is in the municipality of Binn in the Binn Valley, canton of Valais.
The minerals are found in white dolomite from the Triassic period.
More than 40 kinds of mineral were described here for the first time.
Minerals containing the rare element thallium are typical.
Around 160 to 170 kinds of mineral are known from the quarry.
Since 1958, digging has gone on without a break for science and collectors.

abschnitte.text: The **Binn Valley** is a side valley of the Goms in Upper Valais. Today it is a **regional nature park**, the Binntal Landscape Park. Among mineral collectors the valley is known all over the world. The **Lengenbach Quarry** lies in the municipality of **Binn**. It is only a small quarry, but it is extremely important for mineralogy.

The finds are in a white, sugary-grained **dolomite marble** from the **Triassic period**. Crystals were able to grow in its cavities. A striking one is **realgar**, a bright red arsenic mineral. It forms red bands in the pale rock. Many minerals from the quarry contain **arsenic**, **sulphur** and other rare elements.

More than **40 kinds of mineral** were described for the very first time at Lengenbach. Some of them are still known from no other place in the world. The rare element **thallium** is especially typical. Over 30 thallium minerals are known from the quarry, many of them only from here. A study in 2018 counted around 160 kinds of mineral, and there are now about 170. For such a small quarry, that is an extraordinary number.

As early as the **18th century**, people tried mining here, but it hardly paid off. Since **1958**, working groups have been recovering mineral specimens without a break. The finds go to researchers, museums and collectors. For visitors, there is a **rock-breaking area** in front of the quarry in summer. Rock from the digging is put out there. With a hammer and magnifying glass, you can search for small crystals yourself.

gewusst: Some minerals from Lengenbach have not been found anywhere else in the world.
At the rock-breaking area, children can search for real crystals themselves.

teile.einleitung: The carbon cycle describes how carbon constantly moves back and forth between the air, plants, animals, seas and rocks. Carbon is the basic building block of all life. When people burn coal, oil and gas, they upset the balance of this cycle.
wichtigste: Carbon moves between the atmosphere, living things, oceans, soils and rocks.
During photosynthesis, plants take CO2 from the air, and the enzyme RuBisCO binds it.
The ocean contains far more carbon than the atmosphere and takes up a lot of human CO2.
Taking up CO2 makes seawater more acidic.
In the long term, most carbon is stored in carbonate rocks such as limestone.
Raised bogs store a particularly large amount of carbon per area.
Thawing permafrost releases stored carbon as CO2 and methane.

abschnitte.text: During **photosynthesis**, plants, algae and some bacteria take CO2 from the air and use it to make sugar. The enzyme **RuBisCO** binds the CO2 and is thought to be the most common protein on Earth. Animals eat plants and breathe the carbon out again as CO2. When leaves and dead animals rot, the carbon also returns to the air and soil.

The **ocean** contains around 50 times more carbon than the atmosphere. It takes up about a quarter of the CO2 that humans emit. This creates carbonic acid in the water, and the sea becomes more acidic: this is called **ocean acidification**. It makes it harder for corals, mussels and snails to build their chalky shells.

In the long term, most of the Earth's carbon is stored in **carbonate rocks** such as limestone. They formed from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures that settled on the sea floor. Coal, oil and natural gas are also carbon stores, made from plants and tiny living things of prehistoric times. This slow cycle through rocks and volcanoes takes millions of years.

When **fossil fuels** are burnt, carbon that was stored for millions of years gets into the air in a short time. When 12 g of carbon burns completely, 44 g of CO2 is produced, because two oxygen atoms are added. Cutting down forests also releases CO2. That is why the CO2 content of the air is rising, and the climate is warming.

**Raised bogs** cover only a few per cent of the land area, but they store a particularly large amount of carbon per area in their peat. In Switzerland, bogs have been protected by the constitution since the Rothenthurm initiative of 1987. A lot of organic carbon is also frozen in the **permafrost** of the Arctic and the Alps. If it thaws, microbes break it down, producing CO2 and methane, which makes the warming even stronger.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar from CO2 and water.
A store that takes in more carbon than it gives off, for example forests or oceans.
Seawater becomes more acidic because it takes up CO2.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.
A carbon-rich layer in a bog, formed from dead plants.

gewusst: A CO2 molecule is almost four times as heavy as the carbon atom inside it.
The chalk cliffs of Rügen and Dover are made of the shells of tiny sea creatures.
A raised bog grows upwards by only about one millimetre a year.

teile.einleitung: The Glacier Garden in Lucerne shows traces of the Ice Age right in the middle of the city. It is especially famous for its large, round glacier potholes in the rock.
wichtigste: The Glacier Garden is in Lucerne.
There you can see large glacier potholes in the rock.
It was discovered in 1872 during building work for a wine cellar.
The glacier potholes date from the Ice Age, about 20,000 years ago.
There is a mirror maze in the Glacier Garden.
The Lion Monument is right next door.

abschnitte.text: In the **Glacier Garden** in Lucerne you can see large, round holes in the rock. These are **glacier potholes**. They formed when meltwater from a glacier plunged through cracks in the ice down to the rock. The swirling water spun sand and stones around in circles and so ground out deep holes. At the bottom of the potholes there are often still round grinding stones.

During the **Ice Age** it was much colder than today. The glaciers from the Alps reached far into the Swiss Plateau. Thick ice also lay over the place where the city of **Lucerne** is today. The glacier potholes in the Glacier Garden formed about 20,000 years ago. When the ice melted, they were left behind and later filled with earth.

In **1872**, Josef Wilhelm **Amrein-Troller** wanted to dig a **wine cellar**. During the building work, the glacier potholes came to light. Instead of building a cellar, he opened up the site to visitors. Shortly afterwards the Glacier Garden was opened. Today there is also a museum.

A fun attraction is the **mirror maze**. It is designed in the style of the **Alhambra**, a famous palace in Spain. Many mirrors make the passages seem endless. It is easy to get lost inside. For children it is great fun.

Just a few steps from the Glacier Garden is the **Lion Monument**. It shows a dying lion carved directly into the rock. The monument remembers Swiss soldiers who lost their lives in Paris in 1792. It is one of the best-known monuments in Switzerland.

gewusst: In the Glacier Garden you can also find traces from a time long before the Ice Age, when there was a warm sea with palm beaches in the Lucerne area.
The largest glacier pothole in the Glacier Garden is several metres deep.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake the ground wobbles and shakes, sometimes only very slightly, sometimes so strongly that houses collapse. Earthquakes usually happen when strains between the plates of the Earth's crust are suddenly released. The earth also shakes regularly in Switzerland, but most earthquakes are so weak that you cannot feel them.
wichtigste: In an earthquake the ground moves jerkily and shakes.
The most common cause is strain between moving tectonic plates.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the earthquake's source is called the epicentre.
Earthquakes are measured with a seismograph.
If the magnitude rises by 1, about 32 times more energy is released.
In Switzerland the earthquake risk is greatest in Valais.
In 1356 a strong earthquake destroyed the city of Basel.

abschnitte.text: The outer layer of the Earth is broken into large **tectonic plates**, which move a few centimetres every year. At their edges they get caught on each other, and enormous strains build up. When the rock suddenly breaks or slips, the energy is released all at once. It travels through the ground in **earthquake waves**. The place underground where the earthquake begins is called the **focus** or hypocentre.

Earthquakes are measured with a **seismograph**, an instrument that records even the slightest shaking. The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus is called the **epicentre**, and the earthquake is usually strongest there. The strength is given as the **magnitude**, in the past mostly on the Richter scale. If the magnitude rises by 1, about 32 times more energy is released. So an earthquake of magnitude 6 is about 1000 times stronger than one of magnitude 4.

In Switzerland about 1000 to 1500 earthquakes are recorded every year. Most are too weak to be felt. The risk is greatest in **Valais**, followed by Basel, the Grisons, the St Gallen Rhine Valley and Central Switzerland. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes with a network of over 200 measuring stations. Statistically, a strong earthquake can be expected in Switzerland about every 50 to 150 years.

On 18 October 1356 the strongest known earthquake in Central Europe shook the city of **Basel**. Many houses, churches and the Minster were badly damaged. Fires started by overturned hearth fires destroyed large parts of the city. Many castles in the surrounding area collapsed. Such an earthquake could happen again today, which is why there are building regulations for **earthquake-proof building**.

If the earth shakes, you should stay inside and take cover. It is best to crawl **under a sturdy table** and hold on to a table leg. Keep away from windows, glass and shelves that could fall over. Outside, move away from buildings, walls and power lines. After the earthquake, leave the house carefully by the stairs, not by the lift.

There are a particularly large number of strong earthquakes around the Pacific, in the so-called **Pacific Ring of Fire**, for example in Japan, Chile and California. The strongest earthquake ever measured happened in Chile in 1960, with a magnitude of about 9.5. If the earth shakes under the sea, a **tsunami** can form, a huge flood wave. In 2004 a tsunami in the Indian Ocean killed over 200,000 people. In 2011 an earthquake in Japan set off a tsunami that damaged the Fukushima nuclear power station.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place on the Earth's surface directly above the earthquake's focus.
An instrument that records the shaking of the ground.
A number for the strength of an earthquake, that is, how much energy is released.
A huge flood wave that can be set off by an earthquake under the sea.

gewusst: Worldwide the earth shakes hundreds of thousands of times every year, but only a small number of the earthquakes can be felt.
Some animals such as dogs behave restlessly shortly before an earthquake, but a reliable prediction of earthquakes is still not possible today.
People can also cause small earthquakes, for example during the geothermal drilling in Basel in 2006.

teile.einleitung: A stream is a small flowing body of water. It is narrower than a river and often babbles through woods, meadows and mountains. Many animals and plants live in and beside a stream.
wichtigste: A stream is a small, flowing body of water.
Because of gravity, water always flows downhill.
The steeper the land, the faster the stream flows.
When many streams flow together, a river forms.
Brown trout and freshwater shrimps need clean, cool water.
The dipper dives into the stream for small animals.

abschnitte.text: A stream often begins at a **spring**, where water comes out of the ground, or it collects rain and meltwater. Because water always flows downwards due to **gravity**, a stream always runs downhill. On the way, more streams join it. So the body of water keeps getting bigger until it becomes a **river**. In Switzerland there are countless streams that finally flow into rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhône or the Aare.

In the mountains the land is often very steep. That is why a **mountain stream** rushes quickly and powerfully over stones. In flat country, on the other hand, a stream flows calmly and often bends. The fast water carries sand and small stones with it. Where it slows down, they are left behind again.

The **brown trout** needs cool water with plenty of oxygen and lives in many Swiss streams. The **freshwater shrimp** hides under the stones. If you find a lot of them, the water is clean. The **dipper** is a small songbird that even walks along the bed of the stream under water, looking for small animals. The **beaver** also lives by streams. It dams them with branches and mud to make a pond, in which it can build its lodge safely.

The ground on a stream bank is often wet. Plants that like a lot of water grow there. In spring the yellow flowers of the **marsh marigold** shine brightly. Trees such as alders and willows hold the bank in place with their roots and give shade. The shade keeps the water cool, which the fish like.

gewusst: Freshwater shrimps help experts to tell how clean a stream is.
The dipper can dive and walk along the bottom of the stream under water.

teile.einleitung: The Alps consist of a stack of huge slabs of rock that have been pushed on top of each other over many kilometres. Geologists call such slabs nappes. The theory of nappes was developed to a large extent from the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: A nappe is a mass of rock that has been pushed a long way over other rocks.
Autochthonous rocks still lie where they formed, while allochthonous ones were transported.
A klippe is an isolated remnant of a nappe left by erosion, such as the Mythen.
In 1893 Hans Schardt interpreted the Préalpes romandes as nappes.
In 1902 Maurice Lugeon applied the theory of nappes to the whole of the Alps.
In eastern Switzerland, from bottom to top, lie the Helvetic, the Penninic and the Austroalpine.
The Morcles nappe is a prime example of a fold nappe.

abschnitte.text: A **nappe** is a large slab of rock that has been **sheared off** from what lay beneath it and pushed over other rocks for many kilometres. This happened as the Alps formed, when Africa and Europe were moving towards each other. Rocks that still lie where they formed are called **autochthonous**, which means “formed on the spot”. Nappes that have been carried a long way are called **allochthonous**. The area a nappe comes from is called its **root zone**. Many nappes of the Swiss Alps have their roots far to the south.

The very front end of a nappe in the direction of movement is called the **nappe front**. As it moves forward, it is often rolled downwards into a lying fold. Some nappes are huge lying folds with an overturned lower limb. Such **fold nappes** are shown particularly beautifully by the **Morcles nappe** in Lower Valais. It can be seen well at the **Rhône bend** between Saint-Maurice and Martigny.

When **erosion** has removed a nappe all around, sometimes only a single remnant is left. Such a remnant is called a **klippe**. A well-known example is the **Mythen** near Schwyz. They are made of foreign rock that was pushed here from far to the south. That is why this older rock now lies on top of younger rocks.

For a long time people did not understand how the Alps were built. In **1893** **Hans Schardt** recognised that the rocks of the **Préalpes romandes** do not match what lies beneath them and come from far away. With this he laid one of the foundations of the theory of nappes. In a great overview in **1902**, the Lausanne geologist **Maurice Lugeon** showed that the whole of the Alps can be explained by nappes pushed on top of each other. His work made the theory of nappes accepted around the world.

In eastern Switzerland the large nappe systems lie like this, from bottom to top: **Helvetic**, **Penninic** and **Austroalpine**. The stack reflects the original order from north to south. What was deposited furthest north lies at the bottom. What came from the south was pushed over it. In the area of the **Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona** in the Glarus region, such a thrust can be seen particularly well; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: On the summits of the Mythen, older rock lies on top of younger rock, because it was pushed here from far to the south.
At the Glarus thrust, older rocks lie sharply separated on top of much younger ones.

teile.einleitung: Ice is frozen water. When water cools below 0 °C, it becomes solid and forms crystals. In everyday life we meet ice as ice cubes, icicles or black ice, and in nature as glaciers or as huge icebergs in the sea.
wichtigste: Ice is water in solid form; it forms below 0 °C.
Ice floats in water because it is lighter than liquid water.
Pointed rods of ice hanging from a roof are called icicles.
A huge chunk of ice floating in the sea is called an iceberg.
It is dangerous on a frozen lake, because the ice can break.
In winter salt is spread on the roads so that the ice melts.
Glaciers are huge masses of ice that move slowly.

abschnitte.text: Ice is **frozen water**. When water cools to 0 °C, the water particles arrange themselves into a regular pattern. This creates **ice crystals**, which are often six-sided, as you can see in snowflakes. When it gets warmer than 0 °C, the ice melts back into water. The point at which water freezes is called the **freezing point**.

Most substances become denser when they turn solid. Water is an exception: ice is about 9 per cent lighter than liquid water, because its crystal pattern has many gaps. That is why ice **floats** on top. So lakes freeze from the top down, and underneath the water stays liquid, so fish can survive. This special property is called the **anomaly of water**.

In nature ice comes in many forms. **Glaciers** form when snow builds up over many years and is pressed together into ice. The largest glacier in the Alps is the Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais. When ice breaks off glaciers into the sea, an **iceberg** forms, of which only about a tenth sticks out of the water. In winter **icicles** grow on gutters when meltwater drips down and freezes again.

On a frozen lake the **ice can break**, especially when it is still thin or lies over places where streams flow in. You should only go onto ice that has been declared safe by the municipality. On roads and pavements, **black ice** sometimes forms, on which you can easily slip. Falling icicles can injure people. If someone falls through, do not go onto the ice yourself, but get help and call the number 112.

In winter, municipalities spread **salt** on the roads. Salt water only freezes at lower temperatures than pure water. That is why ice melts when salt lies on it, as long as it is not too cold. But because salt harms plants and soils, some municipalities prefer to use **grit** made of small stones on pavements. It does not melt the ice, but it makes it less slippery.

abschnitte.titel: Ice in everyday life and sport
abschnitte.text: Ice cubes cool drinks, and food stays fresh for a long time in the freezer. In the past people sawed ice out of lakes in winter and stored it in ice cellars to keep things cool in summer. In Switzerland **ice hockey** is one of the most popular sports. People skate on ice rinks and frozen mountain lakes such as Lake St Moritz. On Lake St Moritz there are even horse races in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which water turns into ice: 0 °C.
A tiny, regularly built piece of ice, for example in a snowflake.
A huge, slowly moving mass of ice made of pressed-together snow.
A thin, smooth layer of ice on the ground on which you can easily slip.

gewusst: Freezing water expands so strongly that it can split rocks apart.
In the ice of Antarctica there are trapped air bubbles that are over 800,000 years old and tell researchers about the climate of the past.
The Great Aletsch Glacier is about 20 kilometres long and almost 900 metres thick at its thickest point.

teile.einleitung: Coal, oil and natural gas are called fossil fuels. They formed millions of years ago from dead living things and still supply a large part of the world's energy today.
wichtigste: Fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas.
Oil and natural gas formed mainly from sea plankton.
Hard coal formed from the plants of prehistoric swamp forests.
Wood is not a fossil fuel but a renewable one.
When they are burned, carbon stored for a long time gets into the air as CO2.
Lignite gives off the most CO2 for the same amount of energy.
Switzerland's only refinery still in operation is in Cressier (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: Tiny sea creatures, **plankton**, sank to the sea floor after they died. There they were covered by mud. Under pressure and heat, their remains turned into **oil** and **natural gas** over millions of years. These collect in porous rocks deep in the ground. Today they are extracted by drilling.

A very long time ago, giant ferns, horsetails and club moss trees grew in **swamp forests**. Their remains were covered over and lay in the ground without air. From them first peat formed, then **lignite** and finally **hard coal**. A geological period is even named after coal: the **Carboniferous**, from the Latin word “carbo”. It lasted from about 359 to 299 million years ago.

Fossil fuels form much more slowly than we use them up. That is why they will run out at some point. **Wood**, on the other hand, keeps growing back and is counted among the **renewable** fuels. The Sun, wind and water power are also renewable sources of energy. In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from water power.

The carbon in coal, oil and natural gas was locked in the ground for millions of years. When they are burned, it gets into the air as extra **carbon dioxide** (CO2). This strengthens the **greenhouse effect** and warms the climate. **Lignite** gives off the most CO2 for the same amount of energy, because it contains a lot of water and a lot of carbon. Natural gas causes only about half as much CO2 for the same energy.

Switzerland does not produce any oil itself and has to import it. In **Cressier** in the canton of Neuchâtel stands the country's only refinery still in operation (as of 2025). There crude oil is turned into petrol, diesel and heating oil. The refinery in Collombey in Valais was closed in 2015. Worldwide, the **United States** produced the most oil in 2023, followed by Saudi Arabia and Russia.

gewusst: Some of the coal burned today comes from forests that grew even before the dinosaurs.
Plastics are also usually made from oil.

teile.einleitung: Lightning is a gigantic electrical discharge during a thunderstorm. It is hotter than the surface of the Sun and lasts only an instant. If you know how to behave in a thunderstorm, you are well protected.
wichtigste: A flash of lightning heats the air up to about 30,000 degrees.
A flash of lightning lasts less than a second.
Thunder is made because the hot air expands at lightning speed.
In a thunderstorm, get out of the water immediately.
You are fairly safe in a car.
It is dangerous under single trees.
Lightning strikes the tower on the Säntis about 100 times a year.

abschnitte.text: In a thundercloud, ice pellets and water drops whirl around violently. This makes parts of the cloud **electrically** charged. When the voltage becomes too great, it discharges in a flash of **lightning**. It can flash inside the cloud, between clouds or between the cloud and the ground. A flash of lightning lasts only a **fraction of a second**, and sometimes it flickers several times in a row.

A flash of lightning heats the air up to about **30,000 degrees**. That is much hotter than the surface of the Sun. The hot air expands explosively. We hear this as **thunder**. Because light is much faster than sound, you see the lightning first. If you count the seconds until the thunder, about three seconds correspond to one kilometre of distance.

Lightning likes to strike high points. On the **Säntis** in eastern Switzerland there is a tall transmitter tower. Lightning strikes it about **100 times a year**. Researchers have installed measuring instruments there. In this way they learn how strong lightning is and how it happens.

If you are swimming, you must get **out of the water immediately** in a thunderstorm. In the water you are the highest point, and water conducts electricity. In a **car** you are fairly safe. The **metal body** carries the current around the outside into the ground, as long as you do not touch anything metal inside. Buildings with lightning conductors also protect you well.

Never stand under a **single tree** in a thunderstorm. It is often the highest point for a long way around, and lightning likes to strike there. Also avoid hilltops, summits and open fields. Out in the open: crouch down with your feet together and do not lie down on the ground. It is best to look for shelter in good time when a thunderstorm is coming.

gewusst: The lightning conductor was invented in the 18th century by Benjamin Franklin.
Tall towers and mountain peaks are struck by lightning particularly often.

teile.einleitung: A scree slope is a steep slope of loose stones below a rock face. In the Alps you can see them almost everywhere, and some animals and plants have adapted to this special habitat.
wichtigste: A scree slope is a slope made of loose stones.
It usually lies below rock faces.
Freezing water breaks stones off the rock.
The biggest stones usually lie right at the bottom.
It is also called a talus slope.
Walking across it is dangerous because the stones slip easily.

abschnitte.text: Below many **rock faces** lies a steep slope of loose stones. This is a **scree slope**, also called a **talus slope**. Both words mean a slope of loose rock debris. The stones fall down at one spot and spread out downwards. This often creates the shape of a **cone** or **fan**.

Water seeps into cracks in the rock and freezes there into ice. Ice takes up more space than water. That is why it breaks pieces off the rock. This happens especially often when it freezes and thaws again and again, for example in spring and autumn. The pieces fall down and collect at the foot of the rock face.

Big, heavy stones roll further than small ones when they fall. That is why the **biggest stones** usually lie right at the bottom, at the foot of the slope. Smaller stones tend to stay higher up. In this way the stones on a scree slope are sorted by size.

On a scree slope there is little soil, and the stones move. Only **a few tough plants** with long roots can grow there. The **marmot** likes to live in burrows between stones and meadows. When there is danger, it warns the others with a loud **whistle**. Mountain hares and ptarmigans also often hide among the scree.

The stones lie loosely on top of each other. If you step on them, they can **slip away**. You can fall or knock stones loose that hit other people further down. That is why it is best to stay on the marked path when hiking. Stones can also fall from the rock face above at any time.

gewusst: Some alpine plants can travel across the slipping stones with their roots.
In the past, stones from scree slopes were often used to build dry stone walls.

teile.einleitung: Basalt is a dark rock that forms from lava that has hardened. It is the most common volcanic rock on Earth. Even the floor of the oceans and the dark patches on the Moon are made of basalt.
wichtigste: Basalt is usually dark grey to black.
It forms when runny lava cools and hardens.
The floor of the oceans is mostly made of basalt.
Thick flows of basalt often break up into six-sided columns as they cool.
Iceland is mostly built of basalt.
The lunar seas are plains of hardened basalt lava.
Stone wool is made from melted basalt.

abschnitte.text: Basalt is a **volcanic rock**. It forms when lava cools quickly at the Earth's surface. It contains many dark minerals that are rich in **iron** and **magnesium**. That is why it is dark grey to black. Basaltic lava contains little **silica** and is very hot. That is why it is runny and can flow a long way.

At the **mid-ocean ridges**, the Earth's plates are pulling apart. There basaltic lava constantly comes out and hardens in the cold water. This creates the **oceanic crust**, which forms most of the sea floor. The island of **Iceland** lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and also on a hotspot. Many volcanic eruptions have built it up from basalt lava.

abschnitte.titel: Columns as if they were built
abschnitte.text: When a thick lava flow cools slowly, it shrinks and cracks. The cracks often form a pattern of mostly **six-sided columns**. The **Giant's Causeway** on the north coast of **Northern Ireland** is famous. There about 40,000 basalt columns stand close together. The place is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The dark areas on the Moon are called **lunar seas**. But there was never any water there. Over three billion years ago, runny lava filled huge impact basins. The dark basalt stands out clearly from the lighter highlands. That is why you can see the lunar seas even with the naked eye.

Basalt is hard and is used for paving stones, crushed stone or floor tiles. Melted at very high temperatures, it can be blown into fine fibres. This makes **stone wool**. This insulating material protects houses against the cold and does not burn.

gewusst: The name Giant's Causeway means a raised path of giants. An old legend tells that a giant built it.
Most of the solid surface of the Earth under the oceans is made of basalt.

teile.einleitung: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland, if you count its whole area. It lies between Switzerland and France, and the Rhône flows through it.
wichtigste: Lake Geneva has an area of about 580 km².
At its deepest point it is about 310 m deep.
The surface of the lake is at about 372 m above sea level.
The cantons of Geneva, Vaud and Valais have a shore on the lake; the rest belongs to France.
The Jet d'eau in Geneva sprays up to 140 m high.
The vineyard terraces of Lavaux have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Geneva** has an area of about 580 km², making it slightly larger than Lake Constance. Its deepest point, at about 310 m, lies between Lausanne and Évian. The surface of the lake is at about 372 m above sea level. The lake is shaped like a crescent moon. The **Rhône** flows in at the east and leaves it again in Geneva.

About 60 per cent of the lake's area belongs to **Switzerland**, and the rest to **France**. **Vaud** has the long northern shore, **Geneva** the south-western tip and **Valais** a small part in the east. Most of the southern shore belongs to the French department of Haute-Savoie. Well-known places on the lake are Geneva, Lausanne, Vevey, Montreux and Évian.

A landmark of Geneva is the **Jet d'eau**. This fountain shoots water up to 140 m into the air. You can see it from far away. In the harbour of Geneva there are also the Pierres du Niton, two large erratic boulders from the Ice Age.

Between Lausanne and Vevey, on the northern shore, lies **Lavaux**. There vines grow on steep terraces held up by many stone walls. Monks began building them as early as the Middle Ages. Lavaux has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 2007.

On a rock in the lake at Veytaux near **Montreux** stands **Chillon Castle**. The water castle is very old and for a long time belonged to the Counts of Savoy. It is one of the most visited historic buildings in Switzerland. From there you have a beautiful view across the lake to the Alps.

gewusst: In French, Lake Geneva is called “Lac Léman”.
Old paddle steamers with steam engines still sail on Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: An aquifer is a body of rock with spaces through which groundwater can flow. Depending on the rock, these spaces are pores, fractures or karst caves. In Switzerland, aquifers supply most of the drinking water.
wichtigste: An aquifer has pores, fractures or karst cavities through which water flows.
Clay, on the other hand, is an aquitard, because water can hardly pass through it.
The valley gravels of Switzerland contain productive porous aquifers.
Gravel has the highest permeability of all loose rocks.
Darcy's law of 1856 describes the flow of groundwater.
Around 80 per cent of Swiss drinking water comes from groundwater.

abschnitte.text: Groundwater does not flow in underground rivers, but through small spaces in the rock. In **porous aquifers** it flows through the gaps between grains, for example in sand and gravel. In **fractured aquifers** it flows through cracks in solid rock. In **karst aquifers** the water has dissolved limestone and created larger cavities. Layers such as **clay**, which let hardly any water through, are called **aquitards** or aquicludes.

In the large river valleys of Switzerland there are thick layers of **gravel and sand**. These valley gravels are **porous aquifers**. They are among the most productive groundwater sources in the country. According to the **Federal Office for the Environment** (FOEN), around **80 per cent** of drinking water comes from groundwater, including spring water. Most of the rest comes from lakes.

In **1856**, the French engineer **Henry Darcy** described how water flows through porous rock. The flow Q is the product of the **hydraulic conductivity k**, the cross-sectional area A and the **hydraulic gradient** i. An example: k is 0.001 m/s, A is 100 square metres and i is 0.01. Then Q equals 0.001 cubic metres per second, which is **1 litre per second**. **Gravel** has a very high k value. **Clay** does have a lot of pore space, but its pores are tiny, and water can hardly flow through them.

If an aquifer lies under an **impermeable covering layer**, its water is under pressure. This is called **confined groundwater**. If you drill into it, the water level in the borehole rises above the top of the aquifer. If it rises even above the ground, the water gushes out by itself. This is an **artesian well**.

When groundwater is pumped out of a well, the water level around the well falls. It forms a **cone of depression**. This makes water flow towards the well from all sides. If too much is pumped, the water table can fall in the whole surrounding area. That is why the use of groundwater is strictly regulated.

gewusst: Clay can hold more water than gravel and still lets almost none flow through.
The name “artesian” comes from the French region of Artois, where such wells were known early on.

teile.einleitung: Renewable energy comes from sources that keep renewing themselves, such as the Sun, wind, water, geothermal heat and biomass. It does not run out like oil or coal and causes hardly any greenhouse gases. In Switzerland, water power in particular has been supplying clean electricity for over a hundred years.
wichtigste: Renewable energy comes from the Sun, wind, water, geothermal heat and biomass.
In Switzerland, water power supplies most of the electricity.
Pumped storage power stations store surplus electricity by pumping water uphill.
Efficiency tells you what percentage of the Sun's energy a solar cell turns into electricity.
According to Betz's law, a wind turbine can use at most about 59 per cent of the wind's energy.
In May 2017 Swiss voters approved the Energy Strategy 2050.

abschnitte.text: Hydroelectric power stations use the energy of flowing or falling water, which drives turbines. In Switzerland about 55 to 60 per cent of electricity comes from **water power** (as of about 2024). One cubic metre of water, that is 1000 kg, falling 500 m has about 4.9 megajoules of energy. **Pumped storage power stations** such as Linth-Limmern in the canton of Glarus use surplus electricity to pump water into an upper lake and produce electricity again when it is needed.

**Solar cells** turn sunlight directly into electricity; this is called photovoltaics. The **efficiency** tells you what percentage of the Sun's energy becomes electricity; for common panels it is about 20 per cent. Solar collectors, on the other hand, heat water for showers and heating. In Switzerland the number of solar installations on roofs, on walls and even on dam walls is growing fast.

Wind turbines turn in the wind and drive a generator. According to **Betz's law**, a turbine can use at most about 59 per cent of the wind's energy. The power of the wind rises steeply with its speed: at twice the wind speed, it is eight times as great. In Switzerland there are so far only a few wind farms, for example in the Jura and on the Gotthard.

In the Earth's crust the temperature rises on average by about 3 °C per 100 m of depth. Many houses use this **geothermal energy** for heating, with ground probes and heat pumps. **Biomass** is energy from wood, plant remains, liquid manure or garden waste. It can be used to produce heat, electricity or biogas, for example.

In May 2017 Swiss voters approved the **Energy Strategy 2050**. It bans the building of new nuclear power stations and supports saving energy and renewable energy. The existing nuclear power stations may keep running as long as they are safe. One problem remains: the Sun and wind do not always deliver the same amount, so **storage** is needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technology with which solar cells turn light directly into electricity.
The share of the energy put in that is turned into useful energy.
A power station that stores electricity by pumping water into a higher lake.
Using heat from inside the Earth.
Plant and animal material from which energy is obtained.

gewusst: At 285 m, the Grande Dixence in Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world.
If the wind blows twice as fast, it delivers eight times as much power.
In one hour the Sun sends more energy to the Earth than all of humanity uses in a year.

teile.einleitung: A hydrograph shows how much water a river or stream carries over time. It shows how a body of water reacts to rain or snowmelt. Hydrographs are important for flood protection.
wichtigste: A hydrograph shows the discharge of a body of water over time.
Discharge is usually given in cubic metres per second.
The highest point of a flood is called the peak discharge.
Base flow comes mainly from groundwater.
Sealed ground makes the peak higher and earlier.
Heavily glaciated Alpine rivers carry the most water in high summer.

abschnitte.text: **Discharge** tells you how much water flows past a point in a certain time. It is a volume per time. For rivers it is usually given in **cubic metres per second**, and for small streams also in litres per second. A **hydrograph** plots discharge against time. In Switzerland, many federal gauging stations measure the discharge of rivers and streams all the time.

After heavy rain, the curve rises: this is the **rising limb**. The highest point is called the **peak discharge**. After that comes the **falling limb**, also called the **recession limb**. It shows how the soil and groundwater slowly release their water. Some time passes between the heaviest rain and the highest discharge: the **lag time**. In small, steep catchment areas it is short.

Even without rain, water flows in a river. This part is called **base flow**. It comes mainly from **groundwater** and other slow stores, and it keeps the river flowing in dry periods. The part of the rain that flows away quickly is called **direct runoff**. The area between the hydrograph and the base flow equals the **volume of direct runoff**, because discharge multiplied by time gives a volume.

On roads, roofs and car parks, rain cannot soak away. These are called **sealed surfaces**. There the water quickly runs off over the surface. That is why, where a lot of ground is sealed, the **peak is higher** and comes **earlier**. This increases the risk of flooding. Green spaces and surfaces where water can soak away work against this.

abschnitte.titel: The yearly pattern of Alpine rivers
abschnitte.text: Over a whole year, too, the hydrograph shows a typical pattern: the **flow regime**. For heavily glaciated Alpine rivers, this is called a **glacial regime**. Melting ice and snow supply the most water in the warm months of **July and August**. In winter, on the other hand, the discharge is very low because everything is frozen.

gewusst: A glacial stream carries much more water on a hot afternoon than in the early morning.
From the shape of a hydrograph, experts can tell how much water an area stores in its soil.

teile.einleitung: Rocks do not stay the same forever. Over many millions of years they are worn away, deposited, changed and melted, and so new rocks form again and again.
wichtigste: The rock cycle describes how rocks change into one another over a long time.
There are three main groups: igneous rocks, sedimentary rocks and metamorphic rocks.
It is driven by the heat inside the Earth and by the Sun's energy.
One round usually takes many millions of years.
At subduction zones, crustal rock returns to the mantle.
The Scot James Hutton recognised the cycle in the 18th century.

abschnitte.text: The **rock cycle** shows that the same material becomes new rocks again and again. Rocks are worn away, deposited, buried, changed, melted and lifted up again. This happens extremely slowly. A whole round usually takes **many millions** to hundreds of millions of years. The Scottish scientist **James Hutton** was one of the first to recognise, in the 18th century, that this cycle goes on endlessly.

Rocks are grouped by how they formed. **Igneous rocks** such as granite form when hot molten rock solidifies. **Sedimentary rocks** such as limestone or sandstone form from deposits that have hardened. **Metamorphic rocks** such as gneiss or marble are rocks that have been changed by pressure and heat. In the cycle, each group can turn into another.

At the Earth's surface, wind, water and frost attack every rock. It is slowly **broken up** and **worn away**. Rivers and glaciers carry the fragments away. Later they are deposited as **sediment**, for example in lakes or the sea. The energy for this comes from the **Sun**, because it drives the weather and the water cycle.

When a sedimentary rock is buried deep, pressure and temperature rise. The rock becomes **metamorphic rock**; limestone, for example, turns into **marble**. At **subduction zones**, one tectonic plate dives under another. In this way rock gets to great depths, where it is changed or even **melted**. The energy for this comes from the **heat inside the Earth**.

Rocks that have been changed deep down come back to the surface through **uplift** and **erosion**. When mountains form, slabs of rock are lifted up. At the same time, water and ice wear away the upper layers until the deep rocks can be seen. You can see this well in the Swiss Alps: in the Gotthard area there is **granite** and **gneiss** that once lay deep inside the Earth.

gewusst: A grain of sand on the beach may already have been part of a mountain range several times.
The granite and gneiss you see in the Alps today once lay many kilometres deep inside the Earth.

teile.einleitung: A glacier mill, also called a moulin, is a deep, round shaft in the ice of a glacier. Meltwater swirls down it into the depths and can grind round holes into the rock at the bottom.
wichtigste: A glacier mill is a deep shaft in glacier ice.
In it, the meltwater plunges down to the rock floor under the glacier.
Its walls are round and smooth.
Swirling water with sand and stones grinds a round hole into the rock at the bottom.
Round, smooth stones often lie at the bottom of such holes.
Round holes can also be found where there is no longer a glacier today.

abschnitte.text: In summer, **meltwater** flows across the ice of many glaciers in streams. Sometimes such a stream disappears into a deep, round shaft. This is a **glacier mill**. The water swirls down into the depths, often as far as the **rock floor** under the glacier. The swirling water melts the walls in a circle, which is why they are **round and smooth**.

abschnitte.titel: Why it is called a mill
abschnitte.text: In the glacier mill, the water spins in a circle. It takes sand and stones with it and **grinds** them around. This is like a mill in which grain is ground. That is how the glacier mill got its name. You can often hear the water roaring loudly inside it.

Down at the rock, the water swirls **sand and gravel** around in a circle. These act like sandpaper. Over time the water grinds a round hole into the rock, a **glacier pothole**. Rock is very hard. That is why it took a very long time for a deep hole to form. The stones that spun around in it became **round and smooth**.

Round holes from glacier mills can also be found where there is **no longer a glacier** today. During the Ice Age, glaciers lay in many places in Switzerland. When they melted, the holes in the rock were left behind. Well-known examples are the glacier potholes in the **Glacier Garden Lucerne**.

Glacier mills can be very deep. Their edges are wet and slippery. Anyone who falls in can hardly get out again alone. That is why mountaineers keep their distance on the glacier. Some researchers, however, climb in with good safety ropes to study the inside of the glacier.

gewusst: A glacier mill slowly moves down the valley with the glacier, and a new one can form higher up.
Some glacier mills on large ice sheets are more than a hundred metres deep.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake, waves spread through the Earth from the focus. There are different kinds of these seismic waves, which travel at different speeds and move the ground in different ways. They can even be used to look inside the Earth.
wichtigste: P waves are the fastest seismic waves and arrive first.
In S waves the ground vibrates at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
Surface waves usually cause the greatest damage to buildings.
Rayleigh waves make the ground roll up and down like waves on the sea.
Love waves shake the ground from side to side.
From the arrival times at many stations, a picture of the Earth's interior is created.

abschnitte.text: Two kinds of waves travel through the inside of the Earth. **P waves**, the primary waves, are the fastest and arrive first. They squash the rock together in the direction they travel and pull it apart again. In the Earth's crust they travel at about **6 kilometres per second**. **S waves**, the secondary waves, are slower. In them the particles vibrate **at right angles** to the direction of travel, rather like a rope that is being shaken.

When the waves reach the Earth's surface, **surface waves** form. They arrive last, but they have large movements and usually shake buildings the most. In **Rayleigh waves** the particles of the ground move in an ellipse, and the ground rises and falls like the sea. **Love waves** shake the ground horizontally back and forth. They are named after the British mathematician **Augustus Edward Hough Love**, who described them in 1911.

Because the waves travel at different speeds, in an earthquake you often feel a **jolt** first and only then stronger shaking. The further away the focus is, the greater the gap between them. You can also calculate: a P wave at 6 km/s needs **20 seconds** for 120 kilometres. Sometimes you hear a dull **rumble** during an earthquake, because part of the movement of the ground passes into the air as sound.

Nobody can drill down to the Earth's core. But seismic waves reveal what it is like there. At boundaries between layers of rock they are **bent** and **reflected**, and they change their speed depending on the material. **Seismographs** in many places around the world record when the waves arrive. From this, researchers create a picture of the inside of the Earth. This is how it was found that the outer core of the Earth is liquid, because S waves cannot travel through liquids.

If the earth shakes under the sea floor, the floor can suddenly rise or sink. Then the whole column of water above it is moved. This creates a **tsunami**, a huge wave of water. On the open sea it can hardly be noticed, but it can travel thousands of kilometres. At the coast it towers up high.

gewusst: The word “tsunami” comes from Japanese and means “harbour wave”.
Because P waves arrive first, warning systems can give a few seconds' warning before the stronger waves.

teile.einleitung: The Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary marks the end of the age of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago. In the rocks it can be seen as a thin layer that contains traces of a huge impact.
wichtigste: The boundary lies around 66 million years in the past.
It ends the Mesozoic and begins the Cenozoic.
In 1980, Luis and Walter Alvarez found a lot of iridium in the boundary layer.
The Chicxulub crater on the Yucatán Peninsula is around 180 kilometres across.
Shocked quartz is evidence of a huge impact.
As well as the dinosaurs, the ammonites also died out.

abschnitte.text: The **Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary** is dated to around **66 million years** ago. It ends the **Mesozoic**, the middle era of Earth's history, and begins the **Cenozoic**, the modern era. It used to be called the **K-T boundary**. K stands for Cretaceous (from the German “Kreide”), T for **Tertiary**. Because the Tertiary is now divided into the Paleogene and Neogene, it is called the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary.

Near **Gubbio** in Umbria in Italy, the boundary can be seen as a thin layer of clay between layers of limestone. There the geologist **Walter Alvarez** studied samples. Together with his father, the physicist **Luis Alvarez**, he discovered a high content of **iridium**. This metal is rare in the Earth's crust but more common in asteroids. In 1980 they published the hypothesis that a large **impact** had caused the extinction.

Later, the matching crater was found. The **Chicxulub crater** lies in the north of the **Yucatán** Peninsula in Mexico, partly under the Gulf of Mexico. It is around **180 kilometres** across and is buried under younger deposits. The impacting body is estimated to have been around 10 to 15 kilometres across. Further evidence is **shocked quartz** with fine lamellae, which only form under extremely high pressure.

At the same time, the **Deccan Traps** in India were active. Enormous amounts of basalt lava poured out there. Whether these volcanoes helped cause the extinction or made it worse is still being discussed. Many experts see the impact as the main cause. Possibly both events worked together.

At the boundary, a large share of all animal and plant species died out. The **dinosaurs** disappeared, except for the birds, which are descended from them. The **ammonites** also died out completely after more than 300 million years. These sea creatures had spiral shells divided into chambers. Their relatives, the **nautiluses**, have survived to this day. After that, the age of the **mammals** began.

gewusst: Birds are the only descendants of the dinosaurs that survived the extinction.
The Chicxulub crater can hardly be seen from the surface, because younger rocks cover it.

teile.einleitung: A dune is a hill of sand piled up by the wind. There are dunes in deserts such as the Sahara, but also on sea coasts such as the North Sea. Some dunes even slowly move along.
wichtigste: Dunes form where the wind drops sand.
The side facing away from the wind is usually steeper.
Moving dunes are slowly pushed along by the wind.
On the North Sea, marram grass holds the sand in place with long roots.
The Dune of Pilat in France is the highest moving dune in Europe.
There are huge fields of dunes in the Sahara.

abschnitte.text: The wind carries grains of sand along with it. Where it becomes weaker, the grains are dropped. Behind a stone or a bush, more and more sand gathers in this way, and a **dune** grows. The wind pushes the sand up the gentle side, the **windward side**. Behind the crest the sand slides down and forms a steep slope, the **leeward side**.

Because the wind keeps blowing sand over the dune, it can slowly move along. It is then called a **moving dune**. Dunes have different shapes. A **crescent dune** is shaped like a half-moon, and its two points face downwind. There are also long dunes that lie in rows like waves. In the **Sahara**, the largest hot desert in the world, dunes form huge seas of sand.

On sea coasts, the wind blows sand inland from the beach. There, plants such as **marram grass** hold the dunes in place. It has very long roots that hold the sand together like a net. Such dunes protect the land from storm floods. That is why you should only walk on the paths: if the plants are trampled, the wind can blow the dune away. The **Dune of Pilat** on the Atlantic coast of France is about 100 metres high.

Some dunes can **hum** or boom. When a lot of sand slides down their steep slope, the grains rub against each other. This creates a deep sound that can be heard far away. They are called **singing dunes**. This sound is known from various deserts around the world.

gewusst: There are also dunes on Mars, which space probes have photographed.
The Dune of Pilat moves a little inland every year, burying trees in the forest behind it.

teile.einleitung: A hygrometer is an instrument for measuring humidity. It usually shows what percentage of water vapour the air contains compared with the largest possible amount. A famous early hygrometer was invented by the Geneva naturalist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure.
wichtigste: A hygrometer measures humidity, usually as a percentage.
The hair hygrometer uses hairs that get a little longer in damp air.
Horace-Bénédict de Saussure developed the hair hygrometer in 1783.
A psychrometer works with a dry and a wet thermometer.
Modern hygrometers have electronic sensors.
A weather house contains a simple hygrometer.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains some **water vapour**, which you cannot see. How much it can hold depends on the temperature. **Relative humidity** gives, as a percentage, how much of that amount is already in the air. It is measured with a **hygrometer**. The name comes from Greek: **“hygros”** means damp, **“metron”** means measure. So a hygrometer is a humidity measurer.

Hair takes in moisture and **stretches** slightly as it does so. In dry air it shrinks back again. The **hair hygrometer** makes use of this. Inside it, human hairs with the grease removed are usually stretched out. When their length changes, a pointer moves. This instrument was developed in **1783** by the Geneva naturalist **Horace-Bénédict de Saussure**. He is also known for his research in the Alps and his ascent of **Mont Blanc** in 1787, one of the very first.

Another measuring instrument is the **psychrometer**. It has two thermometers. One is dry, the other is wrapped in a wet cloth. As the water **evaporates**, it takes heat away from the wet thermometer. That is why it shows a lower temperature. The drier the air, the more water evaporates and the bigger the difference. From this, the humidity is calculated.

Today humidity is usually measured **electronically**. Inside the sensor is a thin layer that takes in water vapour. This changes its **electrical properties**, for example its capacitance. The device converts this into a percentage. Such sensors are found in weather stations, air conditioning systems and many household appliances.

An old toy and ornament is the **weather house**. Depending on the weather, a figure comes out, often a woman in fine weather and a man in wet weather. The figures hang on a twisted string made of gut or hair. It turns depending on the **humidity** and so pushes one figure out. So a weather house contains a **simple hygrometer**.

gewusst: A human hair gets measurably longer in damp air.
Saussure, the inventor of the hair hygrometer, stood on the summit of Mont Blanc in 1787.
